sections.text: As seen on Traveler32829163268Apr 2024 USA Most Insane Hotel on Planet Earth?: Explore El Chalten is simply word-class. Tucked deep into the Electric Mountain Range--a nature preserve 40 minutes outside El Chalten--this hotel is stunning the moment you arrive with unobstructed views of glaciers, mountains, rivers, and wildlife at your fingertips. As a nature lover, this might be the coolest hotel on Planet Earth, and I'm not exaggerating. Do yourself a favor, book this trip now. We went in April 2024 (their Fall) and the Fall colors and cool weather were spectacular. Read full review Read Less John BMar 2024 Chester, UK Exceptional Hotel in Every Way: Explora El Chalten is one the best hotels we have visited anywhere in the world. It is expensive but worth it. The location is amazing, the rooms great and the staff could not be more friendly and helpful. The food is also exceptional. As if that was not enough the guides are extremely knowledgeable and amongst the best anywhere and take a lot of trouble to take guests on routes that are most suitable to them and also least crowded. The walks we did and the views particularly of Mount Fitzroy were truly memorable. We wished we could have stayed longer. We are already planning our next stay in an Explora property. sections.text: Patagonia [Argentina + Chile] Encircled by both the Pacific and the Atlantic Ocean, Patagonia spreads out across boundaries in the tip of South America. Find breathtaking lakes, fjords and glaciers in the west; and astounding deserts, tablelands and steppes in the east. El Calafate Argentina El Chaltén Argentina Patagonia National Park Chile Torres del Paine Chile Torres del Paine C. Reserve Chile Discover more about Patagonia Sacred Valley of the Incas [Peru] Sacred Valley and Machu Picchu are extraordinary locations with a monumental past. The calm, flowing waters of the Urubamba River pervade the heart of the ancient Inca Empire, meandering the valley’s flourishing natural beauty. Sacred Valley Peru Discover more about Sacred Valley of the Incas Desert & Altiplano [Bolivia + Chile] Perched high on the Andean plateau, the Altiplano could very well be on another planet. sections.text: Through the largest network of award-winning lodges in South America, we bring you closer to the most remote natural wonders and beyond. With nine lodges across Chile, Easter Island, Argentina, and Peru; one overland Travesía into Bolivia; and three expeditions—to Tierra del Fuego, the Sacred Mountains of the Incas, and Iceland’s Highlands—the Luxury of the Essential awaits. Even in true wilderness, return each evening to welcoming spaces, locally rooted cuisine, and restorative wellness after a day of exploration. Chosen day by day together with our Explora guides, each journey is designed for small groups of no more than eight guests and crafted to delve deeper into the landscapes and culture of every destination. Your journey begins in the late afternoon in Punta Arenas, before crossing the Strait of Magellan into Tierra del Fuego. Over seven days, experience the striking contrasts of the far south—from open pampas and the King Penguin colony to the island’s estancia culture. A moderate level of physical fitness is recommended, as routes cross varied terrain and changing weather conditions. faqs.q: Tierra del Fuego History
faqs.a: Tierra del Fuego holds within its lands a fascinating history. At the southernmost tip of America, where fire and ice intertwine, lies this territory of untamed beauty and awe-inspiring landscapes. Since ancient times, the indigenous tribes of Yámanas and Selk’nam inhabited these inhospitable lands, bravely adapting to their hostile environment. Their rich cultures and ancestral traditions still resonate in its mists. It was in 1520 when the Portuguese navigator, Fernando de Magallanes, spotted the lights of bonfires burning on the coast and named this region Tierra del Fuego. Since then, daring explorers and seekers of wealth ventured into these turbulent waters and wild lands in search of treasures and new trade routes. However, the region’s challenging nature and relentless weather conditions turned Tierra del Fuego into a feared and respected place. In the 19th century, the gold rush, sheep wool production, and timber industry attracted numerous settlers. However, as time passed, the region transformed into a starting point for scientific expeditions and Antarctic explorations, becoming a gateway to the last edge of the world. Today, Tierra del Fuego lures travelers with its wild and majestic nature. Its parks are home to unique places with lush forests, imposing mountains, ancient peat bogs, and pristine glaciers. faqs.q: Wild life at the end of the world
The strait of magellan
faqs.a: The Strait of Magellan is an important maritime route located at the southern tip of South America. In 1520, it was first navigated by a European vessel led by the Portuguese explorer Hernando de Magallanes. The Strait of Magellan connects the Atlantic and Pacific Oceans, providing an alternative for trade and navigation between both oceans. The strait has an approximate length of 570 kilometers and a width that varies between 2 and 32 kilometers in different sections. Navigating through it poses challenges due to strong currents, intense winds, and ever-changing weather conditions in the region. Throughout the centuries, the Strait of Magellan has been used as a crucial route for maritime trade, especially during the era of sailing ships. It has also been the setting for numerous scientific expeditions and explorations. Today, the strait is traversed by cargo ships, cruise liners, and fishing vessels. Additionally, its natural beauty and historical significance attract people who wish to explore this fascinating maritime passage.

panes.label: Wild life at the end of the world
The strait of magellan
panes.text: The Strait of Magellan is an important maritime route located at the southern tip of South America. In 1520, it was first navigated by a European vessel led by the Portuguese explorer Hernando de Magallanes. The Strait of Magellan connects the Atlantic and Pacific Oceans, providing an alternative for trade and navigation between both oceans. The strait has an approximate length of 570 kilometers and a width that varies between 2 and 32 kilometers in different sections. Navigating through it poses challenges due to strong currents, intense winds, and ever-changing weather conditions in the region. Throughout the centuries, the Strait of Magellan has been used as a crucial route for maritime trade, especially during the era of sailing ships. It has also been the setting for numerous scientific expeditions and explorations. Today, the strait is traversed by cargo ships, cruise liners, and fishing vessels. Additionally, its natural beauty and historical significance attract people who wish to explore this fascinating maritime passage.

sections.text: Patagonia PARQUE NACIONAL PATAGONIA Ethnobotanical Garden: The first Ethnobotanical Garden in the Aysén Region was born at the Hospital de Cochrane, transforming its unused courtyards into living spaces that connect health, nature, and ancestral knowledge. The garden houses the first museographic collection of medicinal and ethnobotanical plants from the Patagonian steppe, developed through a participatory process involving local communities, indigenous groups, public institutions, and conservation experts. Through the intersection of art, science, medicine, and traditional knowledge, the project promotes ex-situ conservation of native flora, environmental education, and nature-based wellbeing for patients, hospital staff, and the broader community of the Baker Basin. Amphibious Forest: Amphibious Forest is an ecological restoration initiative developed by Fundación Naturaleza Pública in partnership with Club Náutico Escualo in Cochrane. Through a community-driven methodology, children, families, athletes, and local organizations participate in the full regeneration cycle — from native seed collection and plant production to long-term planting and monitoring. In its first phase, the project restored 235 m² through the planting of 915 specimens from 22 native Patagonian species, strengthening local biodiversity and improving the riparian habitat along the Cochrane River. PROJECTS WE CONTRIBUTE TO Up to 15% of the cost of your stay will go to support projects where our destinations are located Get to know some of them: PATAGONIA EASTER ISLAND DESERT & ALTIPLANO PARQUE NACIONAL PATAGONIA Ethnobotanical Garden: The first Ethnobotanical Garden in the Aysén Region was born at the Hospital de Cochrane, transforming its unused courtyards into living spaces that connect health, nature, and ancestral knowledge. The garden houses the first museographic collection of medicinal and ethnobotanical plants from the Patagonian steppe, developed through a participatory process involving local communities, indigenous groups, public institutions, and conservation experts. Through the intersection of art, science, medicine, and traditional knowledge, the project promotes ex-situ conservation of native flora, environmental education, and nature-based wellbeing for patients, hospital staff, and the broader community of the Baker Basin. Amphibious Forest: Amphibious Forest is an ecological restoration initiative developed by Fundación Naturaleza Pública in partnership with Club Náutico Escualo in Cochrane. Through a community-driven methodology, children, families, athletes, and local organizations participate in the full regeneration cycle — from native seed collection and plant production to long-term planting and monitoring. In its first phase, the project restored 235 m² through the planting of 915 specimens from 22 native Patagonian species, strengthening local biodiversity and improving the riparian habitat along the Cochrane River. More than a planting initiative, Amphibious Forest transforms everyday spaces into living laboratories where nature, education, and community action come together. TORRES DEL PAINE Chile Lagos Limpios: In partnership with Fundación Chile Lagos Limpios and UC Davis, Explora launched a scientific tourism program in Torres del Paine National Park focused on water quality monitoring. Guests are invited to participate in monthly measurements of transparency and water conditions in lakes Pehoé and Sarmiento and the Serrano River, contributing to a long-term baseline dataset analyzed by one of the world’s leading freshwater research institutions. Explora guides received specialized environmental monitoring training, integrating the scientific approach into their daily expeditions across the park. The initiative transforms each visit into an act of conservation, turning guests into active stewards of one of Patagonia’s most pristine ecosystems. Educamper: Born in 2006 from a journey connecting rivers from Vancouver to Patagonia, Educamper is a mobile environmental education initiative that runs on recycled cooking oil, bringing hands-on workshops on recycling, circular economy, and river stewardship to rural schools across Chile. Explora supports Educamper with funding

sections.heading: Setting a New Standard with Explora Conservation

sections.text: Explora Conservation unites responsible exploration, community engagement, strategic collaboration, and visionary initiatives—such as our flagship Torres Del Paine Conservation Reserve—to protect and sustain the fragile and extraordinary destinations we are so privileged to explore. We believe true exploration is the ultimate journey to conservation. And our initiatives are woven into the fabric of every adventure we lead, ensuring that our guests experience the opportunity to protect and preserve alongside us.

sections.heading: Discover Our Conservation Reserves
sections.heading_selector: #content > div.component-o2:nth-of-type(5) > div > div > div > div > div > div > div.explora-wysiwyg > h3
sections.text: Backed by more than 30 years of responsible exploration, we’re spearheading a groundbreaking model of fully protected, financially self-sustaining Conservation Reserves in South America. Offering unique Explora-only Explorations and membership opportunities, these Reserves support Explora’s vision to ultimately safeguard one million hectares — nearly 2.5 million acres — of the planet’s most vulnerable ecosystems.

sections.heading: The Torres Del Paine Conservation Reserve

sections.heading_selector: #content > div.component-multi_columns:nth-of-type(6) > div > div > div > div:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(2) > div > div:nth-of-type(1)
sections.text: The Torres Del Paine Conservation Reserve A remerging Patagonian wilderness within the Torres Del Paine Biosphere, this 14,800-acre (6,000 hectare) Reserve created in partnership with The Nature Conservancy is defined by waterfalls, pampas, and magnificent wildlife — including the puma — and one-of-a-kind memberships featuring Explora’s first-ever homesites. Learn More The Puritama Conservation Reserve In the Atacama Desert, find a protected oasis at Explora’s 17,300-acre (7,000 hectare) Puritama Conservation Reserve, where hot springs formed by the Puritama River are the draw. Visitors enjoy ticketed hot spring experiences, while our guests go deeper with breathtaking hikes into lush canyons and swims in private hot springs. Learn More ‹› Defined by Responsible Exploration The intention to witness, preserve and protect pristine natural places and local culture has been part of Explora’s DNA since its inception in 1993. Naturally opposed to a heavy footprint, overcrowding destinations and depleting natural resources, this innate passion to explore responsibly was born out of a deep love for exploring remote and wild places in harmony with local cultures and traditions, and the dream to share it with friends, family and generations to come. It is among the rewards of Explora’s promise to go deeper, and ultimately the promise of a journey to conservation. READ MORE READ LESS

sections.text: By exploring the world’s most remote places with Explora, our guests travel with purpose and help protect what makes these places so extraordinary. Our 2024 Impact Report tells the full story, revealing how every journey supports ecological restoration, wildlife monitoring, and the meaningful involvement of local communities across our destinations. text: DISCOVER Explora Conservation Previous Next CONSERVATION RESERVES ABOUT OUR RESERVES TORRES DEL PAINE PURITAMA Setting a New Standard with Explora Conservation Explora Conservation unites responsible exploration, community engagement, strategic collaboration, and visionary initiatives—such as our flagship Torres Del Paine Conservation Reserve—to protect and sustain the fragile and extraordinary destinations we are so privileged to explore. We believe true exploration is the ultimate journey to conservation. And our initiatives are woven into the fabric of every adventure we lead, ensuring that our guests experience the opportunity to protect and preserve alongside us. Discover Our Conservation Reserves Backed by more than 30 years of responsible exploration, we’re spearheading a groundbreaking model of fully protected, financially self-sustaining Conservation Reserves in South America. Offering unique Explora-only Explorations and membership opportunities, these Reserves support Explora’s vision to ultimately safeguard one million hectares — nearly 2.5 million acres — of the planet’s most vulnerable ecosystems. The Torres Del Paine Conservation Reserve A remerging Patagonian wilderness within the Torres Del Paine Biosphere, this 14,800-acre (6,000 hectare) Reserve created in partnership with The Nature Conservancy is defined by waterfalls, pampas, and magnificent wildlife — including the puma — and one-of-a-kind memberships featuring Explora’s first-ever homesites. Learn More The Puritama Conservation Reserve In the Atacama Desert, find a protected oasis at Explora’s 17,300-acre (7,000 hectare) Puritama Conservation Reserve, where hot springs formed by the Puritama River are the draw. Visitors enjoy ticketed hot spring experiences, while our guests go deeper with breathtaking hikes into lush canyons and swims in private hot springs. Learn More Defined by Responsible Exploration The intention to witness, preserve and protect pristine natural places and local culture has been part of Explora’s DNA since its inception in 1993. Naturally opposed to a heavy footprint, overcrowding destinations and depleting natural resources, this innate passion to explore responsibly was born out of a deep love for exploring remote and wild places in harmony with local cultures and traditions, and the dream to share it with friends, family and generations to come. It is among the rewards of Explora’s promise to go deeper, and ultimately the promise of a journey to conservation. Dedication to Positive Impact By exploring the world’s most remote places with Explora, our guests travel with purpose and help protect what makes these places so extraordinary. Our 2024 Impact Report tells the full story, revealing how every journey supports ecological restoration, wildlife monitoring, and the meaningful involvement of local communities across our destinations. VIEW 2024 IMPACT REPORT Projects In and Beyond Our Backyard In addition to the fully protected Torres Del Paine Conservation Reserve, Explora Conservation supports numerous projects around the world, including educational outreach alliances with the Terevaka Foundation, conservation plans for the Puritama Conservation Reserve and UNESCO-designated Torres Del Paine Biosphere Reserve, and the Toki Pilot Forest, our latest initiative in Rapa Nui. Powerful Partnerships Rooted in the belief that collaboration is the driving force for positive change, Explora Conservation thoughtfully partners with renowned non-profit organizations that include The Nature Conservancy, Rewilding Chile, Terevaka Foundation and ECOAN. Explora is also a Certified B Corporation and Launching Member of the Glasgow Declaration. Pillars of Explora Conservation Our efforts are rooted in four foundational pillars that collectively empowers individuals, strengthens ecosystems, and elevates the standard for exploration, travel and conservation worldwide. Community & Collaboration We actively engage with strategic NGOs, our neighbors and local communities to effect positive, relevant, and lasting change in conservation. Guided by Science Our initiatives follow scientific methodologies and research, and rely on the continuous collection of scientific data, such as from wildlife trap cameras and performance indicators, with a commitment to be at the forefront of science in conservation. Education Across All Levels From local teens and staff to our guides and guests, we nurture ambassadors that return from our destination, share stories and help influence real change and movement. This is a powerful act of difusión: spreading the word. Excellence in Stewardship We seek to redefine the highest standards of stewardship, infrastructure and experiences at our Conservation Reserves, by training our own park rangers, designing trails that respect remerging ecosystems, and offering unique Explorations. Create a Lasting Legacy at the Torres Del Paine Conservation Reserve Discover Explora’s Torres Del Paine Conservation Reserves, a first-of-its-kind wilderness sanctuary and conservation community limited to just 100 nature-loving members, with rare opportunities to own a home, adventure far off the beaten path, and create a legacy that’s protected forever, all in award-winning Explora style. faqs.q: Crafted Explorations
faqs.a: We craft one-of-a-kind explorations so you can experience genuine immersion into the remote, from start to finish. In 30 years’ experience, we gathered the expertise to guide you through each territory’s most exceptional exploration possibilities so your travel is no less than extraordinary. Everything is included throughout the entire experience.

faqs.q: Territory Expertise
faqs.a: Unravel remote territories with the experts. Our guides are qualified under the highest of standards by our exclusive Explora school of guides. Our long-established presence in remote South America has shaped our knowledge on the territory, on exploration, and on conservation. Such know-how is vital for making sure our existence in the world’s most precious treasures only makes them bloom even more. Still preserving the most exceptional experience for the explorer.

faqs.q: Our Lodges
faqs.a: Our definition of luxury focuses on exploring remote places in-depth without ostentation. Each Explora lodge is a retreat for disconnection and renewal in the midst of nature, providing a warm and welcoming environment upon your return from our explorations. This is what we define as essential luxury. Our cuisine is nourished by local products, and we offer you amenities like massages, jacuzzis, and pools, among others, to ensure that you fully enjoy each day.

faqs.q: Conservation Engagement
faqs.a: We are deeply committed to conserving the marvels we explore daily: unparalleled local nature, astounding culture, and rich heritage. Conservation-driven initiatives – like our lodge architecture, among other conscious processes we adopt – are a vital piece of this greater picture. Our most far-reaching initiative to date are the explora Natural Reserves: acres and acres of Patagonian land under our conservation care. We are proud to be active in the quest of perpetuating the world’s rarest, most inestimable natural riches.

faqs.q: Network of Destinations
faqs.a: Present in the most precious locations of remote South America, we connect them all in an ever-exchanging network, so you can explore and discover in even greater depth. With lodges in multiple positions across the continent, explorers can feel free to combine more than one destination in a single journey and craft a truly original and broad exploration experience.

sections.text: Explora’s commitment to positive impact is grounded in integrity, respect for people and planet, and full compliance with the law. This confidential reporting channel exists to uphold the ethical foundations that support our mission and ensure we continue operating with transparency and accountability. Submit a report What Can Be Reported This channel supports our commitment to integrity. You can use it to report any situation that may go against our Code of Ethics or core values, including: Behavior that may go against our commitment to respect, inclusion, or environmental responsibility. Concerns related to workplace conduct, safety, or ethical decision-making. Situations that may involve conflicts of interest, misuse of resources, or violations of policies. Please note: This channel is not designed for customer service feedback related to travel experiences or lodging. For those matters, we invite you to reach out via email at reserve@explora.com READ MORE READ LESS

You may report anonymously, or choose to include your contact information if you wish to receive updates. In line with our values and legal obligations, Explora enforces a strict no-retaliation policy. Speaking up should always feel safe and supported. READ MORE READ LESS

text: Speak Up: Confidential Reporting Channel Explora’s commitment to positive impact is grounded in integrity, respect for people and planet, and full compliance with the law. This confidential reporting channel exists to uphold the ethical foundations that support our mission and ensure we continue operating with transparency and accountability. SUBMIT A REPORT What Can Be Reported This channel supports our commitment to integrity. You can use it to report any situation that may go against our Code of Ethics or core values, including: Behavior that may go against our commitment to respect, inclusion, or environmental responsibility. Concerns related to workplace conduct, safety, or ethical decision-making. Situations that may involve conflicts of interest, misuse of resources, or violations of policies. Please note: This channel is not designed for customer service feedback related to travel experiences or lodging. For those matters, we invite you to reach out via email at reserve@explora.com Confidentiality and Privacy All information submitted through this channel is treated confidentially and handled by designated compliance personnel. You may report anonymously, or choose to include your contact information if you wish to receive updates. We are committed to ensuring that your report is reviewed with discretion, fairness, and respect for all individuals involved. In line with our values and legal obligations, Explora enforces a strict no-retaliation policy. Speaking up should always feel safe and supported. faqs.q: ENVIRONMENTAL
faqs.a: Our environmental pillar considers two main focal points: The sustainable operation and the conservation of our territories. In the first, we established an environmental management system that considers the voice of the different stakeholders and defines the material aspects of our corporation. We established committees to manage our impact at each destination and consolidated an environmental footprint monitoring system. We have now set further ambitious goals to make our operations more sustainable regarding energy efficiency, carbon emissions, water consumption, and waste generation. Conservation The second focal point is Conservation. We recently evolved our purpose as a company, our reason for being and why we do things; incorporating conservation as a central element of what we do is at the core of this evolution. We are a company dedicated to exploration in remote locations. We are experts and know the territories we inhabit. But exploration is not enough. We need to preserve and protect these places. Exploration and knowledge are the essence of what we propose. We connect and forge bonds with the territories through exploration and knowledge, making us want to protect and conserve them.

faqs.q: SOCIAL
faqs.a: Our efforts and commitment to people comprise different areas: our travelers, our employees and the communities in the territories where we operate. Concerning our travelers, this means going beyond, not only providing them with excellent service through everything we do but also adding and taking them through an in-depth exploration along the path of preserving these remote territories. To evaluate and manage our impact on our collaborators and the communities, we have implemented a Social Management System that allows us to identify the key aspects and manage them through committees in each destination. Our commitment towards our collaborators is to ensure that they can permanently receive training of excellence, both concerning their work environment, as well as in other topics that allow them further professional development. We have also created an ongoing support plan for their economic and social situation, thus establishing an Explora Minimum Ethical Income and generating support opportunities in areas such as education, housing, and health. Finally, and true to our essence, we make sure that all Explora collaborators can explore in-depth the different destinations where we are located. Towards the local communities, our commitment is permanent. We work locally with organizations in each destination to promote youth education, environmental care, and the strengthening of local culture and heritage. In this context, we point out long-standing projects such as our suppo

faqs.q: ECONOMIC
faqs.a: Regarding the economic impact, we would like to highlight our commitment to underpinning local economies in the places where we operate. For this reason, we encourage the hiring of local labor and purchasing to local suppliers and producers. We are also permanently examining and managing these aspects. Most noteworthy are initiatives such as the supplier development program that we already implemented in Rapa Nui - Easter Island, and Atacama and we started recently in Patagonia National Park and Torres del Paine, in order to improve the quality and diversity of local farmers' production. At Explora, we work to provide our travelers with memorable experiences. In doing so, we are aware that we can also make a significant contribution to local economies. This is particularly important as our operations are carried out in remote territories, where economic activity and opportunities are often scarce. We firmly believe we can watch over the salaries of local people and collaborators, and also buy products from their respective areas. We are also aware of the importance of contributing to the protection of these territories, which is why we support various conservation projects.

faqs.q: B CORP CERTIFICATION
faqs.a: This 2025, Explora has been recertified as a B Corp This certification acknowledges companies that have committed to continuous improvement to provide concrete solutions to social and environmental problems. It also values, among other things, the promotion of policies and initiatives to address climate change; the development of support plans for their workforce; the conveyance of benefits to local communities; and the high standards of management and transparency. Concerning the environmental issues of our operation, we have also made important commitments: reducing, by 2030, 46% of our carbon footprint and, historically, compensate retroactively Explora's emissions to date. In line with the development of our working forces, we aspire to imprint a seal of excellence and high-quality in all those professionals that have belonged to our teams. Being part of a B Corporation is not a goal but a permanent challenge to continue working collaboratively in all the proposed aspects.

text: HomeOur commitment OUR COMMITMENT Understanding our destinations so deeply also means loving them, which inevitably awakens the need to protect them. For almost three decades we have traveled the most remote corners of the South American continent, exploring and constantly learning from what these vast territories can teach us. But we felt that this was no longer enough and decided to go further. We are committed to being an active force in the protection of the environment, in the fight against climate change, in the care of the people and communities that accompany us in each of the territories where we are. We do this through three pillars for action: environmental, social and economic. In the first, we established an environmental management system that considers the voice of the different stakeholders and defines the material aspects of our corporation. We established committees to manage our impact at each destination and consolidated an environmental footprint monitoring system. We have now set further ambitious goals to make our operations more sustainable regarding energy efficiency, carbon emissions, water consumption, and waste generation. Conservation The second focal point is Conservation. We recently evolved our purpose as a company, our reason for being and why we do things; incorporating conservation as a central element of what we do is at the core of this evolution. We are a company dedicated to exploration in remote locations. We are experts and know the territories we inhabit. But exploration is not enough. We need to preserve and protect these places. Exploration and knowledge are the essence of what we propose. We connect and forge bonds with the territories through exploration and knowledge, making us want to protect and conserve them. sections.text: Named the World’s Leading Expedition Company for six consecutive years, we bring these extraordinary destinations together. Enjoy all-inclusive stays at our award-winning lodges, effortless connections by aircraft and private vehicles, and explorations led by our passionate guides — revealing the very best of Patagonia, both Chilean and Argentine. Discover Patagonia, from lodge to lodge Whether flying over the impressive ice fields between national parks or crossing borders by land, this experience offers a unique opportunity to explore the immensity of Patagonia without limitations. Between October and April, connect our six destinations in Patagonia without any worries—our team will take care of all the details. If you have any questions, please write to us at reserve@explora.com. Learn More Discover the region’s striking contrasts, starting with the legendary Carretera Austral, where roads wind along rivers, lakes, and forests on one of Chile’s most scenic routes. Visit the Marble Cathedrals, natural sculptures emerging from the turquoise waters of Lake General Carrera, and continue on to our lodge in Patagonia National Park, a sanctuary surrounded by wild nature. Further south, discover the untamed beauty of Torres del Paine National Park from our privileged location. From there, our Explora Conservation Reserve—a private refuge—promotes restoration and applied science projects, where wildlife is returning and the land is recovering. text: PATAGONIA Astonishing immensity. Deep blue skies. The silence of the Andes. This is Patagonia. Previous Next TORRES DEL PAINE TORRES DEL PAINE RESERVE PATAGONIA N. PARK EL CHALTÉN EL CALAFATE TIERRA DEL FUEGO HomePatagonia Discover the Largest Network of Lodges in Patagonia Patagonia is one of the world’s most precious natural relics. Shared by Chile and Argentina, this vast region is home to jagged peaks, turquoise rivers, glaciers, and sprawling steppes. It is a sanctuary of wild nature and quiet beauty—a place that calls to be explored deeply, deliberately and without borders. . . Announcing Two New Lodges in 2026 Explora El Calafate and Explora Torres del Paine Conservation Reserve join our Patagonia’s network, allowing travelers to explore the region in depth, creating an immersive, cross-border experience with privileged access to some of its most remote corners. Not only through its most iconic landmarks, but also into remote, lesser-known, and uncrowded territories. Through Patagonia’s Vast Horizons With over 30 years of expertise exploring this unique region, we bring these extraordinary destinations together into one seamless journey—making it possible to experience this world-class destination as it truly is: untamed, vast, and borderless. Patagonia’s breathtaking magnitude and diversity can only be understood when explored in connection. Our unique network of lodges allows travelers to discover its most remote corners on an authentic multi-destination journey through five lodges across Chile and Argentina and an expedition to Tierra del Fuego. Discover Patagonia through our six destinations: Chile: Patagonia N. Park; Torres del Paine; Torres del Paine Reserve. Argentina: El Calafate and El Chaltén. Explora Expeditions: Tierra del Fuego expedition, Chile. A multi-destination trip Named the World’s Leading Expedition Company for six consecutive years, we bring these extraordinary destinations together. Enjoy all-inclusive stays at our award-winning lodges, effortless connections by aircraft and private vehicles, and explorations led by our passionate guides — revealing the very best of Patagonia, both Chilean and Argentine. Discover Patagonia, from lodge to lodge Whether flying over the impressive ice fields between national parks or crossing borders by land, this experience offers a unique opportunity to explore the immensity of Patagonia without limitations. Between October and April, connect our six destinations in Patagonia without any worries—our team will take care of all the details. If you have any questions, please write to us at reserve@explora.com. Learn More Discover the region’s striking contrasts, starting with the legendary Carretera Austral, where roads wind along rivers, lakes, and forests on one of Chile’s most scenic routes. Visit the Marble Cathedrals, natural sculptures emerging from the turquoise waters of Lake General Carrera, and continue on to our lodge in Patagonia National Park, a sanctuary surrounded by wild nature. Further south, discover the untamed beauty of Torres del Paine National Park from our privileged location. From there, our Explora Conservation Reserve—a private refuge—promotes restoration and applied science projects, where wildlife is returning and the land is recovering. It is a place to explore at your leisure and understand Patagonia through its conservation process. Finally, cross over to Argentine Patagonia to stay in El Chaltén, home to the Fitz Roy massif, glacial valleys, and some of the world’s most renowned trekking routes. In connection with El Calafate, discover Los Glaciares National Park and its breathtaking views of Perito Moreno. Discover Tierra del Fuego – Exclusive Expedition At the very edge of South America, where the Andes meet the sea, lies one of the world’s last true frontiers. Our exclusive Tierra del Fuego expedition invites you to explore a land of fjords, windswept valleys, and pristine silence—an untouched Patagonia where nature still reigns in its purest form. Guided by Explora’s experts, you’ll journey beyond the beaten path, uncovering remote ecosystems, unique wildlife, and breathtaking landscapes found nowhere else on Earth. This is Patagonia at its most raw and powerful—a once-in-a-lifetime exploration to the ends of the continent. Discover our Itineraries here. sections.text: Some 2,300 miles west of South America (3,700 km), discover enigmatic Easter Island with its enormous moai statues from our intimate lodge, Explora Rapa Nui. With a unique countryside location outside the village of Hanga Roa, our modern lodge offers countless opportunities for authentic immersion in Rapa Nui culture and traditions, as well as guided Explorations that include hikes to the Rano Raraku moai quarry, bike rides to ancient settlements and coastal adventures by kayak. World's Leading Expedition Company 2025 Condé Nast Traveler Readers’ Choice Awards 2025: Best Resorts in South America Conservation Sustainability With Soul ‹› Explora Rapa Nui comprises 4 suites and 26 Varúa rooms, each appointed with natural wood interiors, ocean or garden views, and jetted bathtubs. On-site amenities include a full-service spa, outdoor pool, hot tub, and sauna, alongside an award-winning dining program featuring Polynesian and Chilean cuisine with Chilean wine service. The all-inclusive rate encompasses all guided Explorations, all meals and beverages, spa facility access, national park entrance fees, and round-trip transfers from Mataveri International Airport (IPC).

faqs.q: Is Explora Torres del Paine all-inclusive?
faqs.a: Yes. Every Explora stay in Torres del Paine is fully all-inclusive. Your rate covers all accommodations, unlimited guided Explorations, all meals and beverages including Chilean wines and spirits, spa facility access, national park entrance fees, and round-trip transfers between Puerto Natales and the lodge. There are no supplementary charges for activities or guided experiences during your stay

faqs.q: What is included in an Explora Torres del Paine stay?
faqs.a: Your stay includes accommodations in a 50-room lodge on the shores of Pehoé Lake, access to more than 40 guided Explorations — from treks to the iconic Towers to kayaking, horseback riding, and glacier hikes — all meals prepared by Explora’s culinary team, all beverages including wine, spa and pool access, national park entrance fees, and transfers. The only extras are personal purchases and optional spa treatments beyond the included facility access.

faqs.q: How do I get to Explora Torres del Paine from Puerto Natales?
faqs.a: Explora Torres del Paine is located approximately 112 kilometers (70 miles) north of Puerto Natales along Ruta 9 and the Sarmiento road into Torres del Paine National Park. The drive takes approximately 1.5 to 2 hours through Patagonian steppe and grasslands. Round-trip transfers between Puerto Natales and the lodge are included in every all-inclusive stay. Guests typically fly into Punta Arenas International Airport (PUQ), then travel to Puerto Natales by shuttle or private transfer before continuing to the lodge.

faqs.q: What kinds of guided Explorations are available at Explora Torres del Paine?
faqs.a: Explora Torres del Paine offers more than 40 guided Explorations, all included in your stay. Options include day treks to the Base of the Towers (Las Torres), hikes to Grey Glacier, kayaking on the park’s lakes, birdwatching for condors and flamingos, horseback riding with a rare breed of Patagonian horses on Explora’s own reserve, and gaucho cultural experiences. Every Exploration is led by guides trained at Explora’s own School of Guides and customized to your fitness level and interests.

faqs.q: What is the best time to visit Torres del Paine?
faqs.a: The main trekking and expedition season in Torres del Paine runs from October through April (Southern Hemisphere spring through early fall). November to February offers the longest daylight hours and most stable weather, though wind is a constant factor year-round in Patagonia. Explora operates the lodge year-round; shoulder seasons (October–November and March–April) offer fewer visitors and lower rates while still providing full access to guided Explorations.

faqs.q: Is it better to stay inside Torres del Paine National Park or in Puerto Natales?
faqs.a: For travelers who want to maximize time in the park, staying inside is the better option. Puerto Natales is approximately 112 kilometers from the park entrance — a 1.5 to 2-hour drive each way — meaning a full day of exploration is lost for every night based in the city. Explora Torres del Paine is located inside the park on the shores of Pehoé Lake, with guided Explorations departing directly from the lodge each morning. Puerto Natales makes sense as a base for travelers on a tight budget or those doing a single day visit; for an all-inclusive expedition stay focused on depth of experience, the park lodge is the right choice.

faqs.q: Is Explora Torres del Paine suitable for non-hikers?
faqs.a: Yes. While the park is most famous for multi-day trekking routes like the W Trek, Explora’s program of 40+ guided Explorations goes well beyond hiking. Options for guests who prefer lower-intensity or non-hiking experiences include horseback riding on Explora’s private Conservation Reserve, kayaking on the park’s lakes, wildlife watching for pumas, condors, and guanacos, boat excursions to Grey Glacier, and gaucho cultural experiences. Explorations are matched to each guest’s interests and fitness level daily — a non-hiker can have a full, varied stay without setting foot on a technical trail.

faqs.q: Does Explora Torres del Paine have a spa?
faqs.a: Yes. Explora Torres del Paine has a full-service spa and wellness area that includes a heated indoor pool, steam sauna, and open-air hot tubs with views across the national park. Spa facilities are included in the all-inclusive rate. Individual spa treatments are available to book separately and carry an additional charge. Appointments can be arranged at the lodge during your stay.

sections.text: What airport do you fly into for the Sacred Valley and Machu Picchu? The primary gateway is Alejandro Velasco Astete International Airport in Cusco (CUZ), approximately 90 kilometers from Explora Valle Sagrado in the Sacred Valley. Cusco is served by direct flights from Lima (LIM), with a flight time of approximately 1 hour 20 minutes. Most luxury lodges in the Sacred Valley, including Explora Valle Sagrado, arrange round-trip airport transfers from Cusco; transfers should be confirmed at the time of booking. The drive from Cusco Airport to the lodge takes approximately 1.5 to 2 hours through the Andean highlands. Machu Picchu itself has no commercial airport; the standard access route is by train from Cusco or Ollantaytambo to Aguas Calientes. What is the best time of year to visit the Sacred Valley and Machu Picchu? The Sacred Valley and Machu Picchu are year-round destinations, with each season offering different conditions. May through October is the dry season, with clear skies, cooler temperatures, and the most stable weather for trekking and high-altitude explorations — this is peak season for both destinations. June through August sees the highest visitor demand; advance booking is strongly recommended. November through April is the wet season, with more rainfall but lush green landscapes, fewer crowds, and generally lower rates at luxury lodges. Brief afternoon showers are common during this period but rarely disrupt full-day programs. Advance booking is recommended

faqs.q: What airport do you fly into for the Sacred Valley and Machu Picchu?
faqs.a: The primary gateway is Alejandro Velasco Astete International Airport in Cusco (CUZ), approximately 90 kilometers from Explora Valle Sagrado in the Sacred Valley. Cusco is served by direct flights from Lima (LIM), with a flight time of approximately 1 hour 20 minutes. Most luxury lodges in the Sacred Valley, including Explora Valle Sagrado, arrange round-trip airport transfers from Cusco; transfers should be confirmed at the time of booking. The drive from Cusco Airport to the lodge takes approximately 1.5 to 2 hours through the Andean highlands. Machu Picchu itself has no commercial airport; the standard access route is by train from Cusco or Ollantaytambo to Aguas Calientes.

faqs.q: What is the best time of year to visit the Sacred Valley and Machu Picchu?
faqs.a: The Sacred Valley and Machu Picchu are year-round destinations, with each season offering different conditions. May through October is the dry season, with clear skies, cooler temperatures, and the most stable weather for trekking and high-altitude explorations — this is peak season for both destinations. June through August sees the highest visitor demand; advance booking is strongly recommended. November through April is the wet season, with more rainfall but lush green landscapes, fewer crowds, and generally lower rates at luxury lodges. Brief afternoon showers are common during this period but rarely disrupt full-day programs. Advance booking is recommended regardless of season, as capacity at luxury lodges is limited year-round.

faqs.q: What is included in a Sacred Valley all-inclusive package?
faqs.a: At Explora Valle Sagrado, the all-inclusive rate covers accommodation, all meals prepared with local Andean ingredients, non-alcoholic beverages, and more than 40 guided explorations each day. Access to the Pumacahua Spa and Bath House, saunas, steam baths, an outdoor swimming pool, and hot tubs is also included. Round-trip airport transfers from Cusco are arranged by Explora. A full-day visit to Machu Picchu can be arranged as an extension to any stay; applicable entry permit and train transport fees may apply separately.

faqs.q: Do Sacred Valley lodges include airport transfers from Cusco?
faqs.a: Most luxury all-inclusive lodges in Peru’s Sacred Valley, including Explora Valle Sagrado, arrange airport transfers from Cusco (CUZ). At Explora, transfers are organized by the lodge and should be confirmed at the time of booking. The drive from Cusco Airport to Explora Valle Sagrado takes approximately 1.5 to 2 hours through the Andean highlands. Transfer inclusions and any associated costs vary by property; verify directly with your lodge at the time of reservation.

faqs.q: How many nights should I plan for the Sacred Valley?
faqs.a: Most travel specialists recommend a minimum of four to five nights in the Sacred Valley to experience a meaningful range of Inca sites and exploration zones. Explora recommends five nights as a minimum; additional nights allow time to acclimatize to the altitude, complete a full-day visit to Machu Picchu, and explore lesser known sites such as Chinchero, Moray, and the Maras salt mines. Travelers planning a Machu Picchu visit typically combine three to four nights in the Sacred Valley with a dedicated day trip or overnight in Aguas Calientes.

faqs.q: What is the altitude of the Sacred Valley?
faqs.a: Explora Valle Sagrado is situated at approximately 9,514 feet (2,900 meters) above sea level near the village of Urubamba. Cusco, the main gateway city, sits at approximately 11,200 feet (3,400 meters). Machu Picchu is considerably lower, at approximately 7,970 feet (2,430 meters). Altitude effects such as headache, fatigue, or shortness of breath are common for newly arrived visitors. Most guests acclimatize within one to two days; staying well-hydrated, avoiding strenuous activity on arrival, and limiting alcohol on the first evening are generally recommended.

faqs.q: Can I visit Machu Picchu from Explora Valle Sagrado?
faqs.a: Yes. Explora Valle Sagrado is an ideal base for a full-day visit to Machu Picchu. The standard route involves a train from Ollantaytambo to Aguas Calientes (approximately 1.5 to 2 hours) followed by a short bus ride to the Machu Picchu entrance (approximately 30 minutes). Entry to Machu Picchu is controlled through a government permit system with daily visitor caps, timed entry windows, and phased ticket releases. During peak season — May through August — available slots regularly sell out within hours of release, and the most popular entry times (early morning) go first. Booking six to eight weeks ahead is standard for peak-season visits; last-minute access is not reliable. Explora’s planning team coordinates your entry permit, train from Ollantaytambo to Aguas Calientes, and guided site access as part of your stay — the logistics are handled in advance so guests arrive with confirmed access rather than contingency plans.

faqs.q: Is it better to stay in the Sacred Valley or in Cusco for a Machu Picchu visit?
faqs.a: The Sacred Valley offers a meaningful logistical advantage over Cusco for travelers prioritizing Machu Picchu access. The Ollantaytambo train station — the primary departure point for Aguas Calientes — is within the Sacred Valley, reducing morning travel time on the day of your Machu Picchu visit compared to departing from Cusco. Sacred Valley lodges also sit at a lower elevation than Cusco (approximately 9,500 feet vs. 11,200 feet), which benefits guests who are sensitive to altitude. Cusco provides more urban amenities and a wider range of restaurants and independent excursions. Travelers combining Machu Picchu access with sustained Andean exploration — including multiple Inca sites across the Sacred Valley — typically find an all-inclusive lodge in the Sacred Valley the more efficient and immersive base.

faqs.q: Do Sacred Valley lodges include guided explorations in the rate?
faqs.a: Inclusion policies vary by property. At Explora Valle Sagrado, more than 40 guided explorations are included in the all-inclusive rate, led by Explora’s own bilingual guides trained at the company’s in-house School of Guides. Explorations are customized each day to your interests and fitness level and cover sites across the Inca heartland, including Pisac, Ollantaytambo, Moray, the Maras salt mines, and a full-day visit to Machu Picchu. Many Sacred Valley boutique hotels do not include guided excursions in their nightly rate — activities are typically booked separately through local operators. If guided access to archaeological sites is a priority, verify inclusions directly with your property at the time of booking.

sections.text: Experience the best of Chile’s surreal desert landscape at Explora Atacama, our multi-award-winning lodge near the oasis town of San Pedro de Atacama. Surrounded by the wild beauty of the vast Atacama Desert — salt flats, volcanoes, geysers, windswept dunes and more — discover a contemporary retreat with every comfort in mind. Enjoy a unique culinary experience, four pools and a spa, and stargazing from our onsite Observatory. Then venture out on horseback from Explora’s own stables, bike or hike the Altiplano with views of the Valley of the Moon, and soak in the natural hot springs, exclusively located in Explora’s Puritama Conservation Reserve. text: OVERVIEW Atacama The Atacama Desert, Chile ATACAMA DESERT OVERVIEW LODGE EXPLORATIONS DINING GETTING HERE TRAVEL TIPS Welcome to Explora Atacama Experience the best of Chile’s surreal desert landscape at Explora Atacama, our multi-award-winning lodge near the oasis town of San Pedro de Atacama. Surrounded by the wild beauty of the vast Atacama Desert — salt flats, volcanoes, geysers, windswept dunes and more — discover a contemporary retreat with every comfort in mind. Enjoy a unique culinary experience, four pools and a spa, and stargazing from our onsite Observatory. Then venture out on horseback from Explora’s own stables, bike or hike the Altiplano with views of the Valley of the Moon, and soak in the natural hot springs, exclusively located in Explora’s Puritama Conservation Reserve. At our 50-room lodge near the historic town of San Pedro de Atacama, discover an elevated stay beyond compare, including all meals, spa facilities with a sauna and four pools, and our own onsite observatory and horseback riding stables. VIEW LODGE Embark on Desert Explorations You’re invited to choose from nearly 50 guided Explorations at Explora Atacama, all included as part of your stay. Led by our own expertly trained guides, these experiences and Explora-only adventures include horseback riding, biking, hiking and high-elevation climbs across the soul-stirring geology of the otherworldly Atacama. Every Exploration is also customized to match your interests and fitness levels, ensuring an unforgettable adventure made just for you. VIEW ALL EXPLORATIONS Enjoy Authentic Cuisine At Explora Atacama, we present an authentic, handcrafted daily menu that highlights the bold flavors and rich culinary traditions of Chile’s Atacama region. Savor fresh locally inspired dishes while enjoying spectacular views from our intimate dining room, where every meal is an experience in itself. VIEW DINING Stargaze from Explora’s Observatory The Atacama Desert is synonymous with starry skies, with San Pedro de Atacama offering some of the clearest skies on the planet. Join us at Explora Atacama in the lodge’s own state-of-the-art Observatory for guided experiences and jaw-dropping views of the constellations, planets and Andean night skies. sections.text: The journey begins from the heart of our Conservation Reserve, a gateway to Patagonia’s wildest landscapes. description: Cross from Chile’s Atacama Desert to Bolivia’s Uyuni Salt Flat in an all-inclusive overland journey. Expert guides, and seamless travel.

sections.text: An exclusive journey from Chile’s Atacama Desert to Bolivia’s salt flats, Travesìa Atacama-Uyuni offers travelers a rare opportunity to transit a spectacular and otherworldly high-altitude route in surprising comfort, and entirely under the wing of seasoned Explora guides. On our nine-day travesìa — the Spanish word for long crossing — venture over 300 miles through some of the most remote and awe-inspiring landscapes of the Altiplano, including the Laguna Colorado with its pink flamingos, towering Irruputuncu volcano, and endless, staggeringly bright Salar de Uyuni salt flat. World's Leading Expedition Company 2025 The Best Hotels and Resorts in South America: Readers' Choice Awards 2025 Conservation Sustainability with Soul ‹› With Explora, your adventure from the world’s driest desert to its largest salt flat delivers on profoundly immersive discoveries and Explorations, which are customized daily to accommodate you. sections.text: A Natural Corridor Between Desert and High Puna The reserve lies within the intermediate gorges of the rhyolitic plateau ecozone. In Puritama, a narrow corridor connecting to the Jorquencal ravine creates a direct link with the high puna, forming a distinct transition between desert lowlands and high-altitude landscapes. The Puritama River emerges from a geothermal source near the center of the reserve, feeding the Puritama hot springs before converging with the Puripica River near Guatín. This high-altitude desert environment is characterized by low humidity, sharp day–night temperature contrasts, seasonal summer rains, freezing winter nights, and strong southwest winds that shape the terrain through erosion. sections.text: Puritama Conservation Reserve’s extreme geography creates ideal conditions for a rich and diverse Andean biodiversity. Located between 3,700 and 4,200 meters above sea level, variations in altitude, solar exposure, water availability, and substrate shape unique plant communities adapted to aridity and high radiation. These adaptations allow flora to thrive through efficient photosynthesis, reduced water loss, and highly specialized growth strategies. This diversity of habitats also supports a wide range of fauna, including nearly 30 bird species, amphibians and reptiles associated with river and hot spring areas, and emblematic mammals such as guanacos, foxes, vizcachas, pumas, and the endangered Andean cat—one of South America’s most iconic species. Cultures Adapted to Altitude and Extremes The Puritama Conservation Reserve lies within Chile’s Norte Grande, a region defined by diverse ecozones distributed across different altitudes. Each of these environments offers distinct resources that have historically complemented one another, shaping patterns of human movement, settlement, and exchange. Seasonal climate extremes—such as cold winters in the high puna and limited vegetation availability—led populations to concentrate in intermediate plateaus, foothill oases, and fertile vegas near the Salar de Atacama. sections.text: Ancestral Myths of the Atacama Landscape For the Atacama people, or Likan Antai, the surrounding volcanoes and mountains are sacred beings. Licancabur, Kimal, Juriques, and Lascar are not merely landmarks, but ancestral figures—volcanoes as men, mountains as women—whose stories shape the landscape. According to legend, Licancabur and Kimal were once united, until betrayal and jealousy led to their separation across the vast salt flat. Yet every winter solstice, Licancabur’s shadow stretches more than 100 kilometers to touch Kimal’s peak, renewing their bond. This sacred moment is believed to bring fertility to the Atacama salt flat and marks the beginning of a new agricultural cycle, still celebrated today. READ MORE READ LESS

sections.text: Our Project As philanthropy often fades in the long run, we start a venture that joins the virtues of business enterprise and non-profit commitment. The design enables us to expand and accelerate conservation as well as project it in perpetuity. The reserves’ territory retains 97% of its area only to exploration and conservation, while the remaining 3% is subject to developments that include tourism, leisure, research, and education. In the spirit of a traditional Estancias, the Reserve’s Hull congregates services and activities. From the Hull, a wide range of explorations will be available: both led by our guides with their distinctive training and knowledge, along with self-guided trails with exploration and conservation content supported by technology. Also, as the Gaucho tradition is alive at the Reserve, horse-riding explorations with them are living testimonies of the local way of life. faqs.q: Geography
faqs.a: Located near the northeastern edge of the Torres del Paine National Park, The Torres del Paine Conservation Reserve is a majestic land in Patagonia's heart. Between the Paine Horns and the Sierra Baguales, this is the only area in the region where you can spot both of those iconic landscapes at once, while also representing some of the most symbolic elements of the southern corner of the planet. This valley is situated in a geological stage with views and sights from any point you stand. Depending on the time of year, many wetlands form in the valley area. There’s also Jara Lagoon, a big body of water in the heart of the reserve, where you can usually spot wildlife, especially resident birds. The Rio de las Chinas river, which originates in the Andes, gives life to a branch known locally as the Zamora River that crosses the entire reserve and defines the landscape. The Steppe is a defining feature of the Patagonia landscape, and the Torres del Paine Explora Conservation Reserve is no exception. For decades, this region has seen the development of livestock within the communities, where the gauchos and animal keepers have traveled endlessly through these vast areas. Mountains flank part of the Steppe to then gives way to what is known locally as “La Vega”: a big patch of land, fertile enough to have grass year-round, especially on a rainy year. faqs.q: Biodiversity
faqs.a: In this over 6000 hectare reserve, one can find Lenga's deep forests (Nothofagus pumilio) and Ñire (Nothofagus Antartica). The strong winds have shaped these endemic trees, telling a story about the land, which also features a vast steppe landscape. You can appreciate the passage of time in the countryside. Some areas where the wind strikes mercilessly are close to barren, while others thrive and can give life to forests and shrub-like vegetation. The altitude and the proximity to mountain chains in the border with Argentina, give the reserve a unique advantage in protecting biodiversity. A distinctive part of the vegetation landscape is the neneo (Anarthrophyllum desideratum), an endemic ball-shaped shrub, that can withstand extreme weather and direct wind. These shrubs, along with the lengas and grass, change colors and transform this area into a red and yellow stage. Some say it’s the most beautiful time of year to visit. Many local species of fauna, especially birds, can be found here. Over a hundred resident bird species have been identified, making this reserve one of the richest in the biodiversity of its kind. In the wetlands and Jara Lagoon, you can spot many species of resident birds, such as flamingos, ducks, and other local species such as bandurrias and ñandues (local ostrich). Other common species in the region, which thrive in this area, are the guanacos, a local camel present throughout the Andean region, and can survive in different geographical conditions. <

faqs.q: Culture
faqs.a: For centuries, this area was home to the Tehuelche people, specifically the Aonikenk tribe. After the arrival of European settlers in the mid 19th century, successive unfortunate events eradicated this and other local tribes. Today there is growing recognition that they were mistreated and taken advantage of. Another aspect of the European influence in the area is the introduction of the horse. Horseback riding became crucial in the area, and the horse itself even became an essential element in the diet of the locals. The archaeological finding of artifacts such as stone arrows seems to reveal that this was a privileged area for the hunting of guanacos and rheas. In future conservation endeavors we may be able to research more in-depth about the Tehuelche presence in the reserve. Early in the 20th century, the first forms of tourism and investigation began in this area. Lady Florence Dixie, a Scottish writer and feminist icon was a pioneer in documenting the field and played an essential role in revealing Patagonia to the rest of the world. Through her findings and illustrations, we can assert that the reserve was part of her travels. Throughout the last century, this area has been home to gauchos and their livestock and horses, they have carried out ancestral European settler’s traditions of managing horses and livestock and have been highly influential in the lifestyle of the region and, in many ways, have paved the way for sustainable tourism in the area. Many local species of fauna, especially birds, can be found here. Over a hundred resident bird species have been identified, making this reserve one of the richest in the biodiversity of its kind. In the wetlands and Jara Lagoon, you can spot many species of resident birds, such as flamingos, ducks, and other local species such as bandurrias and ñandues (local ostrich). Other common species in the region, which thrive in this area, are the guanacos, a local camel present throughout the Andean region, and can survive in different geographical conditions. <

For centuries, this area was home to the Tehuelche people, specifically the Aonikenk tribe. After the arrival of European settlers in the mid 19th century, successive unfortunate events eradicated this and other local tribes. Today there is growing recognition that they were mistreated and taken advantage of. Another aspect of the European influence in the area is the introduction of the horse. Horseback riding became crucial in the area, and the horse itself even became an essential element in the diet of the locals. The archaeological finding of artifacts such as stone arrows seems to reveal that this was a privileged area for the hunting of guanacos and rheas. In future conservation endeavors we may be able to research more in-depth about the Tehuelche presence in the reserve. Early in the 20th century, the first forms of tourism and investigation began in this area. Lady Florence Dixie, a Scottish writer and feminist icon was a pioneer in documenting the field and played an essential role in revealing Patagonia to the rest of the world. Through her findings and illustrations, we can assert that the reserve was part of her travels. Throughout the last century, this area has been home to gauchos and their livestock and horses, they have carried out ancestral European settler’s traditions of managing horses and livestock and have been highly influential in the lifestyle of the region and, in many ways, have paved the way for sustainable tourism in the area. text: HomeConservation Reserves PatagoniaTorres del Paine Conservation Reserve TORRES DEL PAINE CONSERVATION RESERVE On the north-eastern side of the Torres del Paine National Park, these two Patagonian Estancias are true expressions of Patagonian richness. They contain different ecosystems such as Magellan forest, pre-Andean scrubs, steppes, and Patagonian deserts. Two rivers wind up across the estancias, along with wetlands, lagoons, and other water bodies. The land is home to Patagonia’s Gauchos, who keep practicing their old traditions in their everyday life and welcome the visitor with the natural hospitality of a region bound by distance and solitude. Over the last decades, our engagement and understanding of Patagonia reinforced our care for the territory and the people who belong and visit it. Its exceptional millenary landscapes, unique ecosystems, and local traditions are a world’s heritage that only sustainable conservation will preserve for present and future generations. In 2019 we started our reserve journey by undertaking a comprehensive study of the Flora and Fauna, which delivered a detailed map of local species: around 130 types of plants, 50 types of birds and 15 species of mammals, including Darwin’s rheas, flamingoes, Condors, Armadillos, Guanacos, and Pumas. For this last iconic species, we installed trap cameras across our protected lands to better understand its presence and behavior in the area. The resident Gauchos of our estancias periodically check the cameras for new findings. Discover Ownership Opportunities at Our Reserve Explora’s Torres Del Paine Conservation Reserve offers a one-of-a-kind opportunity to own protected land in Patagonia at Explora’s 15,000-acre Torres Del Paine Conservation Reserve. Learn more about the benefits of membership in this special community, including opportunities to build your own home at our Reserve. Learn More. LOCATION Located on the north-eastern side of the Torres del Paine National Park, this Explora Conservation Reserve is a true expression of Patagonian richness, it contains different ecosystems such as Magellan forest, pre-Andean scrubs, steppes, and Patagonian deserts. Between the Paine Horns and the Sierra Baguales, this is the only area in the region where you can spot both of those iconic landscapes at once, while also representing some of the most symbolic elements of the southern corner of the planet. The Zamora River and the Las Chinas river wind up across the estancias, along with wetlands, lagoons, and other water bodies. The land is home to wide range of animals, birds and varios endemic species which make this territory rich in biodiversity and great for exploration. To plan your visit to the reserve, go to conservationreserves.org Perspective Center © Mapbox © OpenStreetMap Improve this map © Maxar 6.000 Hectares Total territory that will be legally protected by DRC (derecho real de conservación) so that it can be conserved in perpetuity. 32% Forest Total percentage of the land that is forest, out of this, 19% is native forest composed of Lenga and Ñirre. 131 Flora Species 95 of those species are native, making 96% of the Flora in the Reserve endemic to the region. 40 Fauna Species The reserve is home to 40 species, among which the Puma and 33 types of birds stand out, including the Chilean Flamingo and the Southern Partridge. GALLERY ABOUT OUR CONSERVATION RESERVE In the spirit of a traditional Estancias, the Reserve offers a unique opportunity to explore and conserve Patagonia’s essence. It is meant to be a living space where travelers, visitors, park rangers, guides, researchers and volunteers can support and participate in a wide range of exploration and conservation experiences. OUR PROJECT GEOGRAPHY BIODIVERSITY CULTURE As philanthropy often fades in the long run, we start a venture that joins the virtues of business enterprise and non-profit commitment. The design enables us to expand and accelerate conservation as well as project it in perpetuity. The reserves’ territory retains 97% of its area only to exploration and conservation, while the remaining 3% is subject to developments that include tourism, leisure, research, and education. In the spirit of a traditional Estancias, the Reserve’s Hull congregates services and activities. From the Hull, a wide range of explorations will be available: both led by our guides with their distinctive training and knowledge, along with self-guided trails with exploration and conservation content supported by technology. Also, as the Gaucho tradition is alive at the Reserve, horse-riding explorations with them are living testimonies of the local way of life. For the development of ecological planning, the Open Standards for Conservation methodology is used, which provides a complete and integrated methodological approach to strategic planning and conservation management, based on the adaptive management cycle. The Conservation Standards bring together common concepts, approaches, and terminology in conservation project and program design, management, and monitoring in order to help improve the practice of conservation. Soon, we’ll have more details and will invite you to join our Reserves, where you will be able to participate as an owner, traveler, researcher, visitor, volunteer, or intern. To plan your visit to the reserve, go to conservationreserves.org LET’S TALK Reach out now to learn more about membership and ownership as well as the chance to visit Explora’s Conservation Reserve in Torres Del Paine: Contact our Conservation Reserve Team Here. Explore Easter Island > ATACAMA The Atacama Desert stretches from the rugged Pacific coast of northern Chile to the steep Andean slopes of southwestern Bolivia. sections.text: Payments & Reservation Lodges: We require an initial payment of up to 30% to confirm the reservation. The remaining balance must be paid 30 days before check-in. During the "Holidays" period, a 50% deposit is required. The remaining balance for this period must be paid 60 days before check-in. Travesía Atacama - Uyuni: We require an initial down payment up to 30% to confirm the booking. The remaining difference must be paid 60 days before check-in. Expeditions: We require an initial down payment up to 30% to confirm the booking. This deposit includes a non-refundable Reservation Fee, which secures availability and expedition logistics planning. The remaining difference must be paid 120 days before check-in. Reservation Fee: - USD 500 per person for Tierra del Fuego and Sacred Mountain Expeditions - USD 1,000 per person for Iceland Expedition The Reservation Fee forms part of the 30% deposit and is non-refundable under all circumstances. The remaining balance must be fully paid 120 days prior to the check-in date. Special Promotions: For the Explora Days promotion or Cyber Week, full payment (100%) is required at the time of booking. sections.heading: A Lodge in the Heart of Torres del Paine National Park

sections.text: Explora is an award-winning collection of Lodges and Expeditions, operating since 1993 from a single founding conviction: the only honest way to experience a wilderness is to be inside it. Located in the heart of Torres del Paine National Park, Explora Torres del Paine offers a privileged location with no equal anywhere in the park, on the shores of Lake Pehoé. The difference is immediate. When the granite towers catch first light, you soak it up through floor to ceiling glass windows. With just 50 rooms, the scale is deliberate: quiet trails, an intimate feel, and enough space to move through the extensive park. There are over 40 Explorations included in every stay, all led by an expert guide trained at Explora’s own School of Guides. Each Exploration covers significant ground: hikes to Grey Glacier, the search for puma, horseback rides alongside local gauchos, and the trek to the base of the granite Towers. Your guide becomes your companion on the trail, not just a leader of it. Beyond the route, they bring the knowledge that lets you see the place in full: trained at Explora’s own School of Guides, bilingual, they sit with you each evening to shape the next day’s Exploration around your pace, your interests, your questions. This is the heart of what Explora offers: access to the natural and cultural richness of these territories, seen through someone who knows them intimately. sections.heading: The Hidden Side of Patagonia
sections.heading_selector: #content > article > div:nth-of-type(2) > div.exp_component:nth-of-type(4) > div.explora-wysiwyg:nth-of-type(2) > h2
sections.text: Further north along Chilean Patagonia, Patagonia National Park expands on this story. Less visited than Torres del Paine, with a landscape that opens differently: wide river valleys, guanaco herds moving in greater numbers, and Andean condors riding thermals above basalt ridgelines. Explora Parque Nacional Patagonia is a 13-room lodge that also operates from right inside the park. This creates a real sense of intimacy. From here, Patagonia looks unique. The attractive landscape is different: fjords reaching deep into the continent, coigüe forests of extraordinary density and age, ice fields with hanging glaciers. The Cochrane River runs through it, one of the most pristine glacial rivers on the planet, alongside a chain of lakes and lagoons in colors that seem to belong to another world. This is ecology you won’t find in Torres del Paine, a Patagonia built on entirely different terms. Guanaco and puma share the pampa of Valle Chacabuco, while huemul roam the wider region, all brought back through active rewilding. The Andean condor soars over the same hills where cattle ranches once stood. This is an ecosystem in active recovery, one you can feel. Every stay is all-inclusive and expert-led as standard. After active days in the field, three outdoor hot tubs with mountain views offer a quiet place to unwind. The Explorations here take a different shape entirely. sections.text: At Explora, conservation is not simply an initiative, but rather a way of being. As a Certified B Corporation backed by decades of responsible exploration, our work (including our numerous conservation projects) is guided by a deep commitment to protect and restore the landscapes and cultures that welcome us. Traveling with Explora means something specific. Every Exploration is led by a guide trained at Explora’s own School of Guides, someone who reads a landscape rather than simply walking through it. It means daily itineraries matched to your fitness and interest, meals and wine already accounted for. It means joining the largest network of Lodges, Expeditions, and Conservation Reserves in South America, a company named World’s Leading Expedition Company for seven consecutive years and celebrated in Condé Nast Traveler’s Readers’ Choice Awards. A different hemisphere. Granite towers instead of savanna. The same guide beside you, the same seriousness about being present in a place. Plan your stay at Explora Torres del Paine or Explora Parque Nacional Patagonia. Emily from Explora

sections.text: Built for travelers drawn to the places that anchor a lifetime of exploration, Explora’s Expeditions travel in a small group of no more than eight, led by the company’s expert guides into a territory that is hard to reach on one’s own. Together, they open authentic access to some of the most remote landscapes on Earth, from a winter ice hike on Europe’s largest glacier to the old Inca trails above the Sacred Valley and the fjords at the end of the world, with nights in place-making lodges, camps and historic hotels along the way. “Travel, at its best, is a way of paying attention, and the places that change you are usually the hardest to reach,” said Sebastián Correa, VP of Expeditions & Explorations, Explora. “That belief runs through all of these expeditions, from the winter glaciers of Iceland, the newest of the four, to the high passes of the Andes and the fjords at the southern end of Patagonia. On every one of our journeys, the idea is the same: to go slowly, in a small group, until a landscape stops being scenery and starts to feel alive. What we are really after is that shift, from looking at a place to caring what becomes of it.” Iceland Winter Expedition Explora’s first winter itinerary in Iceland meets the island in its most dramatic season, unfolding over seven days across four regions and guiding a small group through volcanic landscapes, glacier fields and winter coastlines.
