On every one of our journeys, the idea is the same: to go slowly, in a small group, until a landscape stops being scenery and starts to feel alive. What we are really after is that shift, from looking at a place to caring what becomes of it.” Iceland Winter Expedition Explora’s first winter itinerary in Iceland meets the island in its most dramatic season, unfolding over seven days across four regions and guiding a small group through volcanic landscapes, glacier fields and winter coastlines. While exploring Iceland’s outdoors in winter might seem suited only to experienced adventurers, Explora is designed to make the season approachable, with expert guides and specially equipped vehicles opening the country in its quieter, less-crowded months. The route favors places few travelers reach over the busiest stops, leaving room to take in sites without the high-season crowds. Beginning and ending in Reykjavík, the journey traces Iceland’s natural wonders from the tectonic rift at Þingvellir National Park, where the world’s first parliament once met, and the waterfalls and geysers of the Golden Circle to the black-sand beaches of the south coast and the iceberg-filled lagoon of Jökulsárlón. At the heart of the experience is a guided ice hike on Vatnajökull, Europe’s largest glacier, exploring its blue ice and crevasses on foot with crampons and ice axes — an accessible introduction to the glacier that requires no prior experience. Additional highlights include snowmobiling beneath the Eyjafjallajökull volcano, a morning at the interactive Lava Center, and a geothermal soak at the Sky Lagoon as the cold settles over the coast. Timed around Iceland’s shifting winter light, when the days are short and the nights long, every departure carries strong odds of the Northern Lights. Travelers move by specially modified 4×4 vehicles and stay at a collection of distinctive properties, including Reykjavík’s landmark Hotel Borg, the family-run working farm of Hotel Skálakot and the glacier-facing Hotel Jökulsárlón. Inaugural departures are scheduled for December 5–11, 2026; February 22–28, 2027; and March 3–9, 2027. Iceland Summer Expedition Where the winter itinerary turns toward the coast and the cold, Explora’s summer expedition, first offered in 2025, heads inland, spending eight days in the long light of the northern summer. The expedition reaches some of the highlands’ least-visited terrain, well away from Iceland’s more frequented sights. Beginning and ending in Reykjavík, the route spans the Þórsmörk valley, the banded rhyolite mountains and geothermal fields of Landmannalaugar, the Southern Fjallabak highlands, Vatnajökull and the remote Langisjór lake. The trip includes hikes and overland drives across stark, volcanic country with glaciers, canyons, waterfalls and ice-blue lagoons, as well as the landscapes around Eyjafjallajökull, which shares a magma system with neighboring Katla. Nights are spent in small boutique hotels, countryside guest houses and Reykjavík hotels, with 2027 departures set for June 18–25; June 28–July 5; July 9–16; July 19–26; August 7–14; August 17–24; and September 4–11, 2027. Sacred Mountains Expedition Crafted for experienced trekkers seeking a path to Machu Picchu that few ever travel, the Sacred Mountains Expedition is a nine-day journey through Peru’s Sacred Valley of the Incas. Rather than the classic Inca Trail, it follows one of the route’s lesser-known paths, reaching Machu Picchu by ways that few trekkers ever see. Beginning and ending at Explora’s award-winning Valle Sagrado lodge, the route opens with acclimatization hikes to the archaeological site of Machu Kolka above Chinchero, along the ancient Qhapaq Ñan road to the ruins of Wata, and on old shepherd trails between Lamay and Pisac. It then turns nomadic and camp-supported, climbing into the Misquiyaco Private Conservation Area through cloud forest and above the tree line before pressing deep into the Vilcabamba range beneath Apu Salkantay, the snow-capped peak revered as a mountain guardian. After a descent toward the Vilcanota River and a day in Ollantaytambo, with its Temple of the Sun and a traditional pachamanca lunch cooked in the earth, travelers board the Vistadome train to the Inca Trail and climb through cloud forest by way of Wiñay Wayna to Inti Punku, the Sun Gate, for a first sight of Machu Picchu on foot, the way the Inca approached it. Daily hikes range from about 3.5 to 15 kilometers (2.2 to 9.3 miles), with altitudes reaching 4,671 meters (15,324 feet). text: HomeStoriesTierra del Fuego Expedition: Patagonia’s Changing Light TIERRA DEL FUEGO EXPEDITION: PATAGONIA’S CHANGING LIGHT I’ve always said Patagonia has a particular light. It isn’t brighter or softer, just different. In Tierra del Fuego, it feels sharper, more deliberate, as if it reveals the landscape in layers rather than all at once. That light framed my experience as Expedition Leader on Explora’s Tierra del Fuego Expedition: a seven-day, point-to-point journey through one of the least visited regions of Chilean Patagonia. Yendegaia National Park, Chile A Small Group at the End of the World This expedition took us through stretches of the island that remain largely unexplored, even for seasoned travelers. On the Chilean side of Tierra del Fuego, there are no crowds and no circuit to follow. Instead, scale defines the experience—nature feels immense, and human presence almost incidental. We traveled in a small group of five, supported by Explora’s expedition crew. Before long, a shared rhythm settled in: unhurried explorations, quiet moments outdoors, and conversations that deepened day by day. In a single week, we moved from open Patagonian pampa to subantarctic forest, then into fjords framed by the glacial presence of the Darwin Range. Tierra del Fuego asks for something simple: full attention. Crossing the Strait of Magellan From Punta Arenas, we could already see Tierra del Fuego across the water. The crossing took about two hours, and the day greeted us with a rare gift in Patagonia: sun and almost no wind, ideal for staying on deck and taking in the widening horizon. It felt like a clear line between what was familiar and what was remote. And as we headed toward the island, it was hard not to feel we were stepping into something entirely new. Just before we reached shore, a few Commerson’s dolphins surfaced alongside the boat and then disappeared again, a brief reminder that, out here, we were visitors. King Penguins, Tierra del Fuego Bahía Inútil: King Penguins, Up Close Not long after, we stopped at Bahía Inútil, home to the only king penguin breeding colony on the South American continent. The adults were imposing—nearly three feet tall—with black backs, bright white chests, and those unmistakable golden and orange markings at the neck. Among them, the chicks were mid-change: almost full-sized, still wrapped in brown down, with patches where new feathers were coming through. Near the shoreline, a few hesitated at the edge before stepping into the water, wobbly for a second, then suddenly sure. Around us, the colony’s calls formed a constant chorus. It was unforgettable and completely wild. Magellan Woodpecker Southbound: Into Forest and Fjords From there, the expedition turned south and the island changed character. In the north, the pampa had felt exposed—wind-driven, dry, and wide open. However, as we drew closer to the Darwin Range, the air cooled and the landscape tightened. In Karukinka, lenga and ñirre forests took over: damp undergrowth, filtered light, lichens hanging from branches, and a quiet that slowed us down without asking. It was hard not to think about the people who moved through these same environments long before us: Selk’nam across the interior, and Yagán through the channels, adapting to cold, tides, and a coastline that offers little shelter. Later came sheep ranching and estancias, and the island’s human story shifted again. Germán Genskowsky The Island, Lived In We experienced that continuity firsthand when we arrived at Estancia Lake Fagnano, where we were hosted by Don Germán Genskowsky and his family—among the last settlers living in this far southern corner. In a place where, for years, access was limited and everything had to be built with what you could bring in, their welcome didn’t feel staged. It felt lived-in. Don Germán showed us photographs and documents he had gathered over decades, keeping the island’s recent history tangible and local memory alive. It was one of those rare moments that grounded the entire expedition. We weren’t only moving through landscapes; we were stepping into the island’s living history. Alberto de Agostini National Park, Chile Toward the Darwin Range What followed became the expedition’s turning point: navigating Parry Fjord on a rare calm day. The Darwin Range rose ahead with colossal walls of ice. We heard the low thunder of glaciers calving, seabirds circling above the channel, and then—unmistakably—a leopard seal resting on an iceberg, unbothered and perfectly at home. No one rushed to speak. We let the moment settle. Later, we stepped ashore for a hike that brought everything closer. After hours on the water, walking toward the glacier shifted the perspective—the ice was no longer something in the distance. It filled the valley ahead, and every step made its scale feel more real. Yendegaia: Color Underfoot We also explored Yendegaia National Park, and the first thing that stood out was the color. It kept shifting: deep green lenga and ñirre forest, copper and rust-toned peatlands, and snow-dusted peaks appearing and disappearing as the light moved. There weren’t clear trails in the way most parks have them. Instead, peat, moss, and cushion plants absorbed each step and naturally slowed the group. Everyone moved in their own rhythm. Some travelers stayed focused on the route ahead; I kept looking down, drawn into the miniature world underfoot—quiet layers of life building over time. At the end of the world, the light changes. And so do we. By the end of the expedition, what stayed with me wasn’t just the places themselves, but how Tierra del Fuego reminded me what it means to feel small before vast beauty and to connect meaningfully. It is a destination that asks for presence and, in return, opens space for introspection. faqs.q: What is included?
faqs.a: In this trip, everything is included: Accommodations and transfers detailed in the itinerary, meals, beverages, and guided explorations.

faqs.q: Where do I need to arrive?
faqs.a: The journey starts in Punta Arenas and ends in Punta Arenas. To get to the city of Punta Arenas, you will need to take a flight from Santiago de Chile. The direct flight has an estimated duration of 4 hours.

faqs.q: Will you pick me up from the airport?
faqs.a: If your arrival is on the same day as the start of the trip, we will pick you up from the airport starting at 10 am and take you to the hotel. If you arrived the day before, we will pick you up from your accommodation in Punta Arenas where you are staying. Please note that the check-in time is from 3:00 pm onwards

faqs.q: Is there phone signal and Wi-Fi in Tierra del Fuego?
faqs.a: The phone signal is intermittent and will only be available until the 3rd day of the trip. On the last day, when returning to Pampa Guanaco, we will have signal again. There is no freely available Wi-Fi. There will be satellite Wi-Fi available for emergency cases at the cabins in Estancia Lago Fagnano.

faqs.q: Will we carry satellite phones?
faqs.a: Yes. For the safety of our travelers, we will have a satellite phone in one of the vehicles for exclusive use in case of emergencies.

faqs.q: What are the lodging options for the Journey?
faqs.a: There are different types of accommodation during the trip, as options in Tierra del Fuego are very limited. Therefore, we have selected those that best align with creating a deep experiential connection with the territory and can provide extraordinary value to our travelers. First night: We will stay in Punta Arenas at a small hotel, a colonial house that keeps the local culture alive both in its decor and offerings.

faqs.q: What type of transportation will we use?
faqs.a: We will use 4×4 trucks for both our travelers and our staff accompanying us on this journey. The trucks are suitable for the road and various weather conditions that we may encounter.

faqs.q: How much luggage can I bring?
faqs.a: We recommend a maximum of 1 suitcase weighing up to 20 kg. The plane that will transport you back to Punta Arenas from Tierra del Fuego has limited capacity.

faqs.q: Is the return trip to Punta Arenas by plane included?
faqs.a: The transfer on a private plane from Tierra del Fuego to Punta Arenas is included and has an approximate flight duration of 1 hour. We do not include the return experience by land, which could take an additional 6 to 10 hours. In case of weather restrictions and the plane cannot take off, the return will be by land. We recommend you take this into consideration for your return flight from Punta Arenas to Santiago de Chile.

faqs.q: Can I modify the itinerary and explorations?
faqs.a: It is not possible to modify the itinerary or explorations, they may be adjusted or modified only due to season and weather conditions.

faqs.q: What type of person is this journey recommended for?
faqs.a: This trip is recommended for active individuals who are capable of hiking on uneven terrain, such as mud, rocks, snow, or peat bogs. Hikes of up to 10 kilometers with inclines and declines are included.

faqs.q: How will the food be?
faqs.a: The food during the trip consists of a unique menu with local components from Patagonia. There will be lamb roasts on a spit and other preparations that help us understand part of the local culture of Tierra del Fuego. Travelers with any type of food intolerance should inform us in advance to evaluate the adaptation of their meals. Excellent Chilean wines are included in the menu.

faqs.q: Will this journey be the same as going to an Explora?
faqs.a: It won’t be the same as going to an Explora. This trip takes place in a remote location with basic infrastructure, but we will accommodate it with different Explora touches for each and every moment.

faqs.q: What happens in case of an emergency?
faqs.a: In case of an emergency, our team is trained to handle a range of situations. Our guides are certified in first aid, allowing them to properly assess and manage any incident that requires medical attention. Basic medical care is available in the town of Porvenir. For other treatments, or depending on the severity of the case, a transfer to Punta Arenas may be necessary. Given the remote nature of this territory and the absence of nearby pharmacies, we strongly recommend that travelers bring an adequate supply of any personal medications for the entire duration of the expedition. Please note that we do not provide or administer medications. If you take prescription medication or have a specific medical condition, be sure to carry everything you may need.

faqs.q: Can I cancel my booking free of charge?
faqs.a: Yes. You may cancel up to 60 days before your check-in date free of fines.

faqs.q: What happens if I cancel less than 60 days before check-in?
faqs.a: The following conditions apply based on how close to check-in you cancel: 60 days or more before check-in: no fine 59–30 days before check-in: 50% fine 29–0 days before check-in: 100% fine

faqs.q: Do I need to sign anything before traveling?
faqs.a: Yes. The traveler must sign the flight disclaimer and exploration waiver.

faqs.q: Should I purchase travel insurance?
faqs.a: We recommend it. Travel insurance is advised in case an emergency evacuation is needed.

sections.text: This journey has been designed so that you can discover this remote territory alongside our expert exploration team. This is a place where highways don’t exist, services are scarce, and there are still native settlers who arrived decades ago to colonize a pristine territory. Day 1: Welcome We will meet this day at the Yegua Loca Hotel in Punta Arenas, where we will be waiting for you. Depending on your arrival time, you can explore the beautiful city of Punta Arenas while we prepare for the evening, where we will enjoy the introduction to our journey with our exploration team and a dinner to kick off the trip. Accommodation: Yegua Loca Hotel READ MORE READ LESS

sections.heading: Day 1: Welcome
sections.heading_selector: #content > div.component-t7:nth-of-type(5) > div > div > div > div > div:nth-of-type(4) > div > div > div:nth-of-type(1)
sections.text: Day 2: Strait of Magellan and Pampa Rise at dawn for breakfast before departing by boat across the Strait of Magellan, the most important natural passage between the Pacific and Atlantic Oceans. Enjoy the fresh sea air as you witness this passage from the deck. When explorer Ferdinand Magellan discovered the island of Tierra del Fuego, he named it after the large bonfires he saw from the sea, likely lit by the indigenous Selk’nam people who inhabited the area. Arrive at the port of Porvenir, where we will take a brief tour of the city to learn about its history and culture. Your journey continues as you cross vast expanses of pampa and several estancias, with a stop to marvel at the island’s only king penguin colony. Enjoy lunch and connect with the culture of Tierra del Fuego. Later, arrive at our accommodation in a local estancia. Accommodation: Local estancia (single rooms only) READ MORE READ LESS

sections.heading: Day 2: Strait of Magellan and Pampa
sections.heading_selector: #content > div.component-t7:nth-of-type(6) > div > div > div > div > div:nth-of-type(2) > div > div > div:nth-of-type(1)
sections.text: Day 3: Transition to Patagonian Forest Today you cross the border and the endless plains of pampa to enter the forests of Tierra del Fuego. Arrive at Karukinka Park, a private natural reserve spanning more than 741,000 acres (300,000 hectares) that seeks to preserve the native environment and raise awareness about the island’s biodiversity. Take a 4.3-mile (7 km) hike to Cerro Pietro Grande to admire its diverse ecosystems, as well as the effect of beavers on its forests. End the day at our cabin accommodations near Lake Fagnano. These special accommodations belong to the Genkowsky family, who welcome us upon arrival. Considered the last settlers on the island, they built roads, settled against all odds to live in this part of the planet, and share their stories with us firsthand. Accommodation: Estancia Fagnano (select cabins have outdoor bathrooms) READ MORE READ LESS

sections.heading: Day 3: Transition to Patagonian Forest
sections.heading_selector: #content > div.component-t7:nth-of-type(7) > div > div > div > div > div:nth-of-type(4) > div > div > div:nth-of-type(1)
sections.text: Day 4: Navigating the Patagonian Fjords After an early breakfast, head to Caleta María, a bay that was previously only accessible by sea until 2014, when a new land route was developed. Today, we travel by boat to navigate to Parry Fjord and cross the Almirantazgo Sound, Tierra del Fuego’s first protected marine area. Enjoy a moderate hike along the fjord’s edge through forests overlooking the glaciers. In the afternoon, we return to the protected area of the Almirantazgo Sound, where we find sea elephants, leopard seals, and black-browed albatrosses. Disembark at Caleta María and return to Estancia Fagnano for dinner and a relaxing evening. Accommodation: Estancia Fagnano (select cabins have outdoor bathrooms) READ MORE READ LESS

sections.heading: Day 4: Navigating the Patagonian Fjords

sections.text: Day 5: Mountains and Forests Today, embark on an active, full-day adventure at Yendegaia National Park. This park is closed to visitors, but Explora has special access to explore a part of this wonderful park at the end of the world. Led by our expert guides, enjoy a full-day hike of advanced intensity through the park’s varied terrain and its high-altitude lagoons. Accommodation: Estancia Fagnano (select cabins have outdoor bathrooms) READ MORE READ LESS

sections.heading: Day 5: Mountains and Forests

text: ITINERARY Tierra del Fuego Expedition Chile TIERRA DEL FUEGO OVERVIEW ITINERARY DEPARTURE DATES WHAT TO BRING FAQ ALL EXPEDITIONS Expedition Itinerary This journey has been designed so that you can discover this remote territory alongside our expert exploration team. This is a place where highways don’t exist, services are scarce, and there are still native settlers who arrived decades ago to colonize a pristine territory. Day 1: Welcome We will meet this day at the Yegua Loca Hotel in Punta Arenas, where we will be waiting for you. Depending on your arrival time, you can explore the beautiful city of Punta Arenas while we prepare for the evening, where we will enjoy the introduction to our journey with our exploration team and a dinner to kick off the trip. Accommodation: Yegua Loca Hotel Day 2: Strait of Magellan and Pampa Rise at dawn for breakfast before departing by boat across the Strait of Magellan, the most important natural passage between the Pacific and Atlantic Oceans. Enjoy the fresh sea air as you witness this passage from the deck. When explorer Ferdinand Magellan discovered the island of Tierra del Fuego, he named it after the large bonfires he saw from the sea, likely lit by the indigenous Selk’nam people who inhabited the area. Arrive at the port of Porvenir, where we will take a brief tour of the city to learn about its history and culture. Your journey continues as you cross vast expanses of pampa and several estancias, with a stop to marvel at the island’s only king penguin colony. Enjoy lunch and connect with the culture of Tierra del Fuego. Later, arrive at our accommodation in a local estancia. Accommodation: Local estancia (single rooms only) Day 3: Transition to Patagonian Forest Today you cross the border and the endless plains of pampa to enter the forests of Tierra del Fuego. Arrive at Karukinka Park, a private natural reserve spanning more than 741,000 acres (300,000 hectares) that seeks to preserve the native environment and raise awareness about the island’s biodiversity. Take a 4.3-mile (7 km) hike to Cerro Pietro Grande to admire its diverse ecosystems, as well as the effect of beavers on its forests. End the day at our cabin accommodations near Lake Fagnano. These special accommodations belong to the Genkowsky family, who welcome us upon arrival. Considered the last settlers on the island, they built roads, settled against all odds to live in this part of the planet, and share their stories with us firsthand. Accommodation: Estancia Fagnano (select cabins have outdoor bathrooms) Day 4: Navigating the Patagonian Fjords After an early breakfast, head to Caleta María, a bay that was previously only accessible by sea until 2014, when a new land route was developed. Today, we travel by boat to navigate to Parry Fjord and cross the Almirantazgo Sound, Tierra del Fuego’s first protected marine area. Enjoy a moderate hike along the fjord’s edge through forests overlooking the glaciers. In the afternoon, we return to the protected area of the Almirantazgo Sound, where we find sea elephants, leopard seals, and black-browed albatrosses. Disembark at Caleta María and return to Estancia Fagnano for dinner and a relaxing evening. Accommodation: Estancia Fagnano (select cabins have outdoor bathrooms) Day 5: Mountains and Forests Today, embark on an active, full-day adventure at Yendegaia National Park. This park is closed to visitors, but Explora has special access to explore a part of this wonderful park at the end of the world. Led by our expert guides, enjoy a full-day hike of advanced intensity through the park’s varied terrain and its high-altitude lagoons. Accommodation: Estancia Fagnano (select cabins have outdoor bathrooms) Day 6: Andean Treeline Today’s Exploration takes you to the extreme southeast side of Karukinka Park for a moderate walk along the tree line. At the highest point of this walk, take in incredible views of the mountains, valleys, and an ecosystem that is home to the greatest variety of plants in all of Karukinka, as well as its greatest concentration of endemic plant species. Snow is always possible in the area, so exploring with snowshoes may be necessary. Return to the cabins this evening for a farewell dinner with your fellow travelers. Accommodation: Estancia Fagnano (select cabins have outdoor bathrooms) Day 7: Returning Home/Flight to Punta Arenas Today, we finish this marvelous journey and prepare to return home. After breakfast, travel to Pampa Guanaco, where a flight awaits to take you to Punta Arenas. Operated by Aerolíneas DAP, this flight has an approximate duration of 1 hour and a maximum capacity of 15 people. VIEW DEPARTURE DATES SPECIAL OFFERS Save now with our latest offers and savings. sections.text: Iceland Overview Itinerary Departure Dates Our Expedition begins in Reykjavik, where we meet at the historic Hotel Borg, a landmark in the heart of the city. Over the coming days, this exclusive Explora itinerary will lead you through a captivating tapestry of volcanic landscape, majestic glaciers, and breathtaking vistas of the Icelandic Highlands. Immerse yourself in the extraordinary beauty of Iceland, culminating with a visit to the iconic Sky Lagoon on the last day. Throughout this adventure, the expert Explora team and our dedicated, certified staff will be at your side, ensuring a seamless and unforgettable experience. Day 1: The Adventure Begins Your journey begins with a check-in at the iconic Hotel Borg, a historic landmark nestled in the heart of Reykjavik. Enjoy an evening aperitif as you meet your fellow travelers and our experienced team. After a detailed briefing on the upcoming adventure, prepare to embark on your expedition early the next morning. Accommodation: Hotel Borg or equivalent READ MORE READ LESS

sections.text: Day 2: The Thorsmork Valley Travel south to the stunning Thorsmork Valley and marvel at hanging glaciers cascading from the Eyjafjallajokull Volcano, accompanied by breathtaking waterfalls and one of Iceland’s most remarkable ecosystems. In addition to the day’s curated Explorations, your journey includes a twoand-a-half-hour drive with a scenic stop along the way. Later, arrive at your cozy hotel and enjoy a relaxing evening. Accommodation: Hotel Skálakot The journey includes a 2.5-hour drive with a scenic stop along the way. Depending on weather conditions and the physical abilities of the group, we’ll choose from four carefully crafted exploration options. READ MORE READ LESS

sections.text: Day 3: Southern Highlands Experience profound solitude as we venture beyond the typical tourist paths. Discover dramatic Tindfjall Mountain and one of the country’s deepest canyons. Marvel at the otherworldly landscapes surrounding Maelifell Mountain and Myrdalsjokull Glacier, which conceals the Katla Volcano beneath its icy surface. Enjoy curated Explorations as well as scenic stops during your four-hour drive today. For more adventurous spirits, a challenging 10-kilometer (6.2-mile) hike to the Strutslaug Hot Springs offers a rewarding experience. Accommodation: Hotel Arctic Exclusive Ranch. Choose from five carefully curated exploration options, tailored to the weather and the physical abilities of all travelers. For the most adventurous spirits, a challenging 10-kilometer (6.2-mile) hike to the Strútslaug Hot Springs offers a rewarding experience. Total time on drive: 4 hours READ MORE READ LESS

sections.text: Day 4: Vatnajökull Adventure Vatnajökull, Europe’s largest ice cap, offers a spectacular display of hanging glaciers, dramatic canyons, and unique waterfalls. Experience the glaciers with guided hikes in the surrounding canyons, admiring breathtaking views from multiple vantage points, or even walking on the ice for an unforgettable adventure. Scenic views during the day’s two-and-ahalf-hour drive complete your discovery. Later, return to your charming hotel to rest and relax. Accommodation: Hotel Arctic Exclusive Ranch. The journey includes a 2.5-hour drive with a scenic stop along the way. We will choose from five carefully crafted exploration options, taking into account the weather, the physical abilities of our travelers, and their preferred way to experience the glaciers. sections.text: Day 5: Into the Highlands Today, return to the Highlands to explore the aweinspiring Lakagígar region, the volcanic fissure responsible for the devastating European famine of 1783. This extraordinary day features the stunning Langisjor Lake, northern edge of the Vatnajokull ice cap, and the pristine beauty of the Fjallabak Nature Reserve. In addition, enjoy several scenic stops during the day’s three-and-a-half-hour drive. Accommodation: Highlands Center Hotel During the day the drive will take approximately 3.5 hours, with at least three scenic stops along the way. We will choose from five carefully crafted exploration options, tailored to the weather and the physical abilities of our travelers. READ MORE READ LESS

sections.text: Day 6: Landmannalaugar Begin the day by heading south to Landmannalaugar. Nestled within the Fjallabak Nature Reserve, this kaleidoscopic landscape is renowned for some of Iceland’s most iconic hiking trails. Today’s hikes are the most challenging of our journey, promising breathtaking discoveries and views. Inside the Fjallabak Nature Reserve, choose from four hiking options ranging from 1.5 miles (2.5 kilometers) to 12.4 miles (20 kilometers). Today’s three-hour drive reveals majestic scenery and stops along the way. Return to your hotel after an invigorating day. Accommodation: Highlands Center Hotel The drive will take approximately 3 hours, with three scenic stops along the way. Inside the Fjallabak Nature Reserve, we’ll choose from four hiking options ranging from 2.5 kilometers (1.5 miles) to 20 kilometers (12.4 miles). READ MORE READ LESS

The drive will take approximately two-and-a-half hours, including a stop at three of the valley’s most beautiful waterfalls. In the afternoon, unwind with a relaxing soak in the geothermal waters of Sky Lagoon, a perfect way to rejuvenate after an incredible adventure. In the evening, gather in Reykjavik with your fellow travelers for a final dinner, reminiscing about the unforgettable moments of your Expedition. Accommodation: Hotel Borg or equivalent The drive will take approximately 2.5 hours, including a stop at three of the valley’s most beautiful waterfalls. READ MORE READ LESS

sections.text: Peru Overview Itinerary Departure Dates To help you plan and make the most of this trip to the Sacred Mountains in Peru, we have compiled some frequently asked questions that might arise. faqs.q: What is included?
faqs.a: In this trip, everything is included: Explora Team: A dedicated team leader and expert guides will support our travelers throughout the entire journey, from start to finish. All Transportation: All transfers, including train tickets and transportation to and from Cusco. All Accommodations and Meals. Expertly Guided Explorations and Entrance Fees Campsite Amenities:Everything from high-quality mountain tents to technical sleeping. Access to a hot shower at the campsite every day. Two days of leg massages included at the camps. A dedicated staff of 15–20 members managing dining, camping, and logistics. Not Included: Gratuity for the guides Massages and extra services requested at Explora Valle Sagrado or Machu Picchu Pueblo hotel. Private services, such as privately guided explorations. This is a group experience shared with other guests on your departure.

faqs.q: Where do I need to arrive?
faqs.a: The journey begins and ends at our lodge Explora Valle Sagrado. To get to our lodge, you must take a flight to the city of Cusco, Peru, in the morning.

faqs.q: What are the passport requirements for the Machu Picchu entrance permit?
faqs.a: To secure your entrance permit, we require a copy of your passport at least four months before departure. Please ensure all details match your passport exactly, as permits are issued in each traveler’s name and cannot be reissued once confirmed. If you renew your passport after your permit has been issued, kindly travel with both your old and new passport.

faqs.q: Will you pick me up from the airport?
faqs.a: Our team will pick you up at the airport to transfer you to the lodge. It is recommended that you arrive 1 day in advance, in which case our team will pick you up at the hotel in Cusco. Please note that the check-in time is from 3:00 pm onwards.

faqs.q: Is there phone signal and WI-FI?
faqs.a: Phone signal and Wi-Fi are available at the lodges, but there is no signal during the days spent in the mountains.

faqs.q: How physically demanding is the expedition?
faqs.a: This journey is recommended for active travelers. You will hike 80 kms (50 miles), reaching up to heights of 4,683 meters above sea level (15,350 feet). Recommended for travelers in strong physical condition.

faqs.q: Do you offer food options for vegans?
faqs.a: Yes, we accommodate dietary preferences, including vegan options. Please inform us in advance of any specific requirements so we can prepare a suitable menu for you at each accommodation.

faqs.q: What happens in case of an emergency?
faqs.a: In case of an emergency, our team is trained to handle a range of situations. Our guides are certified in first aid, allowing them to properly assess and manage any incident that requires medical attention. We have an emergency plan, satellite communication, oxygen assistance, and evacuation points along the entire route, so we are prepared for any contingency. Depending on where the evacuation takes place, basic medical care is available in Ollantaytambo or Urubamba. For more complex treatments, or depending on the severity of the case, a transfer to Cusco may be necessary for further medical attention. Please note that we do not supply medications. We recommend that travelers bring their own, particularly any they take regularly or may need in an emergency.

faqs.q: How much luggage can I carry on?
faqs.a: You should bring a 20-liter daypack to carry essentials such as a jacket, water, and snacks for daily use. Additionally, a 40-liter duffle bag (measuring 25 x 30 x 50 cm) will be provided to store extra clothing and gear. This duffel bag will be transported between camps by mules, allowing you to focus on enjoying the trek comfortably. Any additional luggage or items you do not wish to take to the camping nights can be securely stored at the Explora hotel.

faqs.q: What type of transportation we will use?
faqs.a: During the expedition, we will use a combination of transportation methods to ensure comfort and efficiency. Transfers from the hotel to the starting points of the hikes will be done by vans, allowing us to reach the starting points comfortably. For more scenic routes, such as the journey from Ollantaytambo to Machu Picchu Village, round trip, we will take the train, which offers stunning views of the Andean landscape. Additionally, during the trekking stages, we will use horses and mules to transport the equipment and supplies between camps, allowing us to enjoy the trek without the burden of heavy backpacks.

faqs.q: Why visit Iceland in winter instead of summer?
faqs.a: Winter offers a different set of conditions and activities: glacier hiking with crampons, snowmobiling, and the possibility of seeing the Northern Lights, none of which are available in summer.

faqs.q: What fitness level is required?
faqs.a: The expedition is suitable for all kinds of travelers. The activity level can be adjusted to the group. If necessary, the team can split into two subgroups so each traveler moves at their own pace. No mountaineering experience required.

faqs.q: Is there a minimum age requirement?
faqs.a: Travelers 13 and older are recommended. Exceptions may be considered on a case-by-case basis.

faqs.q: How do you manage the limited daylight in winter?
faqs.a: The itinerary is structured around Iceland’s 4–5 hours of daylight. All explorations are planned within that window, and the remaining hours are used for transfers, dining, briefings, and rest.

faqs.q: How do you handle cold and windy weather during the expedition?
faqs.a: The team adapts the daily plan in real time based on conditions. The itinerary is flexible by design. Technical clothing is recommended for this expedition. Before departure, travelers receive a packing list with everything they should bring.

faqs.q: What happens in case of an emergency?
faqs.a: In case of an emergency, our team is trained to handle a range of situations. Our guides are certified in first aid and emergency response, and members of our team belong to the Icelandic Association for Search and Rescue, ensuring professional support should an incident arise. We carry communication equipment that allows us to reach emergency services at all times, and evacuation or transfer to a medical facility can be arranged if necessary. Given the remote nature of this territory and the absence of nearby pharmacies, we strongly recommend that travelers bring an adequate supply of any personal medications for the entire duration of the expedition. Please note that we do not provide or administer medications. If you take prescription medication or have a specific medical condition, be sure to carry everything you may need.

faqs.q: Are the guides local?
faqs.a: Travelers are accompanied by Explora’s expert expedition team throughout the trip. The team also works closely with local partners in Iceland, including drivers and specialized guides for specific activities such as the glacier hike.

faqs.q: What activities are included beyond hikes?
faqs.a: Easy walks, glacier hiking with crampons and ice axes, snowmobiling, and a visit to Sky Lagoon’s geothermal pools.

faqs.q: What vehicles are used during the expedition?
faqs.a: The expedition uses specialized expedition vehicles suited for Iceland’s rugged terrain, plus snowmobiles for specific activities. All transportation during the expedition is included.

faqs.q: How much luggage can I bring?
faqs.a: One suitcase (up to 20 kg / 44 lbs) and a daypack for daily explorations.

faqs.q: Is there Wi-Fi or cell service during the expedition?
faqs.a: Some accommodations have Wi-Fi and signal, but connectivity will be limited in remote areas.

faqs.q: For private groups, can dates be customized?
faqs.a: Dates for private departures must be coordinated in advance. Contact reserveexpeditions@explora.com for details.

faqs.q: Where can I find the detailed itinerary and accommodations?
faqs.a: The full day-by-day itinerary, including accommodations for each night, is available on our website here and on the last page of the downloadable itinerary here.

faqs.q: When does the expedition begin and how do transfers work?
faqs.a: Transfers are available from Keflavík International Airport (KEF) and Reykjavík Domestic Airport (RKV) to the hotel in Reykjavík, coordinated according to each traveler’s arrival time. Check-in is from 3:00 PM. The expedition begins at 5:30 PM at the hotel.

faqs.q: What's included in the price?
faqs.a: Accommodation, all meals and beverages, guided explorations, equipment (crampons, ice axes, snowshoes), all transportation during the expedition, and airport transfers.

faqs.q: What are the departure dates and price?
faqs.a: December 5–11, 2026 / February 22–28, 2027 / March 3–9, 2027. From USD $17,900 per person in double occupancy.

faqs.q: How large are the groups?
faqs.a: Maximum 8 travelers per departure. Private departures are also available.

faqs.q: Do ECHO Society members get any benefits on this expedition?
faqs.a: Yes. ECHO Society members have a 10% discount on this expedition. Contact reserveexpeditions@explora.com for details.

faqs.q: Can I join this expedition as a solo traveler
faqs.a: Yes. Solo travelers are welcome with a single supplement available upon request

faqs.q: How do I book?
faqs.a: You can request more information by selecting your expedition of interest here.

faqs.q: About Explora Expeditions
faqs.a: Beyond Iceland, Explora operates three other expedition programs: the Iceland Summer Expedition, the Tierra del Fuego Expedition (Chile), and the Sacred Mountains Expedition (Peru). All are small-group, nomadic itineraries limited to 8 travelers, with everything included. For dates, itineraries, and booking, write to reserveexpeditions@explora.com or visit explora.com.

faqs.q: What is included?
faqs.a: In this trip everything is included: The Explora Team, a dedicated team with expert guides will support our travelers throughout the entire Explora Expedition, from start to finish. All transfers, accommodations, meals and expertly guided explorations and entrance fees are also included. Not included: Gratuity for guides, massages and extra services requested and private services. The expedition is a group experience with other guests on your departure.

faqs.q: Where do I need to arrive?
faqs.a: Please arrive at Reykjavík Airport on the first day of your selected departure date. Our team will pick you up and transfer you to the hotel. Check-in begins at 3:00 PM local time.

faqs.q: Is there phone signal and WI-FI in the Expedition?
faqs.a: Yes, phone signal and Wi-Fi are available at the accommodations. However, there may be some days when these services are unavailable in certain remote locations.

faqs.q: What are the lodging options for the Expedition?
faqs.a: There are different types of accommodation during the trip. Therefore, we have selected those that best align with creating a deep experiential connection with the territory and can provide value to our travelers.

faqs.q: What type of transportation will we use?
faqs.a: We use well-maintained, comfortable 4×4 Super Jeeps, designed to handle Iceland’s rugged terrain. These vehicles ensure safety and accessibility, even in remote areas.

faqs.q: What type of person is this journey recommended for?
faqs.a: The level of physical demand varies based on the activities you choose. While some hikes and treks can be challenging, but there are options for all fitness levels. Travelers can select activities that best suit their physical abilities.

faqs.q: Do you offer food options?
faqs.a: Yes, we accommodate dietary preferences, including vegan options. Please inform us in advance of any specific dietary requirements so we can ensure a suitable menu for you.

sections.text: This expedition begins at Explora Valle Sagrado, where we gather at noon on the first day to meet and prepare for the adventure ahead. Over the following days, the itinerary takes you along ancient Inca paths, through breathtaking archaeological sites, and into awe-inspiring natural landscapes. You’ll connect with the Sacred Mountains of the Incas, culminating in an unforgettable arrival at the world-renowned sanctuary of Machu Picchu, entering through the iconic Intipunku Sun Gate. Day 1 – The Adventure Begins Arrive at Cusco Airport, where you are transported to Explora Valle Sagrado. sections.text: Day 7 – Journey to Ollantaytambo and Andean Traditions This morning, we walk for around 2.5 hours through Andean scenery before meeting our vehicle and continuing to Ollantaytambo. We visit the Temple of the Sun and explore its monumental terraces and finely crafted Inca stonework, then walk into the village along narrow cobblestone streets to the main square. Here, we pause to take in daily life around small markets, community gatherings, and local crafts. Later, we transfer to our lodge just outside the village for a traditional pachamanca lunch, prepared earth-oven style with local ingredients. The afternoon is free to rest and enjoy the quieter side of the Sacred Valley. sections.text: Day 8 – Inca Trail to the Sun Gate and Machu Picchu After breakfast, we travel by van to the station and take the Vistadome train to the starting point of the Inca Trail. We then continue to Inti Punku, the Sun Gate and the historic entrance to Machu Picchu. We enter the sanctuary and explore its main areas with our guide, then descend to Machu Picchu Pueblo for the return train to Ollantaytambo and our transfer back to Explora Valle Sagrado for a farewell dinner. sections.heading: Expedition Itinerary
sections.heading_selector: #content > div.component-o2:nth-of-type(4) > div > div > div > div > div > div > div.explora-wysiwyg > h3
sections.text: This expedition constantly inhabits the tension between the rawness of the Arctic winter and the luxury of the essential. A deep, accesible and transformative experience for curious travelers, not just for experts. Day 1: Reykjavik The first night in Iceland is always one of orientation. Hotel Borg in the historic heart — 1930s Art Déco architecture that signals this is no ordinary trip. The group aperitif is the opening ritual: sharing expectations, aligning on the expedition mindset. What strikes most in Reykjavik in winter is the darkness — barely 5 hours of daylight — and the possibility of seeing the Northern Lights from the city itself. Accommodation: Hotel Borg or equivalent – Reykjavik READ MORE READ LESS

sections.heading: Day 1: Reykjavik
sections.heading_selector: #content > div.component-t7:nth-of-type(5) > div > div > div > div > div:nth-of-type(2) > div > div > div:nth-of-type(1)
sections.text: Day 2: Golden Circle An introduction to Iceland’s living geology and history. The earth here is visibly fractured — cracked open along the Mid-Atlantic Ridge, still pulling apart. Hot steam rises from fissures in the ground, a reminder that magma sits just below the surface. Towering waterfalls carve through ancient lava fields. Accommodation: Hotel Skálakot – South Iceland READ MORE READ LESS

sections.heading: Day 2: Golden Circle
sections.heading_selector: #content > div.component-t7:nth-of-type(6) > div > div > div > div > div:nth-of-type(4) > div > div > div:nth-of-type(1)
sections.text: Day 3: Eyjafjallajökull Learn about the full story of Iceland’s volcanic activity during the morning, and then approach Eyjafjallajökull by snowmobile —the same volcano that paralyzed European air traffic in 2010—now silent beneath its glacier. If conditions allow, snowshoes take you closer to the summit. Accommodation: Hotel Skálakot READ MORE READ LESS

sections.heading: Day 3: Eyjafjallajökull
sections.heading_selector: #content > div.component-t7:nth-of-type(7) > div > div > div > div > div:nth-of-type(2) > div > div > div:nth-of-type(1)
sections.text: Day 4: Dyrhólaey The day opens at Dyrhólaey — a volcanic promontory with Mýrdalsjökull and Eyjafjallajökull rising behind. Then Reynisfjara: black sand, rock spires and Atlantic waves at full force. The day ends at Jökulsárlón Glacier Lagoon, where icebergs calve and drift slowly toward the sea. Accommodation: Hotel Jökulsárlón READ MORE READ LESS

sections.heading: Day 4: Dyrhólaey
sections.heading_selector: #content > div.component-t7:nth-of-type(8) > div > div > div > div > div:nth-of-type(4) > div > div > div:nth-of-type(1)
sections.text: Day 5: Vatnajökull As you walk across Europe’s largest glacier with crampons and ice axe, the crevasses and ice formations are a reminder that Earth is alive, still moving, still forming. The day ends at the hotel’s outdoor hot tubs and sauna, to unwind with the glacier on the horizon. Accommodation: Hotel Jökulsárlón – Glacier Lagoon READ MORE READ LESS

sections.heading: Day 5: Vatnajökull
sections.heading_selector: #content > div.component-t7:nth-of-type(9) > div > div > div > div > div:nth-of-type(2) > div > div > div:nth-of-type(1)
sections.text: Day 6: South Coast Skógafoss in winter is a different creature — ice clinging to the rock face, rainbows forming when the sun barely clears the horizon. The long drive south is anything but monotonous and Sky Lagoon closes the expedition the way it should — submerged in 38°C geothermal water, while the air bites at -5°C. Accommodation: Hotel Borg or equivalent – Reykiavik READ MORE READ LESS

text: HomeTierra del Fuego ExpeditionItinerary OVERVIEW ITINERARY DEPARTURE DATES WHAT TO BRING? FAQ ALL EXPEDITIONS EXPEDITION ITINERARY This journey has been designed so that you can discover this remote territory alongside our expert exploration team. This is a location where highways don't exist, services are scarce, and there are still native people who arrived decades ago to colonize a pristine territory. Day 1: Welcome We will meet this day at the Yegua Loca Hotel in Punta Arenas, where we will be waiting for you. Depending on the arrival time, you can explore the beautiful city of Punta Arenas while we prepare for the evening, where we will enjoy the introduction to our journey with our exploration team and a dinnerto kickstart the trip. Accommodation: Yegua Loca Hotel Pingüinos Rey Day 2: Strait of Magellan and Pampa Rise at dawn for breakfast before departing by boat across the Strait of Magellan, the most important natural passage between the Pacific and Atlantic Oceans. Embrace the brisk sea air as you witness this passage from the deck. When explorer Ferdinand Magellan discovered the island of Tierra del Fuego, he named it after the large bonfires he saw from the sea, which were likely made by the indigenous Selk’nam people who inhabited the area. Arrive at the port of Porvenir, where we briefly tour the city to understand its history and culture. Your journey continues as you cross vast extensions of pampa and several estancias, with a stop to marvel at the island’s only colony of king penguins. Enjoy lunch and connect with the culture of Tierra del Fuego. Later, arrive at our accommodation in a local estancia. Accommodation: Local estancia (single rooms only) Day 3: Transition to Patagonian Forest Today you cross the border and endless plains of pampas to enter tthe forests of Tierra del Fuego. Arrive at Karukinka Park, a private natural reserve spanning more than 741,000 acres (300,000 hectares) that seeks to preserve the native environment and raise awareness about the island’s biodiversity. Take a 4.3-mile (7 km) hike to Cerro Pietro Grande to admire its diverse ecosystems as well as the effect of beavers on its forests. End the day at our cabin accommodations near Lake Fagnano. These special accommodations belong to the Genkowsky family, who welcome us upon arrival. Considered the last settlers on the island, they created roads, settled against all odds to live in this part of the planet and share their stories with us firsthand. Accommodation: Estancia Fagnano (select cabins have outdoor bathrooms) Day 4: Navigating Patagonian Fjords After an early breakfast, head to Caleta María, a bay once only accessible by sea until 2014m, when a new land route was developed. Today, we travel by boat to navigate to Parry Fjord and cross the Almirantazgo Sound, Tierra del Fuego’s first protected marine area. Enjoy a moderate hike along the fjord’s edge through forests overlooking the glaciers. In the afternoon, return to the protected area of the Almirantazgo Sound, where we find sea elephants, leopard seals and black-browed albatrosses. Disembark in Caleta Maria and return to Estancia Fagnano for dinner and a relaxing evening. Accommodation: Estancia Fagnano (select cabins have outdoor bathrooms) Day 5: Mountains & Forests Today, embark on an active, full-day at Yendegaia National Park. This park is closed to visitors, but Explora has special access to explore a part of this wonderful park at the end of the world. Led by our expert guides, enjoy a full-day hike of advanced intensity through the park’s varied terrain and surrounding its high-altitude lagoons. Accommodation: Estancia Fagnano (Select cabins have outdoor bathrooms) Day 6: Andean Treeline Today’s Exploration brings you to the extreme south-east side of Karukinka Park for a moderate walk along the tree line. At the highest part of this walk, take in incredible views of the mountains, valleys and an ecosystem that is home to the greatest variety of plants in all of Karukinka as well as its greatest concentration of endemic plant species. Snow is always possible in the area, so exploring in snowshoes may be necessary. Return to the cabins this evening for a farewell dinner with your fellow travelers. Accommodation: Estancia Fagnano (Select cabins have outdoor bathrooms) Day 7: Returning Home/Flight to Punta Arenas Today, we finish this marvelous journey and prepare to return home. After breakfast, journey to Pampa Guanaco, where a flight awaits to take you to Punta Arenas. Operated by Aerolíneas DAP, this flight is approximately 30 minutes for a maximum capacity of 15 people. faqs.q: What is included?
faqs.a: In this trip, everything is included: Accommodations and transfers detailed in the itinerary, meals, beverages, and guided explorations.

faqs.q: Where do I need to arrive?
faqs.a: The journey starts in Punta Arenas and ends in Punta Arenas. To get to the city of Punta Arenas, you will need to take a flight from Santiago de Chile. The direct flight has an estimated duration of 4 hours.

faqs.q: WILL YOU PICK ME UP FROM THE AIRPORT?
faqs.a: If your arrival is on the same day as the start of the trip, we will pick you up from the airport starting at 10 am and take you to the hotel. If you arrived the day before, we will pick you up from your accommodation in Punta Arenas where you are staying. Please note that the check-in time is from 3:00 pm onwards

faqs.q: Is there PHONE SIGNAL and WI-FI in Tierra del Fuego?
faqs.a: The phone signal is intermittent and will only be available until the 3rd day of the trip. On the last day, when returning to Pampa Guanaco, we will have signal again. There is no freely available Wi-Fi. There will be satellite Wi-Fi available for emergency cases at the cabins in Estancia Lago Fagnano.

faqs.q: Will we carry SATELLITE PHONES?
faqs.a: Yes. For the safety of our travelers, we will have a satellite phone in one of the vehicles for exclusive use in case of emergencies.

faqs.q: What are the lodging options for the Journey?
faqs.a: There are different types of accommodation during the trip, as options in Tierra del Fuego are very limited. Therefore, we have selected those that best align with creating a deep experiential connection with the territory and can provide extraordinary value to our travelers. First night: We will stay in Punta Arenas at a small hotel, a colonial house that keeps the local culture alive both in its decor and offerings. Second night: We will be on Tierra del Fuego, one of the most remote places in the world. For this night, we will stay at a fishing lodge that only has single rooms, so each traveler will have to sleep independently. Third, fourth, fifth, and sixth nights: we will stay in different rooms within cabins in the middle of a Patagonian forest on the shores of Lake Fagnano. The cabins and rooms are very simple but with great hosts: the last settlers of Tierra del Fuego who are happy to welcome us and share part of their history These lodging choices have been carefully selected to provide a deep and meaningful experience with the territory, offering something extraordinary to our travelers.

faqs.q: What type of transportation will we use?
faqs.a: We will use 4×4 trucks for both our travelers and our staff accompanying us on this journey. The trucks are suitable for the road and various weather conditions that we may encounter.

faqs.q: How much luggage can I bring?
faqs.a: We recommend a maximum of 1 suitcase weighing up to 20 kg. The plane that will transport you back to Punta Arenas from Tierra del Fuego has limited capacity.

faqs.q: Is the return trip to Punta Arenas by plane included?
faqs.a: The transfer on a private plane from Tierra del Fuego to Punta Arenas is included and has an approximate flight duration of 30 minutes. We do not include the return experience by land, which could take an additional 6 to 10 hours. *In case of weather restrictions and the plane cannot take off, the return will be by land. We recommend you take this into consideration for your return flight from Punta Arenas to Santiago de Chile.

faqs.q: Can I modify the itinerary and explorations?
faqs.a: It is not possible to modify the itinerary or explorations, they may be adjusted or modified only due to season and weather conditions.

faqs.q: What type of person is this journey recommended for?
faqs.a: This trip is recommended for active individuals who are capable of hiking on uneven terrain, such as mud, rocks, snow, or peat bogs. Hikes of up to 10 kilometers with inclines and declines are included.

faqs.q: How will the food be?
faqs.a: The food during the trip consists of a unique menu with local components from Patagonia. There will be lamb roasts on a spit and other preparations that help us understand part of the local culture of Tierra del Fuego. Travelers with any type of food intolerance should inform us in advance to evaluate the adaptation of their meals. Excellent Chilean wines are included in the menu.

faqs.q: Will this journey be the same as going to an Explora?
faqs.a: It won’t be the same as going to an Explora. This trip takes place in a remote location with basic infrastructure, but we will accommodate it with different Explora touches for each and every moment.

faqs.q: WHAT HAPPENS IN CASE OF AN EMERGENCY?
faqs.a: In case of an emergency, our staff is trained to handle various emergency situations. Our guides are certified in first aid, which will enable them to properly assess any event that requires medical attention. Basic medical attention is available in the city of Porvenir. For other treatments and depending on the severity, it may be necessary to transfer to Punta Arenas. As there are no nearby pharmacies, we recommend not forgetting to bring all the necessary medications for the entire trip.

faqs.q: Will you pick me up from the airport?

faqs.q: Is there phone signal and WI-FI?
faqs.a: Phone signal and Wi-Fi are available at the lodges, but there is no signal during the days spent in the mountains.

faqs.q: How physically demanding is the expedition?
faqs.a: This journey is recommended for active travelers. You will hike 80 kms (50 miles), reaching up to heights of 4,683 meters above sea level (15,350 feet). Skill level: Intermediate-level trek.

faqs.q: Do you offer food options for vegans?
faqs.a: Yes, we accommodate dietary preferences, including vegan options. Please inform us in advance of any specific requirements so we can prepare a suitable menu for you at each accommodation.

faqs.q: What happens in case of an emergency?
faqs.a: In case of an emergency, our staff is trained to handle various situations. Our guides are certified in first aid, allowing them to properly assess and manage any incident that requires medical attention. Basic medical care, depending on the location of the evacuation, will be available in the cities of Ollantaytambo or Urubamba. For more complex treatments or depending on the severity, it may be necessary to transfer to Cusco for additional medical attention. We have an emergency plan, satellite communication, oxygen assistance, and evacuation points throughout the entire route to be prepared for any contingency.

faqs.q: How much luggage can I carry on?
faqs.a: You should bring a 20-liter daypack to carry essentials such as a jacket, water, and snacks for daily use. Additionally, a 40-liter duffle bag (measuring 25 x 30 x 50 cm) will be provided to store extra clothing and gear. This duffel bag will be transported between camps by mules, allowing you to focus on enjoying the trek comfortably. Any additional luggage or items you do not wish to take to the camping nights can be securely stored at the Explora hotel.

faqs.q: What type of transportation we will use?
faqs.a: During the expedition, we will use a combination of transportation methods to ensure comfort and efficiency. Transfers from the hotel to the starting points of the hikes will be done by vans, allowing us to reach the starting points comfortably. For more scenic routes, such as the journey from Ollantaytambo to Machu Picchu Village, round trip, we will take the train, which offers stunning views of the Andean landscape. Additionally, during the trekking stages, we will use horses and mules to transport the equipment and supplies between camps, allowing us to enjoy the trek without the burden of heavy backpacks.

text: HomeSacred Mountains Itinerary OVERVIEW ITINERARY DEPARTURE DATES WHAT TO BRING FAQ ALL EXPEDITIONS EXPEDITION ITINERARY This expedition begins at Explora Valle Sagrado, where we gather at noon on the first day to meet and prepare for the adventure ahead. Over the following days, the itinerary takes you along ancient Inca paths, through breathtaking archaeological sites, and into awe-inspiring natural landscapes. You’ll connect with the Sacred Mountains of the Incas, culminating in an unforgettable arrival at the world-renowned sanctuary of Machu Picchu, entering through the iconic Intipunku Sun Gate. Day 1 – The Adventure Begins Arrive at Cusco Airport, where you are transported to Explora Valle Sagrado. Gather to meet with fellow travelers, your guide, and the Expedition Leader for an introductory talk about the exciting journey ahead. Enjoy lunch at the lodge with your group, featuring a specially crafted menu to savor the local flavors of the Sacred Valley. Later, embark on your first Exploration with an overland journey to Chinchero and a 2.9-mile hike (4.6 km). Visit the archaeological site of Machu Kolka and hike through picturesque crop fields, offering stunning views of the pampas, Urquillos Valley, and surrounding snow-capped mountains. Accommodation: Explora Valle Sagrado Distance Max. altitude Elevation gain 4.6 km / 2.9 mi 3,933 masl / 12,979 fasl 236 m / 776 ft Day 2 – Journey to Ancient Wata Set out for a full day on the ancient Inca Qhapaq Ñan trail, exploring sections of the road network that once connected the Andes. The route leads to Wata, where pre-Incan and Incan remains sit high above the valley, offering a strong first sense of the region’s history and scale. Return to Explora Valle Sagrado in the late afternoon. Accommodation: Explora Valle Sagrado Distance Max. altitude Elevation gain 11.5 km / 7.1 mi 3,820 masl / 12,532 fasl 808 m / 2,650 ft Day 3 – Shepherds’ Route between Lamay and Pisac This day is designed for acclimatization before the expedition moves into mountain camps. The route follows old shepherd trails around lagoons that sustain nearby rural communities, with gentle slopes and shifting Andean scenery. Back at Explora Valle Sagrado, the afternoon focuses on practical preparation—reviewing equipment, packing strategy, and what to expect as the journey transitions to camp-supported trekking. Accommodation: Explora Valle Sagrado Distance Max. altitude Elevation gain 10.3 km / 6.6 mi 4,396 masl / 14,422 fasl 432 m / 1,417 ft Day 4 – Misquiyaco Private Conservation Area This morning, we leave Explora Valle Sagrado and drive into the highlands of the Sacred Valley, watching the landscape open into wide plateaus and small farming communities before reaching the Misquiyaco Private Conservation Area—a protected buffer zone to Machu Picchu entered with exclusive Explora access. After meeting our camp team and muleteers, we begin a 4.8-mile hike (7.7 km) through the Sacred Mountains of the Incas, starting in a relict Mesoandean forest, gradually ascending beyond the tree line. We pause for a trail-side lunch, then continue on to our first tented campsite. Accommodation: Private Tented Camp. Distance Max. altitude Elevation gain 7.7 km / 4.8 mi 4,297 masl / 14,097 fasl 1,207 masl / 3,959 ft Day 5 – Sacred Salkantay Mountain This morning, we set out on an 8.1-mile (13 km) mountain trek toward Apu Salkantay, the snow-capped giant of the Vilcabamba range. In Andean belief, Apus are revered as mountain guardians, and Salkantay is often regarded as one of the most significant among them. The route reaches a maximum altitude of 15,324 ft (4,671 m), opening wide views of ridgelines and valleys as we move deeper into the range. We end the day in Pampacahuana, settling into camp at 12,795 ft (3,900 m) for the night. Accommodation: Private Tented Camp. Distance Max. altitude Elevation gain 13 km / 8 mi 4,671 masl / 15,324 fasl 819 m / 2,687 ft Day 6 – Descent Toward the Vilcanota River and the Sacred Valley Today we descend through a long, scenic valley toward the Vilcanota River, gradually approaching the Sacred Valley once again. Along the way, we pass remnants of Inca agricultural terraces that reveal the ingenuity of ancient mountain farming. The route covers 15.2 km (9.4 mi) with a total descent of 1,308 m (4.291 ft), offering shifting landscapes as we lose altitude. We end the day at our new camp, Chamana, located at 2,575 m (8,448 ft), surrounded by a lush and tranquil Andean environment. Accommodation: Private Tented Camp. Distance Max. altitude Elevation gain 15.2 km / 9.4 mi 3,883 masl / 12,739 fasl 215 m / 705 ft Day 7 – Journey to Ollantaytambo and Andean Traditions This morning, we walk for around 2.5 hours through Andean scenery before meeting our vehicle and continuing to Ollantaytambo. We visit the Temple of the Sun and explore its monumental terraces and finely crafted Inca stonework, then walk into the village along narrow cobblestone streets to the main square. Here, we pause to take in daily life around small markets, community gatherings, and local crafts. Later, we transfer to our lodge just outside the village for a traditional pachamanca lunch, prepared earth-oven style with local ingredients. The afternoon is free to rest and enjoy the quieter side of the Sacred Valley. Accommodation: Las Qolqas Hotel Distance Max. altitude Elevation gain 6.4 km / 4 mi 2,703 masl / 8,868 fasl 367 m / 1,204 ft Day 8 – Inca Trail to the Sun Gate and Machu Picchu After breakfast, we travel by van to the station and take the Vistadome train to the starting point of the Inca Trail. From Chachabamba, we begin a 6.5-mile (10.5 km) hike, ascending along lush mountain slopes into the cloud forest to reach Wiñay Wayna, a standout Inca site of steep terraces and finely crafted stonework. We then continue to Inti Punku, the Sun Gate and the historic entrance to Machu Picchu. We enter the sanctuary and explore its main areas with our guide, then descend to Machu Picchu Puebl

title: New Torres del Paine Conservation Reserve - Explora Hotels

sections.text: Patagonia, Chile About our Reserves Torres del Paine Puritama You’re Invited to Our Patagonia Wilderness Sanctuary Deep in the wildest reaches of Patagonia, far off the beaten path and yet neighboring Torres Del Paine National Park, discover Explora’s 14,800-acre protected refuge, the Torres Del Paine Conservation Reserve, a pristine refuge defined by remerging wildlife in a thriving ecosystem, jaw-dropping landscapes, and unique Explora-only experiences. Created in partnership with The Nature Conservancy and open to all to explore, this first-of-its-kind sanctuary is financially self-sustaining, legally protected forever and entirely stewarded by the world’s leading travel expedition company. It’s also home to a trailblazing membership community featuring rare opportunities to own a home and create a legacy for generations to come. READ MORE READ LESS

sections.text: Discover a wilderness all its own, rewilded to welcome the return of endangered species in a thriving ecosystem in the Torres del Paine Biosphere Reserve, and protected into perpetuity under the wing of Explora, its dedicated members and the local community. Journey to a True Wilderness Set within a UNESCO-designated biosphere and neighboring the namesake national park, the Torres Del Paine Conservation Reserve boasts its own striking Patagonian beauty—blue rivers and waterfalls, condors gliding over deep canyons, sweeping pampas and forested mountains, and pumas stalking guanacos. text: HomeCulture & historyAmongst mountains and gauchos: an incredible journey through time in the Torres del Paine Conservation Reserve AMONGST MOUNTAINS AND GAUCHOS: AN INCREDIBLE JOURNEY THROUGH TIME IN THE TORRES DEL PAINE CONSERVATION RESERVE In the majestic landscape of Patagonia, to the northeast of Torres del Paine National Park and cocooned by the Cuernos del Paine and the Sierra Baguales peaks, exists an ecosystem of fascinating history and prehistory, rich biodiversity, and cherished local culture. This is nothing less than the Torres del Paine Conservation Reserve. Through innovative practices of tourism and conservation, such as regenerative cattle ranching, this unique territory today is being restored and protected for present and future generations. By Ladera Sur. Located just 1.3 km from Laguna Azul in the renowned Torres del Paine National Park, the reserve is home to 6,000 hectares of flourishing ecosystems. It´s almost as if the reserve was an extension of the Torres del Paine National Park itself. Located in the Region of Magallanes and Chilean Antarctica, it is here that the Patagonian steppe, the Andean desert, the pre-Andean scrubland and the Magellanic Forest coexist with various water sources such as the Zamora River and Las Chinas River, which snake across this vast and remote territory. In 2019, the Explora team decided to embark on the conservation, protection and research of these southern most lands in the Americas. In these windswept, remote and silent mountains it was no coincidence that in the first scientific studies, 131 species of flora, 50 species of birds and 15 species of mammals were uncovered in the Torres del Paine Conservation Reserve. To develop this project, we created an innovative alliance (corporate partnership) with The Nature Conservancy (TNC), an organization that has worked for conservation of territories around the world for decades, which will design and oversee the conservation plan. Safeguarding the geological, paleontological, cultural and historical identity of this reserve for posterity therefore comes hand in hand with protecting its rich vegetation and animal species such as Chilean flamingos (Phoenicopterus chilensis), condors (Vultur gryphus), pumas (Puma concolor) and guanacos (Lama guanicoe). The metamorphosis of a territory and its inhabitants This territory with its expansive landscapes, wonderful mountain silhouettes and striking bodies of water was unrecognizable 65 million years ago. At that time, during the Mesozoic era, this reserve located in the province of “Última Esperanza” (Last Hope), was part of the supercontinent called Pangea and it was under water. This explains the presence of marine fossils today in the area. Many millennia later, the region would undergo great deformations, giving rise to the Andes Mountains and, during the Cenozoic era, the expansion of glaciers that helped form the great lakes and mountainous reliefs we see today. Paula López Wood – writer, researcher and audiovisual producer with a master’s in creative writing from New York University – unpacked these ideas in a long-term investigation of the reserve. “Small traces of the past concealed in geological formations such as Cerro Guido or Sierra Baguales, provide important signs of life from other periods of its great geological history,” writes López Wood, adding that the discovery of the iconic Milodon Cave, a few kilometers from the reserve, was one of the first historical landmarks in Patagonia that bridged the gap between science and tourism. Some of the most significant prehistoric discoveries in the region by López Wood include the remains of a 15,000-year-old four-metre tall ground sloth (Mylodon darwini), the fossilised 129-139 million year-old remains of ichthyosaurs (a marine reptile) in the Tyndall Glacier, the 85 million year-old remains of Pachydiscus (a specie of large ammonite) in Cerro Toro and the 68 million year-old hadrosaurs (duck-billed dinosaur) in Cerro Guido. Beyond the geological transformations and the ground breaking paleontological findings of López Wood, human beings only began to make their mark in this southern territory no more than 11,000 years ago. This timing is borne out by studies of archaeological discoveries in various Magellanic caves, including tools and rock art. “From the work carried out in the areas surrounding the reserve, we know that the first settlers were small groups of hunter-gatherers who cohabited with the megafauna, living on a diet predominantly of guanaco. They probably disappeared with the same megafauna before another wave came to the region,” argues López Wood in her investigation. Thanks to written accounts by Patagonian explorers and chroniclers in the late 19th and early 20th centuries, as well as recent anthropological studies, today we have insights into how the more recent indigenous groups, such as the Tehuelches, lived, interacted and migrated. The heritage of cattle ranches and gaucho culture The arrival of the first sheep to the region in 1876 from the Falkland Islands heralded the rise of the region´s renowned cattle ranches. From that moment on, the industry witnessed year-on-year growth due to increasing demand, and by 1910 animal husbandry had come to dominate much of the economy across the Magellanic landscape. At the same time, gaucho (Patagonian cowboy) culture was taking root alongside the farmers and muleteers who worked on the ranches. The result was the creation of a culture of local landscape connoisseurs, knowledgeable in the remotest corners of Magallanes. “The life of the muleteers who worked in the current Conservation Reserve was solitary, hard and very connected to nature,” says Paula López Wood. In the current territory where the Torres del Paine Conservation Reserve is located, there used to be three important cattle ranches. text: HomeConservation & sustaintabilityNew felines in the Explora Conservation Reserves NEW FELINES IN THE EXPLORA CONSERVATION RESERVES Explora has two conservation reserves located in Puritama (San Pedro de Atacama) and Torres del Paine in Chile with the objective of protecting local fauna. For this aim, each has camera traps, which allow for documentation of some animals that are at risk of extinction. Mid-way through this year, the cameras recorded a mother puma with her cub in Puritama and a Geoffroy cat in Torres del Paine, which is a great discovery and a joy for Explora and the other organizations with which they have been working for over 10 years for the wellbeing of these animals. THE PURITAMA CONSERVATION RESERVE Located deep in an Andean canyon of the Atacama Desert, the reserve covers an area of 7,000 hectares in the Puritama River valley, including the Puritama hot springs, where the native vegetation and abundant flora and fauna offer an oasis for numerous species. In the year 2010, Explora decided to install cameras in order to record the presence of mammals within the reserve. Currently, there are 20 cameras that are found throughout the reserve, which are monitored in conjunction with the NGO Alianza Gato Andino, in addition to guides and staff from Explora, who have joined the expeditions to install and review cameras. So far, it has been possible to register all three of the feline species present in the Andean Altiplano: the puma, Andean cat and Colocolo cat. The last record they obtained is very important, since a puma mother with a calf is observed, both vocalizing. “Beyond the anecdotal record of the vocalization, this is tremendously relevant since it accounts for successful puma reproduction inside the Reserve, which emphasizes the need to continue protection not only of the puma but also of the rest of the ecosystem that Puritama houses”, commented Nicolás Lagos, coordinator in Chile of the Alianza Gato Andino. THE TORRES DEL PAINE CONSERVATION RESERVE Located in the northeast sector of the Torres del Paine National Park, Explora has two ranches that are the true expression of the biological richness of Patagonia. They include different ecosystems, such as the Magellanic forest, pre-Andean scrub, steppes and the Patagonian desert. Two rivers cross the estancias accompanied by wetlands, lagoons and other bodies of water. This land is the home of the gauchos of Patagonia, who, in their daily lives, continue to practice their ancient traditions. In Patagonia, sightings of pumas, Geoffroy’s cat and the Colocolo or Pampas cat have been recorded, the latter being the rarest of the three, with very few records in the Magallanes Region. This year a Geoffroy cat was observed in the Explora cameras, which is a relatively common feline in the Torres del Paine area and its surroundings, but even so it is still important to be able to verify that there is a place in the Reserve where individuals of this species, which was intensively hunted in the past. FELINE PROTECTION There are several organizations that care about and watch over the welfare of these animals, such as Phantera, AGA and Geoffroy’s Cat Working Group (GCWG), among others. It is very important to protect the well-being of cats, since they are generally at the top of the food chain, and as such, they control everything that happens in the chain. This is why maintaining healthy feline populations in one place means that the ecosystem is healthy and functional. “This is very important since thanks to these organisms and institutions, it is sought not only to protect and care for fauna and ecosystems, but also to contribute to human well-being and to mitigate the effects of human activities on the planet,” said Nicolás Lagos, coordinator in Chile of the Alianza Gato Andino.
