faqs.q: 1. Los Huemules Conservation Reserve
faqs.a: The future of conservation depends on shifting our role in the world: from mere observers to custodians – active protectors of the places we explore and are part of who we are. It is rare to find a place on Earth in which so much is packed into such a relatively compact area. The Los Huemules Conservation Reserve, where the Explora lodge in El Chalten is located, encloses features that cannot be easily found elsewhere in Patagonia. This allows travelers to set off on exploration routes from the very doorstep of our lodge, thus minimizing transport and road time. The ecosystems it hosts are as varied as the climates it can witness. A place for introverts, its privacy means you can walk for days without ever seeing another person, walking side by side with nature itself.
faqs.trigger: #content > div.component-t14:nth-of-type(11) > div > div > div > div:nth-of-type(2) > div:nth-of-type(1) > h4 > span

faqs.q: 2. Parque Nacional Los Glaciares
faqs.a: The Los Glaciares National Park is an area of exceptional natural beauty, with rugged, towering mountains and numerous glacial lakes scattered within its borders. This area allows travelers to explore a part of the park, encountering the many ecosystems it hosts within. Home to fauna from the sub-Antarctic steppe and woods, the park is a bird-watcher’s paradise, with over 100 species – from the Andean condor to the white-throated caracara – inhabiting the forest and steppe.
faqs.trigger: #content > div.component-t14:nth-of-type(11) > div > div > div > div:nth-of-type(3) > div:nth-of-type(1) > h4 > span

faqs.q: 3. Lago del Desierto
faqs.a: Once a center of conflict between two neighboring countries, the Desert Lagoon (Chile) or Desert Lake (Argentina) is a wildlife enclave around which numerous Patagonian ecosystems can be observed and explored. Framed by lush forests of lengas and ñirres, as well as two minor mountain ranges – the Vespignani range and its hanging glaciers to the west, and the Bosque (Forest) range to the east – this coveted fresh water source spreads over 10 km. from north to south, and approximately 1 km. from east to west. In addition, it’s fed by the Diablo River as well as numerous streams that replenish and maintain the purity of its waters. Naturally, the site attracts substantial wildlife and irrigated varied ecosystems within a relatively small area

Explorations are limited to a group size of no more than eight guests to allow for a more personal atmosphere and in-depth discovery. Privately guided Explorations are available at an additional cost. VIEW ALL EXPLORATIONS Explora Guides Our guides have an unyielding passion and knowledge for the great outdoors. Trained at our own School of Guides, these bilingual experts possess a deep connection with the special landscapes we explore. They are also keenly aware of the fragility of these unique places and share in our advocacy for their conservation. VIEW ALL EXPLORATIONS Uncover El Chalten's Most Untouched Corners Explore a remarkable number of diverse ecosystems and three unique regions, with more than 30 guided Explorations and options for self-guided adventure. Must-do Patagonia adventures in this rugged Argentinian region include hikes through forest and rivers valleys to blue lagoons, rock climbing for beginners and experts, birding treks, and challenging high-mountain ascents with views to Mount Fitz Roy. Explore by: Hike Overland Climbing Self Guided By packraft High Mountain Ascent Explore a remarkable number of diverse ecosystems 1. Los Huemules Conservation Reserve The future of conservation depends on shifting our role in the world: from mere observers to custodians – active protectors of the places we explore and are part of who we are. It is rare to find a place on Earth in which so much is packed into such a relatively compact area. The Los Huemules Conservation Reserve, where the Explora lodge in El Chalten is located, encloses features that cannot be easily found elsewhere in Patagonia. This allows travelers to set off on exploration routes from the very doorstep of our lodge, thus minimizing transport and road time. The ecosystems it hosts are as varied as the climates it can witness. A place for introverts, its privacy means you can walk for days without ever seeing another person, walking side by side with nature itself. Explore by: View Los Huemules Conservation Reserve Explorations 2. Parque Nacional Los Glaciares The Los Glaciares National Park is an area of exceptional natural beauty, with rugged, towering mountains and numerous glacial lakes scattered within its borders. This area allows travelers to explore a part of the park, encountering the many ecosystems it hosts within. Home to fauna from the sub-Antarctic steppe and woods, the park is a bird-watcher’s paradise, with over 100 species – from the Andean condor to the white-throated caracara – inhabiting the forest and steppe. Explore by: View Parque Nacional Los Glaciares Explorations 3. Lago del Desierto Once a center of conflict between two neighboring countries, the Desert Lagoon (Chile) or Desert Lake (Argentina) is a wildlife enclave around which numerous Patagonian ecosystems can be observed and explored. Framed by lush forests of lengas and ñirres, as well as two minor mountain ranges – the Vespignani range and its hanging glaciers to the west, and the Bosque (Forest) range to the east – this coveted fresh water source spreads over 10 km. from north to south, and approximately 1 km. from east to west. In addition, it’s fed by the Diablo River as well as numerous streams that replenish and maintain the purity of its waters. During the first day of the travesía, we will only take small walks that won’t require an important physical effort in order to gradually acclimate our bodies to the altitude before the rest of the journey.

faqs.q: Climate
faqs.a: Climate With more than 90% of sunny days, San Pedro de Atacama has a privileged weather all year-round. During the day, temperature goes from 8°C to 23°C in winter (June to September) and from 12°C to 28°C in summer (December to March). Uyuni´s weather is as dry as San Pedro’s but, because it is at higher levels, it is usually colder. During the winter (June to September), daily temperatures fluctuate between 2°C and 18°C, and during the summer (September to December) between 5°C and 20°C. Temperatures at night can be as low as -20°C. Between December and March, the area if affected by “The Altiplano Summer” whose heavy rains deeply damage the tracks.

faqs.q: Other requirements
faqs.a: Other Requirements To be healthy enough to be able to face heights and fluctuating temperatures. Adventure and good spirit. Some people are sleep deprived when in altitude. Only in that case, we advise you to bring some products that can help you sleep.

faqs.q: Wifi and Voltage
faqs.a: Wifi and Voltage Because we are in remote areas, Wi-Fi access is limited. The voltage in our Travesía Atacama & Uyuni is 220V.

faqs.q: Tips
faqs.a: Tips Tips are voluntary. If you wish to leave any, you can do so at the hotel reception at the end of your stay. It will be distributed among all those who contributed to making your trip a unique experience. We suggest leaving USD 100 per day per room.

Cuenca del salar Geometric and seemingly infinite, the Atacama salt flat abruptly interrupts the desert’s chromatic continuum. The crunch of salt under every footstep is swept into silence by the wind, and all that’s left is to go deeper into the territory around you. The lowest part of this area corresponds to the Atacama Salt Flat (2350 m.a.s.l.) itself, an endorheic basin that once accumulated the waters and sediments from volcanoes and mountains over millions of years. Today it hosts a complex ecosystem, including half of the world’s flamingo species. Also within this Exploration zone, the Salt Mountain range rises to the west of the salt flat in a geological spectacle, as crusts of sediments crown the rugged mountains that frame the desert. faqs.q: 1. Cuenca del salar
faqs.a: Geometric and seemingly infinite, the Atacama salt flat abruptly interrupts the desert’s chromatic continuum. The crunch of salt under every footstep is swept into silence by the wind, and all that’s left is to go deeper into the territory around you. The lowest part of this area corresponds to the Atacama Salt Flat (2350 m.a.s.l.) itself, an endorheic basin that once accumulated the waters and sediments from volcanoes and mountains over millions of years. Today it hosts a complex ecosystem, including half of the world’s flamingo species. Also within this Exploration zone, the Salt Mountain range rises to the west of the salt flat in a geological spectacle, as crusts of sediments crown the rugged mountains that frame the desert. Finally, we recommend exploring the Oasis of San Pedro, which stands as a beacon of life and local traditions kept alive by its people
faqs.trigger: #content > div.component-t14:nth-of-type(11) > div > div > div > div:nth-of-type(2) > div:nth-of-type(1) > h4 > span

faqs.q: 2. Quebradas Intermedias
faqs.a: As if sliced off from the desert’s mantle, the ravines in this zone were created over millions of years by the forces of water and wind. Plunging into the abyss, they are sculptures that only time could shape. Numerous ravines connect the Altiplano and Salt Flat Basin zones, crisscrossing the ascent while volcanic stonewalls and brooks lined with wild grass species modestly irrigate the surrounding land, making room for medicinal plants and flowers which have been used by local shepherding communities for centuries. The Domeyko Mountain Range, located in this zone, hosts wildlife and cultural heritage alike, with guanacos and ancient petroglyphs doting certain hillsides. The ravines offer a cradle for life to flourish in, as is the case of the Puritama Natural Reserve, where a series of hot springs irrigate and sustain a series of ecosystems within.
faqs.trigger: #content > div.component-t14:nth-of-type(11) > div > div > div > div:nth-of-type(3) > div:nth-of-type(1) > h4 > span

faqs.q: 3. Altiplano
faqs.a: The Altiplano exists up there, somewhere between the mountains and the sky. Within, a whole new world silently awaits the intrepid explorers that venture its way. For us, this is a territory that words simply fall short of. The Altiplano zone –or Puna as it is known locally– stretches between 3800 and 4300 m.a.s.l. It is an elevated plateau, crowned by imposing mountains, volcanoes and geysers. Lack of oxygen, intense sunlight and extreme temperatures keep this unique territory safe, calling only those who are drawn to unusual beauty.
faqs.trigger: #content > div.component-t14:nth-of-type(11) > div > div > div > div:nth-of-type(4) > div:nth-of-type(1) > h4 > span

faqs.q: 4. Montaña
faqs.a: These colossal massifs not only hoard minerals, but also encompass cultural expressions of people past and present. Axes of mystery, Atacama’s mountains frame its territory, remaining vigilant of all whom explore it. The best views of Atacama can be found by reaching the peaks of the Licancabur Volcano along with the Kimal, Toco, Láscar, Corona, Soquete, Sairecabur and Colorado mountains – summits that scrape the skies at over 5000 m.a.s.l. Though spectacular, this altitude level requires physical stamina and preparation, and is therefore not for the faint of heart. The rewards, however, are worth the patience and dedication: a unique encounter with the world from above
faqs.trigger: #content > div.component-t14:nth-of-type(11) > div > div > div > div:nth-of-type(5) > div:nth-of-type(1) > h4 > span

faqs.q: 5. Cielo
faqs.a: Atacama’s night skies are a constant spectacle. When night falls, the sky becomes alive with the infinite powder of the Milky Way or Celestial River, as it is known in Atacama. Star-gazing has been a pastime of humanity since the dawn of time, as our forefathers often looked to the skies for divine answers. Atacama’s night skies’ sheer definition allows gazers to draw their own constellations and meaning from beyond our planet and even our galaxy. At the center of the Milky Way lies the Yakana or constellation of the Llama, seen breastfeeding its newborn calf. To its right are the Partridge, the Frog and the Serpent constellations, which guide the Andean shepherds and farmers, protecting them seasonal floods.

faqs.q: 1. Macizo Paine
faqs.a: Reach the iconic granite massif from a completely different starting point. This zone covers the northwestern sector of Torres del Paine National Park, where the massif rises from the landscape to form some of Patagonia's most celebrated landmarks — the Torres del Paine, the Cuernos del Paine, and Glaciar Grey. Hike to the base of the Torres, trek through the legendary Valle Francés, and take in the towering walls of the Cuernos. Access combines overland routes and navigation across Lago Pehoé, revealing the massif from angles the classic circuits rarely show. These are the park's most iconic experiences — guided at Explora's pace: thoughtfully, unhurriedly, and with room for what the land itself wants to reveal.
faqs.trigger: #content > div.component-t14:nth-of-type(12) > div > div > div > div:nth-of-type(2) > div:nth-of-type(1) > h4 > span

faqs.q: 2. Cuenca Paine
faqs.a: Discover the southeastern sector of Torres del Paine National Park — an open territory of Patagonian steppe and interconnected lakes, where wildlife, wetlands, and sweeping views of the massif define the landscape. This is the part of the park where the horizon opens up, and where the life of Patagonia reveals itself in slower, more intimate ways. Explore on foot or overland through sectors like Laguna Azul, Lago Sarmiento, and Laguna Amarga, along with wetlands such as Vega Castillo. Follow wildlife corridors where guanacos graze freely, spot extraordinary birdlife, and walk landscapes where the granite towers appear on the horizon like a distant, watchful presence.
faqs.trigger: #content > div.component-t14:nth-of-type(12) > div > div > div > div:nth-of-type(3) > div:nth-of-type(1) > h4 > span

faqs.q: 3. La Reserva
faqs.a: Step directly into Explora’s private 6,000-hectare Conservation Reserve — a protected territory that connects Torres del Paine National Park with broader Patagonian landscapes. Here, steppe, lakes, and native wildlife coexist within a territory actively managed under a philosophy of restoration and conservation.Hike, ride horseback, or follow self-guided trails across lagoons, valleys, and former estancias whose histories are still written into the land. This is where Explora’s restoration work unfolds, where native wildlife is returning, and where every exploration becomes part of a living commitment to regenerate the landscape. A place to slow down — and to understand what it means to travel as part of the place, not apart from it.
faqs.trigger: #content > div.component-t14:nth-of-type(12) > div > div > div > div:nth-of-type(4) > div:nth-of-type(1) > h4 > span

faqs.q: 4. Sierra Baguales
faqs.a: Venture into one of Patagonia’s most remote and least explored territories. Located northeast of the Conservation Reserve, near the border between Chile and Argentina, Sierra Baguales is a landscape of ancient geological formations, vast open valleys, and fossils that predate the Andes themselves — a place where the earth’s oldest chapters surface with every season.Hike through interior valleys, climb to natural viewpoints, and cross the region overland to reach lagoons, cerros, and panoramic horizons that reveal the deep geological history of the land. Wildlife moves freely across these plains, and the sense of remoteness is almost absolute. This is Patagonia with the volume turned down — and the scale turned all the way up.

Access combines overland routes and navigation across Lago Pehoé, revealing the massif from angles the classic circuits rarely show. These are the park's most iconic experiences — guided at Explora's pace: thoughtfully, unhurriedly, and with room for what the land itself wants to reveal. Explore by: View Macizo Paine Explorations 2. Cuenca Paine Discover the southeastern sector of Torres del Paine National Park — an open territory of Patagonian steppe and interconnected lakes, where wildlife, wetlands, and sweeping views of the massif define the landscape. This is the part of the park where the horizon opens up, and where the life of Patagonia reveals itself in slower, more intimate ways. Explore on foot or overland through sectors like Laguna Azul, Lago Sarmiento, and Laguna Amarga, along with wetlands such as Vega Castillo. Follow wildlife corridors where guanacos graze freely, spot extraordinary birdlife, and walk landscapes where the granite towers appear on the horizon like a distant, watchful presence. Explore by: View Cuenca Paine Explorations 3. La Reserva Step directly into Explora’s private 6,000-hectare Conservation Reserve — a protected territory that connects Torres del Paine National Park with broader Patagonian landscapes. Here, steppe, lakes, and native wildlife coexist within a territory actively managed under a philosophy of restoration and conservation.Hike, ride horseback, or follow self-guided trails across lagoons, valleys, and former estancias whose histories are still written into the land. This is where Explora’s restoration work unfolds, where native wildlife is returning, and where every exploration becomes part of a living commitment to regenerate the landscape. A place to slow down — and to understand what it means to travel as part of the place, not apart from it. Explore by: View La Reserva Explorations 4. Sierra Baguales Venture into one of Patagonia’s most remote and least explored territories. Located northeast of the Conservation Reserve, near the border between Chile and Argentina, Sierra Baguales is a landscape of ancient geological formations, vast open valleys, and fossils that predate the Andes themselves — a place where the earth’s oldest chapters surface with every season.Hike through interior valleys, climb to natural viewpoints, and cross the region overland to reach lagoons, cerros, and panoramic horizons that reveal the deep geological history of the land. Wildlife moves freely across these plains, and the sense of remoteness is almost absolute. This is Patagonia with the volume turned down — and the scale turned all the way up. sections.heading: Climate
sections.heading_selector: #content > div.component-t4:nth-of-type(5) > div > div > div > div > div > div > div:nth-of-type(1)
sections.text: Located in the heart of Chile’s Carretera Austral road, the climate of Chacabuco Valley, within Patagonia National Park, is defined by its striking seasonal contrasts and ever-present winds. Known for its dynamic weather changes, it’s not uncommon to experience sunshine, rain, and wind in a single day. During the spring and summer months, from October to March, temperatures range from 50°F to 68°F (10°C to 20°C), with long daylight hours and plenty of time to explore. The fall months, beginning at the end of March, are a special time in the valley as the forests and grasslands burst into vibrant fall colors of red, yellow, and gold. This season, with cooler temperatures and crisp air, offers some of the most breathtaking scenery along the Carretera Austral road. In winter, the famous Patagonian winds settle and the day becomes shorter, with temperatures ranging from -5°C to 5°C (23°F to 41°F). The varied climate throughout the year contributes to the region’s diverse ecosystems, creating an ever-changing backdrop for the park’s explorations.

sections.text: Cusco’s high altitude and proximity to the Equator create a diverse climate with two main seasons, each offering its own unique experiences. faqs.q: How is the climate in Cusco and when is the best time to travel?
faqs.a: The Sacred Valley enjoys two distinct seasons, each with its own character and appeal — shaped by the region’s high altitude and proximity to the equator. Dry Season (April – October) This is the sunniest time of year, with clear skies and crisp mountain air. The landscape takes on warm shades of yellow and ochre as the Andean plains dry out. Temperatures are pleasant during the day, ranging from 41°F to 68°F (5°C to 20°C), though nights can be cold and occasional frosts are not uncommon, sometimes dropping to 32°F (0°C). Wet Season (November – March) The valley transforms into a lush, vivid green as rainfall brings the landscape to life. The atmosphere is warmer and more subtropical, with temperatures ranging from 45°F to 70°F (7°C to 21°C). While rain is frequent, it rarely lasts all day — mornings are often clear, and the light during this season is particularly beautiful. Both seasons offer genuinely rewarding experiences, and the “best” time to visit ultimately depends on the kind of landscape and atmosphere you’re drawn to. We’re happy to help you decide based on your preferences.

faqs.q: How many nights do you recommend staying at Explora Sacred Valley?
faqs.a: We recommend a minimum of five nights to truly experience the Sacred Valley. The region is remarkably diverse, and a shorter stay simply doesn’t allow enough time to explore its many hidden corners and lesser-known sites. For those wishing to include our full-day explorations to Machu Picchu or Cusco — two of the highlights of any visit to this region — five nights is the baseline we suggest. If you’d like a deeper, more unhurried experience of both the Sacred Valley and the greater Cusco region, six nights is an excellent choice. Please note: Our Machu Picchu exploration combines Explora services with third-party providers, as required by the site’s access regulations. This excursion carries an additional cost depending on your program and must be confirmed with our reservations team at the time of booking.

faqs.q: What emergency medical services are available?
faqs.a: Guest safety is a priority at Explora. Most of our expert guides hold Wilderness First Responder (WFR) certification, equipping them with the skills and knowledge to respond effectively in remote environments. For medical emergencies requiring clinical attention, the nearby town of Urubamba — just a few kilometers from the lodge — has a Social Security Hospital as well as two local branches of established Cusco-based clinics: MAC Salud and CIMA Clinic. In the event of a severe case requiring more specialized care, patients are referred to facilities in Lima.

faqs.q: How can my relatives contact me in case of a emergency?
faqs.a: In case of an emergency, your relatives can reach the lodge directly by phone at +51 989 467 497 or by email at recvallesagrado@explora.com. Our front desk team is available around the clock to assist with any urgent communication.

faqs.q: Can I change the type of my bed on my room?
faqs.a: When making your reservation, you’ll be asked to choose between a king-size bed or a room with two double beds. If you’d like to change your bed configuration after booking, we’ll do our best to accommodate your request, subject to availability. We recommend reaching out to our reservations team as early as possible to ensure your preference is noted.

faqs.q: Do the rooms have air conditioning?
faqs.a: The Sacred Valley’s natural climate makes air conditioning unnecessary. Temperatures in the valley typically range between 9°C and 22°C (48°F and 72°F), creating a comfortable environment year-round. Beyond that, the lodge has been thoughtfully designed to make the most of natural ventilation and the area’s gentle air currents, keeping rooms fresh and pleasant throughout your stay.

faqs.q: What time do the transfers run between cusco airport and Explora?
faqs.a: Transfers between Cusco airport and Explora Sacred Valley are scheduled individually to align with each guest’s flight times, ensuring a seamless arrival and departure experience. For travelers not flying directly through Cusco airport, transfers operate according to a set timetable. Full details can be found on our Travel Tips page.

faqs.q: How can I arrange my exploration to Machu Picchu?
faqs.a: A visit to Machu Picchu is offered as a full-day overland exploration, featuring a guided tour of approximately three hours through the sanctuary’s most iconic archaeological sites. As access to the citadel is strictly limited, we strongly recommend coordinating this exploration with our reservations team well in advance — ideally at least four months ahead during high season. This allows us to secure your train tickets to Aguas Calientes, as well as your entrance to the citadel, both of which are subject to limited daily availability. Please note that specific schedules and routes within the site are also subject to availability at the time of booking. Please note: This exploration may carry an additional cost depending on your program.

faqs.q: Is there Wi-Fi?
faqs.a: As Explora Sacred Valley is nestled in a remote and pristine corner of the Andes, Wi-Fi connectivity is limited in both rooms and common areas. We invite you to embrace this as part of the experience — a rare opportunity to disconnect from the everyday and immerse yourself fully in the landscapes and culture of the Sacred Valley.

faqs.a: Chituca was once a shepherding settlement, boasting impressive views of both the Altiplano and the salt flat. Explorations take different shapes and durations: one option is to follow the shepherds’ paths, once used by the area’s original inhabitants as trading routes with other villages. Another alternative is to visit the secluded village of San Pedro de Quemes, an old Spanish settlement with panoramic views of the Altiplano and salt flat, exploring archaeological sites and human settlements that use quinoa cultivation as a main source of income.
faqs.trigger: #content > div.component-t14:nth-of-type(11) > div > div > div > div:nth-of-type(2) > div:nth-of-type(1) > h4 > span

faqs.q: 2. Ramaditas
faqs.a: It is a rare thing to experience silence on a planet where it seems to have become extinct. High up in the Altiplano the only sounds you are able to hear are those of nature herself: the whistle of the wind, the cry of a baby alpaca in the distance, or the crunch of dry earth beneath your every footstep. We invite our travelers to stay in the Altiplano area for as long a possible, so as to reacquaint with a slower pace of mind and body which is rarely found elsewhere.
faqs.trigger: #content > div.component-t14:nth-of-type(11) > div > div > div > div:nth-of-type(3) > div:nth-of-type(1) > h4 > span

faqs.q: 3. Lodge Uyuni
faqs.a: Our final lodge is on the border of the Uyuni salt flat, the largest and highest salt flat on Earth. This lodge is located on the slopes of the Tunupa volcano, named after the Andean god of lightning, in whose honor the area’s original inhabitants celebrated countless sacrifices and rituals. The lodge allows travelers to fully appreciate the sheer immensity of Uyuni. For those yearning for a bit more of adventure, climbing the multicolored Tunupa volcano will take you to 17,822 f.a.s.l. A less extreme but equally interesting alternative is to circle the volcano from below, visiting the villages, wetlands and archaeological sites that surround it.

faqs.q: 1. Janca

Janca is the highest part of the Peruvian Andes. Its inaccessibility simultaneously defines its essence and beauty. Due to the zone’s extreme altitude, life acquires a calmer pace; human settlements are scarce and dedicated mainly to high mountain mining. Reaching the Janca zone requires special acclimatization due to the area’s extremely low temperatures and lack of oxygen. Likewise, this zone is mostly steep terrain, which requires technical knowledge and experience.
faqs.trigger: #content > div.component-t14:nth-of-type(10) > div > div > div > div:nth-of-type(2) > div:nth-of-type(1) > h4 > span

faqs.q: 2. Quechua
faqs.a: The Quechua zone is the starting point for all our explorations in the Sacred Valley. Following the winding course of the Urubamba River, this area showcases Inca architecture at its best, enclosing some of Peru’s most important archaeological landmarks, from Pisac to Macchu Picchu. As we ascend progressively through cornfields, orchards and small villages bustling with life, we reach some of the most enigmatic and remote archaeological sites of the valley, as is Pumamarca, a hillside fortress that once guarded the entrance to the valley’s fertile lands.
faqs.trigger: #content > div.component-t14:nth-of-type(10) > div > div > div > div:nth-of-type(3) > div:nth-of-type(1) > h4 > span

faqs.q: 3. Suni
faqs.a: With the valley at its feet, Suni is a transition zone between the Quechua and Puna zones. Within, some of the area’s most memorable panoramic views can be found from winding paths perched high on deep gorges plunging into the green abyss below. This zone showcases the valley’s verticality – a pivotal component around which the Incas developed their particular cosmovision. Technological development and communal work structures can be evidenced in the extremely well-preserved ruins of the Moray experimental crop center and the Salineras de Maras, as well as the precision and craftsmanship of Tipon’s fluvial canals, which remain active to this day.
faqs.trigger: #content > div.component-t14:nth-of-type(10) > div > div > div > div:nth-of-type(4) > div:nth-of-type(1) > h4 > span

faqs.q: 4. Puna
faqs.a: Abruptly rising from the ground beneath your feet, mountains define almost every aspect of the Sacred Valley’s identity. As they grow in height the sheer power of altitude, combined with the cold from the perpetual glaciers perched high on their rugged shoulders, are proof of how living conditions become harsher the further from the ground you dare to go. Explorations in the area of the Puna take travelers through narrow shepherd mountain trails and chromatic progressions of green, brown and white. This highly dynamic zone is a feast to the eyes that varies significantly depending on the seasons and harvesting times.

text: EXPLORATIONS Valle Sagrado The Sacred Valley of the Incas, Peru Previous Next SACRED VALLEY OVERVIEW LODGE EXPLORATIONS DINING GETTING HERE TRAVEL TIPS Discover Unique & Authentic Explorations Discover Cusco, Machu Picchu, and other renowned and hidden gems on full- and half-day explorations, with every experience fully customized to your ability and designed for small groups of no more than eight guests. Explorations span four unique zones of the Sacred Valley, including guided hikes, biking, climbing, multi-sport experiences, high-mountain ascents, and remote Explora-only Signature Explorations. Over 40 Explorations included with your stay Led by Explora’s own certified bilingual guides Customized for every interest and fitness level +20 Photos Customized to Your Interests Our Explorations feature classic routes to iconic sites as well as Signature Explorations, designed and operated exclusively by Explora in the region’s most remote and pristine locations. Every adventure is customized to match with your skills and interests — something you’ll experience every evening as part of our flexible, day-by-day itinerary building, when your Explora guide meets with you to tailor the next day’s Explorations to your preferences. Explorations are limited to a group size of no more than eight guests to allow for a more personal atmosphere and in-depth discovery. Privately guided Explorations are available at an additional cost. VIEW ALL EXPLORATIONS Led by the Region’s Best Guides Deeply familiar with the region and its traditions, our local guides have an unyielding passion and knowledge for the Sacred Valley and the magical landscapes we explore. They’re trained at our own School of Guides and fluent in Spanish and English. They are also keenly aware of the fragility of these unique places and share in our advocacy for the conservation of Peru’s many wonders. Each day, one of our guides will gladly help you choose the right exploration for your interests and provide further information on each zone. VIEW ALL EXPLORATIONS EXPLORATIONS Explore the Best of the Sacred Valley Choose from 49 in-depth Explorations across four unique Andean zones. These adventures and experiences take you to the ancient Incan Empire of Machu Picchu, vibrant Cusco as well as Pisaq and Urubamba, but also extraordinary and rarely visited marvels, including the ancient hillside fortress of Pumamarca Explore by: Our Exploration Zones 1. Janca Towering titans that reach into the clouds above, defying altitude and gravity in order to provide a vital experience of heaven on Earth for all who venture their slopes. Janca is the highest part of the Peruvian Andes. Its inaccessibility simultaneously defines its essence and beauty. Due to the zone’s extreme altitude, life acquires a calmer pace; human settlements are scarce and dedicated mainly to high mountain mining. Reaching the Janca zone requires special acclimatization due to the area’s extremely low temperatures and lack of oxygen. Likewise, this zone is mostly steep terrain, which requires technical knowledge and experience. Explore by: View Janca Explorations 2. Quechua The Quechua zone is the starting point for all our explorations in the Sacred Valley. Following the winding course of the Urubamba River, this area showcases Inca architecture at its best, enclosing some of Peru’s most important archaeological landmarks, from Pisac to Macchu Picchu. As we ascend progressively through cornfields, orchards and small villages bustling with life, we reach some of the most enigmatic and remote archaeological sites of the valley, as is Pumamarca, a hillside fortress that once guarded the entrance to the valley’s fertile lands. Explore by: View Quechua Explorations 3. Suni With the valley at its feet, Suni is a transition zone between the Quechua and Puna zones. Within, some of the area’s most memorable panoramic views can be found from winding paths perched high on deep gorges plunging into the green abyss below. This zone showcases the valley’s verticality – a pivotal component around which the Incas developed their particular cosmovision. Technological development and communal work structures can be evidenced in the extremely well-preserved ruins of the Moray experimental crop center and the Salineras de Maras, as well as the precision and craftsmanship of Tipon’s fluvial canals, which remain active to this day. Explore by: View Suni Explorations 4. Puna Abruptly rising from the ground beneath your feet, mountains define almost every aspect of the Sacred Valley’s identity. As they grow in height the sheer power of altitude, combined with the cold from the perpetual glaciers perched high on their rugged shoulders, are proof of how living conditions become harsher the further from the ground you dare to go. Explorations in the area of the Puna take travelers through narrow shepherd mountain trails and chromatic progressions of green, brown and white. This highly dynamic zone is a feast to the eyes that varies significantly depending on the seasons and harvesting times. sections.text: Situated in one of the driest regions on Earth, San Pedro de Atacama is defined by its extreme aridity and striking landscapes. Here, the climate is remarkably stable, with almost no rainfall throughout the year. Days are typically warm, while nights can be cold, with significant temperature drops after sunset. The desert’s unique environment supports a surprising diversity of life, with flora and fauna adapted to thrive in these harsh conditions. San Pedro de Atacama is also renowned for its crystal-clear skies, making it one of the best places in the world for stargazing, offering unparalleled views of the night sky.

faqs.q: What’s the best time of year to visit the Atacama?
faqs.a: The Atacama Desert is a year-round destination, with each season offering unique conditions that shape the travel experience. In the summer months (December to February), temperatures during the day are warm and pleasant, but this is also when there’s a slightly higher chance of rain due to the so-called Altiplanic Winter—short, sporadic showers that can bring dramatic skies and rare desert blooms. In contrast, winter (June to August) brings colder nights, often with temperatures dropping below freezing, especially at higher altitudes, while daytime remains sunny and dry. Spring and fall offer a balance of mild weather and fewer crowds. Regardless of when you visit, the Atacama’s striking landscapes, starry skies, and otherworldly beauty make it an unforgettable destination any time of year.

faqs.q: How many days should I spend in the Atacama Desert?
faqs.a: To truly connect with the vastness and diversity of the Atacama Desert, we recommend staying for at least five nights. This allows enough time to explore a variety of landscapes—from salt flats and geysers to canyons and lunar-like valleys—without feeling rushed. With six or more nights, you’ll have the opportunity to go deeper into the territory, reaching the high plateau, visiting remote lagoons, or even ascending one of the region’s iconic volcanoes. A longer stay also means you can enjoy the pace of exploration while taking in the desert’s silence, colors, and night skies at a more immersive rhythm.

faqs.q: Is credit card acceptance widespread or should I bring cash?
faqs.a: Credit cards are widely accepted at Explora and in most shops, restaurants, and services in downtown San Pedro de Atacama. However, it’s a good idea to carry some cash for small purchases at local markets, artisan stands, or rural communities, where card payment may not be available. Cash is also useful for tipping staff at the Explora lodge, should you wish to do so. That said, there’s no need to worry about paying for additional services during your stay—everything at the lodge is included as part of the all-inclusive experience.

faqs.q: How extreme is the temperature difference between day and night in Explora Atacama Lodge?
faqs.a: During winter, the temperatures in Explora’s Atacama Desert Lodge fluctuate between -10°C (14°F) at night and 20°C (68°F) in daytime. During summer, the temperatures fluctuate between 10°C (50°F) at night and 30°C (86°F) in daytime.

faqs.q: Are there vegetarian/vegan food options available?
faqs.a: Yes! There are vegetarian/vegan food options available in every Explora destination. If you have any dietary preferences or restrictions, please contact our reserves team before your arrival.

faqs.q: Do I need to make restaurant reservations in advance?
faqs.a: Theres is no need to make restaurant reservations in advance if you are staying in any Explora Lodge, our travelers are always considered in every meal, it is part of the all-inclusive service we offer.

faqs.q: What are the must-see attractions in the Atacama Desert?
faqs.a: Explora has plenty of “must-see” attractions that you certainly cannot miss, however, it will depend on your preferences and experience, as you can choose from almost 50 guided explorations included in your stay, from a visit to the observatory to see a wonderful starry night to a panoramic view from the peaks of different mountains.

faqs.q: What is the best way to experience stargazing in the Atacama?
faqs.a: The Atacama Desert is world-renowned for its clear skies and minimal light pollution, making it one of the best places on Earth for stargazing. At Explora, you can take this experience to the next level with access to our private observatory, designed specifically for astronomical observation. Accompanied by expert guides, you’ll have the chance to view constellations, planets, and deep-sky objects through high-quality telescopes—an awe-inspiring experience that reveals the full beauty of the desert’s night skies.

faqs.q: Can I visit Bolivia’s Salar de Uyuni from the Explora Atacama Lodge?
faqs.a: Yes, it is possible to visit Bolivia’s Salar de Uyuni from Explora Atacama through a special overland journey designed by Explora. However, this experience must be booked separately and confirmed prior to your arrival at the lodge. Due to the logistics involved, it is not possible to arrange this trip once you are already at the lodge. We recommend planning ahead to ensure availability and a seamless travel experience across the border into Bolivia.

faqs.q: How far in advance should I book with Explora?
faqs.a: We recommend booking your stay at least 60 days in advance to ensure availability and allow enough time to plan every detail of your trip. However, for greater flexibility and peace of mind—especially during peak travel periods—reserving 6 months ahead is ideal. Whether you’re traveling in high or low season, early booking helps us prepare everything to deliver the seamless, immersive experience Explora is known for.

faqs.q: Does Explora offer private experiences or only group activities?
faqs.a: Yes, Explora offers private experiences with an additional cost and coordinated in advance.

faqs.q: Does Explora offer transportation from the airport?
faqs.a: Yes, Explora provides complimentary transportation at preset schedules to and from the nearest airport as part of your all-inclusive experience. Upon arrival, a member of our team will be waiting to welcome you and ensure a smooth transfer to the lodge. Likewise, at the end of your stay, we’ll coordinate your return journey to the airport so you can travel comfortably and on time. All transfers are scheduled based on your flight details and arranged in advance for your convenience.

sections.heading: Climate
sections.heading_selector: #content > div.component-t4:nth-of-type(5) > div > div > div > div > div > div > div:nth-of-type(1)
sections.text: Easter Island, or Rapa Nui, enjoys a mild, subtropical climate that remains pleasant throughout the year, making it a great destination no matter when you visit. The average annual temperature hovers around 70°F (21°C), with February being the warmest month, often reaching highs of 81°F (27°C). Rain is scattered and brief, with an annual average of 45 inches (1,140 mm), but no distinct rainy season, so it’s always wise to be prepared for light showers. The island’s average humidity is about 76%, contributing to its lush green landscapes. Whether you’re visiting during the warmer months or the cooler periods, the gentle breezes and moderate temperatures make it comfortable year-round.

faqs.q: Is Explora Rapa Nui all-inclusive?
faqs.a: Yes. Every Explora stay on Easter Island is fully all-inclusive. Your rate covers all accommodations, unlimited guided Explorations, all meals and beverages including Chilean wines, spa facilities, national park entrance fees, and round-trip transfers between Mataveri International Airport and the lodge. There are no supplementary charges for activities or guided experiences during your stay

faqs.q: What is included in an Explora Easter Island stay?
faqs.a: Your stay includes accommodations in one of 30 rooms (including suites with Pacific views), access to all guided Explorations — from hikes to the Rano Raraku quarry to coastal kayaking — all meals prepared by our culinary team, beverages including wine, spa and pool access, national park entrance fees, and airport transfers. The only extras are personal purchases and optional spa treatments beyond the included access.

faqs.q: How Many Nights Do You Recommend Staying at Explora?
faqs.a: We recommend a minimum of four nights to have an exploration experience that allows you to deeply discover Easter Island, although we are sure that when discovering its mysteries, you will want to extend your stay. Five nights are a good alternative to explore all its corners and enjoy the local culture.

faqs.q: Can I Change The Type of Bed In My Room?
faqs.a: At the time of booking, you must select a room with either a king-size bed or two double beds. In Rapa Nui, if needed, you may request a bed change, subject to availability.

faqs.q: Do The Rooms Come with Air Conditioning?
faqs.a: Yes, all rooms are equipped with air conditioning.

faqs.q: Is It Possible To Scuba Dive In Rapa Nui?
faqs.a: Our exploration programs in Easter Island offer various scuba diving options for both beginners and experienced divers. These activities come at an additional cost and can be arranged through our reservations team or directly on-site. *Explora is not responsible for services provided by third-party operators.

faqs.q: What is the best hotel on Easter Island?
faqs.a: Explora Rapa Nui has been named among the best resorts in South America by the Condé Nast Traveler Readers’ Choice Awards and recognized as the World’s Leading Expedition Company. Located outside Hanga Roa with sweeping Pacific Ocean views, the lodge offers an all-inclusive experience focused on deep exploration of Rapa Nui culture, archaeology, and natural landscapes — a different category from conventional hotels on the island.

faqs.q: How do I get to Easter Island?
faqs.a: Easter Island (Rapa Nui) is served by Mataveri International Airport (IPC) in Hanga Roa. LATAM Airlines operates regular flights from Santiago, Chile (approximately 5 hours) and seasonal flights from Lima, Peru. Once you land, Explora coordinates round-trip airport transfers to and from the lodge as part of your all-inclusive rate. There are no connecting flights required — just one direct route from Santiago.

faqs.q: What kinds of explorations are available from the lodge?
faqs.a: Explora Rapa Nui offers more than 30 guided Explorations, all included in your stay. Options include hiking to the Rano Raraku moai quarry, biking to ancient ahu platforms, kayaking and stand-up paddleboarding along the volcanic coastline, snorkeling, diving, and cultural immersions with locally trained guides. Every exploration is customized daily based on your interests and fitness level.

faqs.q: Are alcoholic beverages included at Explora Rapa Nui? A: Yes.
faqs.a: Yes. The all-inclusive rate at Explora Rapa Nui covers all beverages, including Chilean wines, beer, and spirits, served throughout the day in the dining room and common areas. There is no separate bar tab or beverage charge during your stay. Premium or specialty selections beyond the standard offering may carry an additional cost — contact reservations for specifics prior to arrival.

faqs.q: What is not included in an Explora Rapa Nui stay?
faqs.a: The all-inclusive rate covers accommodations, all guided Explorations, all meals and beverages, spa facility access, national park entrance fees, and round-trip airport transfers. Items not included are personal purchases, gratuities, and optional spa treatments beyond general facility access. There are no hidden activity charges — every guided Exploration offered by Explora is included in the base rate.

faqs.q: How many rooms does Explora Rapa Nui have?
faqs.a: Explora Rapa Nui has 30 rooms in total: 4 suites (including the Raa Suite at 44 m²/474 ft² with ocean and garden views) and 26 Varúa rooms (32 m²/345 ft²). All rooms include jetted bathtubs, twin or king bed configurations, and non-smoking policy. Room size reflects the lodge’s design philosophy: essential luxury and deep rest rather than maximalist features.

sections.heading: The Climate of El Calafate Argentina: Where Seasons Shape the Landscape
sections.heading_selector: #content > div.component-t4:nth-of-type(5) > div > div > div > div > div > div > div:nth-of-type(1)
sections.text: In El Calafate, the weather is part of the adventure. Located deep in Argentine Patagonia, this remote place experiences all four seasons with striking contrasts — from crisp, wind-swept summers to silent, snow-dusted winters. Summer (December to February) brings long days and mild temperatures that rarely exceed 20 °C (68 °F). The wind can be strong, sweeping through the steppe and over the turquoise waters of Lago Argentino, but the light is golden and endless — perfect for exploring the glacier, hiking trails and all the explorations we crafted in this part of the world. Autumn (March to May) paints the landscape with ochre and copper tones. Temperatures cool, the wind softens, and the region becomes quieter, offering a sense of stillness and reflection. Winter (June to August) transforms El Calafate into a serene retreat. Snow may blanket the landscapes and mountains, creating a peaceful atmosphere where silence reigns and the glaciers appear even more imposing under the pale winter light. On calm days, you will quickly feel warm during the hikes. Spring (September to November) brings renewal. Wildflowers bloom across the steppe, days grow longer, and wildlife reappears — guanacos, condors, and flamingos return to the shores of Lago Argentino. Throughout the year, El Calafate’s weather reminds visitors that Patagonia is a land of extremes and beauty. No two days are ever alike, and that unpredictability is precisely what makes it unforgettable.

faqs.a: Unlike hotels in the town of El Calafate, Explora El Calafate is a remote all-inclusive lodge set within the historic Chorrillo Malo estancia, surrounded by the Patagonian steppe with sweeping views of the pampas, the Andes, and glimpses of the Perito Moreno Glacier. The experience goes far beyond accommodation: 30+ guided explorations are included with your stay, led by bilingual expert guides trained at Explora’s own School of Guides. All meals, drinks, transfers, and National Park entrance fees are also included — making it a seamless, immersive Patagonian journey rather than just a place to sleep.

faqs.q: What explorations and activities are available at Explora El Calafate?
faqs.a: Explora El Calafate offers more than 30 guided explorations across five distinct zones of Argentine Patagonia: Hielos Milenarios — up-close encounters with the iconic Perito Moreno Glacier, one of the few advancing glaciers on Earth, by boat and on foot. Brazo Sur — the most remote corner of Los Glaciares National Park, with hidden valleys, lagoons, and glaciers. Valles y Montañas — forested hikes and panoramic viewpoints where ice, water, and forest converge. Pampa — overland journeys across the vast Patagonian steppe, tracing the region’s ranching history. La Estancia — horseback riding and hiking through the lodge’s own historic estancia territory. All explorations are customized to your skill level and interests, and group sizes are limited to eight guests for a deeply personal experience.

faqs.q: What is the best time of year to visit El Calafate?
faqs.a: El Calafate can be visited year-round, with each season offering a distinct experience: Summer (December–February): Long golden days, mild temperatures up to 20°C (68°F), and ideal conditions for glacier explorations and hiking. Autumn (March–May): The steppe turns ochre and copper, crowds thin out, and the landscape feels wonderfully still. Winter (June–August): Snow blankets the mountains and glaciers appear more imposing under pale winter light — a serene, intimate retreat. Spring (September–November): Wildflowers bloom across the steppe, guanacos, condors, and flamingos return to the shores of Lago Argentino. No matter when you visit, Patagonia’s signature unpredictability ensures no two days are ever alike.

faqs.q: How do I get to Explora El Calafate?
faqs.a: The most convenient way to reach the lodge is by flying into El Calafate Airport (FTE), approximately 1 hour from the lodge. Regular flights connect El Calafate with Buenos Aires. Explora includes round-trip airport transfers on preset schedules as part of your stay. Guests traveling within the Patagonia Network can also arrive: From Explora El Chaltén by road (approx. 3.5 hours), with transfers available on select days October–April. From Torres del Paine, Chile by road (approx. 6 hours), crossing the Chile–Argentina border — a spectacular scenic journey. Private transfers are also available at an additional cost.

faqs.q: What is included in a stay at Explora El Calafate?
faqs.a: An all-inclusive stay at Explora El Calafate covers everything you need for a complete Patagonian experience: Accommodation in 20 thoughtfully designed rooms (Standard or Suite) with views of the pampa and mountains All guided explorations — 30+ excursions by foot, horseback, boat, and overland vehicle All meals and drinks — cuisine inspired by local Patagonian ingredients (lamb, trout, native herbs, seasonal produce) and Patagonian wines Spa facilities — outdoor hot tubs to unwind under the open sky National Park entrance fees Round-trip airport transfers according to preset schedules The only things not included are flights, optional private transfers, and personal expenses.

faqs.q: Who designed Explora El Calafate and what is the lodge like?
faqs.a: Explora El Calafate was designed by acclaimed Chilean architect José Cruz Ovalle, with a philosophy of blending seamlessly into the Patagonian landscape. Natural materials, organic forms, and expansive windows frame panoramic views of glaciers, rolling plains, and distant mountains — making guests feel part of the landscape rather than observers of it. The lodge offers 20 rooms — Standard (with views of the pampa and mountains) and Suites — each designed for rest and comfort after a day of exploration. Shared spaces encourage connection: stories shared over exceptional cuisine, a glass of wine by the fire, and the quiet luxury of a hot shower after a day in the wild.

Travelers who do need a VISA: Though a Bolivian visa can be obtained on the border, due to the remoteness of this border crossing and to avoid possible delays, we recommend obtaining the visa at the consulate in your country of origin before traveling. For this, you need to complete the following paperwork: Visa Application sworn statement Photocopy of current passport + 4 passport size photos Photocopy of Explora booking Photocopy of round-trip tickets. Economic solvency: Photocopy of front and back of a valid Credit Card. Yellow fever vaccination. USD 160 in cash: It is recommended that you carry the precise amount. We remind you that US Citizens require a Visa to enter Bolivia. Please check requirements to enter Bolivia, per your citizenship, several months prior to travel. More information here. faqs.q: TIPS / WIFI & VOLTAGE
faqs.a: WIFI AND VOLTAGE Because we are in remote areas, Wi-Fi access in rooms and common areas is limited. The voltage is 220V. TIPS Tips are voluntary. If you wish to leave any, you can do so at the hotel reception at the end of your stay. It will be distributed among all those who contributed to making your trip a unique experience. We suggest leaving USD 100 per day per room.

faqs.q: What to bring
Key Points
faqs.a: Climate Uyuni´s weather during the winter (June to September): daily temperatures fluctuate between 2°C and 18°C, and during the summer (September to December) between 5°C and 20°C. Temperatures at night can be as low as -20°C.Between January and March, the area if affected by “the Altiplano Winter” whose heavy rains deeply damage the tracks. Safety & Expertise We have roamed and deeply studied the the Altiplano for over 15 years. Such experience has allowed us to become experts guides in the region and to ensure traveler safety at all times. Our vehicles are equipped with satellite communication systems, GPS technology, VHF radio, and oxygen supplies. All guides and drivers, are vetted for their senior guiding experience and local knowledge. After so many years of preparation, we have been rewarded: in 2022 we were named as World’s Leading Expedition Company in the World Travel Awards, for the fourth year in a row. Altitude Uyuni is located at 3,681 m.a.s.l. (12,076 f.a.s.l.) Acclimatization is fundamental and will be prioritized. During the first day, we will only take non-strenuous walks in order to gradually acclimate our bodies to the altitude before the rest of the journey. Health Adventure and good spirit: It is important to be healthy enough to withstand higher altitudes and fluctuating temperatures.

sections.text: Our rooms Explora stands apart from other accommodations in the region. Our unrivaled attention to detail spans from lavish lodge amenities to our hospitable staff and dedication to sustainable tourism. All-inclusive rates encourage you to soak in every moment of the experience without worry. We believe luxury means having what is necessary for an incredible experience, like a cozy atmosphere. That’s why each room at the El Chaltén lodge is a place to rest and recharge within the Los Huemules Conservation Reserve. Rooms are designed to provide silence, privacy, and space, giving you deep rest after exploring all day. THE EL CHALTÉN LOCATION Explora El Chaltén sits in a picturesque setting, surrounded by views of the Marconi Glacier and Electric Valley. The destination seamlessly blends luxurious accommodations with its rugged natural surroundings. Guests are steps away from unforgettable adventures, whether lounging in a sumptuous room, dining on locally sourced cuisine, or fully recharging at the spa. We’ll use the lodge as our cozy home base for explorations in El Chaltén. They ensure deep rest after a long day of exploration in Patagonia. At Explora, we actively seek disconnection from everyday routine. STANDARD ROOM 17 Standard Rooms measuring 36m² (388 feet²) See more details > SUITE 3 suites measuring 60m² | 646 feet² See more details > EL CHALTÉN LODGING & SERVICES OUR ROOMS Explora stands apart from other accommodations in the region. Our unrivaled attention to detail spans from lavish lodge amenities to our hospitable staff and dedication to sustainable tourism. All-inclusive rates encourage you to soak in every moment of the experience without worry. We believe luxury means having what is necessary for an incredible experience, like a cozy atmosphere. That’s why each room at the El Chaltén lodge is a place to rest and recharge within the Los Huemules Conservation Reserve. Rooms are designed to provide silence, privacy, and space, giving you deep rest after exploring all day. THE EL CHALTÉN LOCATION Explora El Chaltén sits in a picturesque setting, surrounded by views of the Marconi Glacier and Electric Valley. The destination seamlessly blends luxurious accommodations with its rugged natural surroundings. Guests are steps away from unforgettable adventures, whether lounging in a sumptuous room, dining on locally sourced cuisine, or fully recharging at the spa. We’ll use the lodge as our cozy home base for explorations in El Chaltén. Explora’s passionate local guides are always eager to lead guests into the surrounding mountains, valleys, glaciers and lagoons of the Argentinian Patagonia. Our hotel staff is equally as passionate, warmly welcoming you into the unique part of the world they call home. With us, you can safely and sustainably embark on hiking, climbing, riding, kayaking and other adventures. Explora is located amidst a private natural reserve, on the north bank of the Eléctrico River and surrounded by dense forests of lenga and ñirre trees. Its strategic position is perfect to explore the Southern Patagonia Ice Field, the world’s third largest fresh water reserve. The surrounding scenery is just one reason our lodge is among the best places to stay in El Chaltén. OUR CUISINE Our unique menu at Explora El Chaltén is sustained on the interpretation of the surroundings, nature, and culinary landscape. We will only use seasonal raw materials purchased from small farmers, produced with agroecological standards, and even wild harvested products. THE SPA AT EL CHALTÉN Built for disconnection and immersion in nature with amazing views of the ñirre forest, we offer a space of relaxation where our travelers can enjoy of two massages rooms, two saunas and five open-air Jacuzzis. In addition, there are six lounge chairs outside and a shower with a view of the valley and the Eléctrico River, perfect after a day of exploration. faqs.q: Where is El Chaltén?
faqs.a: El Chaltén is a village in Argentina’s side of Patagonia. Known as the capital of trekking in Argentina, El Chaltén is a gateway to exploration in Los Glaciares National Park. Find our luxurious Explora lodge in the Los Huemules Conservation Reserve of El Chaltén.

faqs.q: What to do in El Chaltén?
faqs.a: Hike to lagoons and glaciers, embark on high-mountain ascents, go rock climbing, or spot local wildlife on an unforgettable Explora tour of El Chaltén. Back at the lodge, you can relax in the spa, sample outstanding cuisine and plan the next day’s adventures.

faqs.q: How do I get from El Calafate to El Chaltén?
faqs.a: Explora offers pick-up and drop-off at El Calafate Airport and hotels. We also provide transfers to and from our Torres del Paine location several days per week.

faqs.q: How many days to spend in El Chaltén?
faqs.a: To explore El Chaltén in depth, we recommend a minimum stay of 5 nights.

faqs.q: What clothing and footwear should I bring for the Atacama explorations?
faqs.a: We provide travelers with some equipment for their Atacama Desert tours, including trekking poles, helmets, bottles of water and riding gaiters for the horseback rides. We recommend bringing along the following items of clothing, footwear and accessories: Baseball cap Buff or neck gaiter Layered clothing (1st layer: layer top and bottom, 2nd layer: fleece, 3rd layer: windbreaker jacket, 4th layer: down jacket) Liner or windstopper gloves Polar/wool/Windstopper hat Small backpack (25 liters) Sunglasses Sunscreen T-shirts and long-sleeve T-shirts Thin fleece Trekking boots Trekking pants and trekking shorts Trekking socks (long) Water bottle Optional items you may choose to bring include a bathing suit, sandals and a Camel Back.

faqs.q: What cultural experiences can I expect during the explorations?
faqs.a: The Andean culture is rooted deeply in the Atacama Desert. The local residents value their connection to the Earth. With Explora, you can immerse yourself in the nature of the Atacama Desert. These experiences can give you greater insight into the organic beauty of the territory and perhaps a better understanding of the people who live in this remote part of the world.

faqs.q: What languages are spoken by the guides and locals in the area?
faqs.a: The most commonly spoken language in the region is Spanish, and our guides speak both Spanish and English.

faqs.q: What safety measures are in place for visitor well-being in the desert?
faqs.a: We have established safety measures in place to protect our visitors from unstable weather conditions during our Atacama Desert excursions. Depending on the conditions, some explorations may be subject to changes or even cancelled. This is most common during the period between mid-December and the beginning of March due to the rain and snow experienced in the higher areas. This is known as the Altiplano Winter.

faqs.q: What unique geographic features can be found in Atacama, and how does it feel to explore them?
faqs.a: There are numerous interesting geographic features in the area, including active geysers, salt flats, multi-colored lagoons, thermal baths, dunes, and even volcanoes. Many visitors say the experience is like visiting an alien planet, giving you a one-of-a-kind adventure that takes you off the beaten path. These are just a few of the many reasons to discover the wonders of Atacama.

Every room, including six suites, at our Sacred Valley lodge, also offers stunning views, glorious beds and every comfort you need to commune with this magical destination — what we call the Luxury of the Essential. Immerse yourself in a magical setting while acclimatizing for high Andean Explorations in ancient Machu Picchu at 7,970 feet (2,430 meters) and Spanish colonial Cusco at 11,2000 feet (3,400 meters). faqs.q: Is Explora Valle Sagrado adults-only?
faqs.a: No. Explora Valle Sagrado welcomes guests of all ages, including families with children. Explorations are customized daily by interest and fitness level, making them accessible across different age groups and abilities. The outdoor swimming pool and hot tubs are popular with younger guests. Cribs and extra beds for children are available on request. Families traveling with young children are encouraged to discuss exploration planning with Explora at booking to ensure a schedule that works well for everyone.

faqs.q: Does Explora Valle Sagrado include alcohol?
faqs.a: Alcoholic beverages are not included in the standard all-inclusive rate. The rate covers accommodation, all meals, non-alcoholic beverages, more than 40 guided explorations, and access to the spa facilities, pool, and hot tubs. Wine, beer, and spirits are available at the bar and restaurant and charged separately. Individual spa treatments are also available at an additional cost and are recommended to be booked in advance directly with the lodge.

faqs.q: Do you get altitude sickness at Explora Valle Sagrado?
faqs.a: Explora Valle Sagrado sits at 9,514 feet (2,900 meters) above sea level, above the general threshold where some visitors begin to notice mild altitude effects such as headaches, fatigue, or shortness of breath. Most guests acclimatize comfortably within one to two days. Some explorations reach higher elevations, including Cusco at approximately 11,200 feet (3,400 meters). Staying well-hydrated, avoiding alcohol on arrival, and resting on the first afternoon are generally recommended. Guests with a history of altitude sensitivity are encouraged to consult a physician before travel.

faqs.q: What is included in a stay at Explora Valle Sagrado?
faqs.a: A stay includes accommodation, all meals and non-alcoholic beverages, and more than 40 guided explorations each day. Access to the Pumacahua Spa and Bath House, saunas, steam baths, outdoor swimming pool, and hot tubs is included. Explorations are customized daily to your interests and fitness level, with small group sizes. A full-day visit to Machu Picchu can be arranged as part of your stay; applicable entry permit and train transport fees may apply separately. Alcoholic beverages, individual spa treatments, and privately guided explorations are available at an additional cost.

faqs.q: How do I get to Explora Valle Sagrado from Cusco?
faqs.a: The lodge is approximately 90 kilometers from Alejandro Velasco Astete International Airport in Cusco (CUZ). Explora arranges round-trip airport transfers that should be confirmed at the time of booking. The drive from Cusco Airport to the lodge takes approximately 1.5 to 2 hours through the Andean highlands. Guests flying from abroad should book a connecting domestic flight to Cusco via Lima (LIM); the Lima-to-Cusco flight takes approximately 1 hour 20 minutes, with several daily connections available through major Peruvian carriers.

faqs.q: How far in advance should I book Explora Valle Sagrado?
faqs.a: Explora Valle Sagrado has 50 rooms, and demand from international travelers is consistent year-round. Booking four to six months in advance is recommended, particularly for the May through August dry season and the December through January peak period. Advance booking is also essential for the Machu Picchu component of any stay, as timed entry permits are required by the Peruvian government and can sell out several months ahead. Reservations can be made directly through Explora’s website or through a travel specialist.

faqs.q: Can you stay overnight at Machu Picchu?
faqs.a: There is no accommodation at the Machu Picchu archaeological site itself. The closest hotel is Belmond Sanctuary Lodge, located at the entrance gate to the ruins in Aguas Calientes — a town at the base of the mountain accessible by train from Cusco or Ollantaytambo. Most travelers visit Machu Picchu as a day trip from a base in the Sacred Valley or Cusco. Explora Valle Sagrado in the Sacred Valley offers a full-day guided excursion to Machu Picchu, included as part of the all-inclusive lodge rate, with train transport from Ollantaytambo and guided site access; entry permits are arranged in advance and may involve a separate fee.

faqs.q: Are guided excursions to Machu Picchu included in the Explora lodge rate?
faqs.a: A full-day visit to Machu Picchu is available as a guided exploration from Explora Valle Sagrado and can be arranged as part of any stay. The guided excursion — led by Explora’s bilingual guides — includes assistance with train logistics from Ollantaytambo and guided access at the site. The applicable Machu Picchu entry permit and train transport fees are charged separately, as these are set by the Peruvian government and the train operator. All other explorations across the Sacred Valley — including Pisac, Ollantaytambo, Chinchero, Moray, and the Maras salt mines — are fully included in the all-inclusive rate at no additional cost.

Our spacious 50-room hideaway boasts a modern design inspired by traditional hacienda style, hot tubs and an outdoor pool, the historic Pumacahua Bath House with a spa and sauna, and a breathtaking setting wrapped in fertile Andean peaks on a remote ancient Incan corn plantation. Every room, including six suites, at our Sacred Valley lodge, also offers stunning views, glorious beds and every comfort you need to commune with this magical destination — what we call the Luxury of the Essential. Imagine a dialogue between Andean peaks, valleys, and one of the most remote and ancient corn plantations in Sacred Valley. Expect an inspired design with soaring lines and high ceilings, organic materials and natural blond woods, and panoramic views alongside wide verandas, tiled roofs, and other nods to Peru’s traditional hacienda architecture. sections.text: The nearest airport is Comandante Armando Tola International Airport in El Calafate, located 137 miles from El Chaltén. Connecting to El Calafate via Buenos Aires: Upon arrival at Buenos Aires Ezeiza Airport, take a connecting flight to El Calafate. From there, you’ll embark on a 137-mile (220 km) scenic drive to El Chaltén, with a travel time of approximately 3 hours. *Flights are primarily from Buenos Aires, with a non-stop travel time of approximately 3.5 hours to El Calafate. Airlines operating this route include Aerolíneas Argentinas, Jetsmart, and Flybondy. By Vehicle from El Chaltén: If you’re traveling by private or rental car, make sure to download the directions and Google Maps route before starting your journey. The distance from El Chaltén to our lodge is 10.5 miles (17 km).

faqs.q: Pick-up & Drop-off
faqs.a: Pick-up & Drop-off Below, we share the schedules for in-out transfers. Transfer on arrival to El Calafate: El Calafate Airport: Free shuttle service from El Calafate Airport to Explora El Chaltén is available at 12:00 PM and 4:30 PM. Hotels in El Calafate: Free shuttle service from hotels in El Calafate to Explora is available at approximately 11:00 AM and 3:30 PM.* Last-minute flight changes made within 24 hours of check-in may incur an additional fee if a special transfer arrangement is required. Transfer on departure: El Calafate Airport: Departure from the hotel at 8:00 AM, with arrival at the airport by 11:30 AM. Hotels in El Calafate: Departure from the hotel at 8:00 AM, with arrival at your destination by 12:00 PM. If needed, you may also opt for a private transfer, which has an additional cost. For availability, please contact your reservation executive or get in touch with reserve@explora.com prior to arrival. *Confirm with your booking agent. * Only for programs with transfer service included.

faqs.q: Transfer to/from Explora Torres del Paine
faqs.a: Transfer to/from Explora Torres del Paine Transfers to/from Explora Torres del Paine Van transportation between Explora Torres del Paine and Explora El Calafate or Explora El Chaltén, available daily at 9:00 a.m., at an additional cost. Transfers may be private or shared, with a minimum of two passengers. Private transfers can accommodate up to six passengers. Both routes depart at 9:00 a.m. to allow sufficient time for border crossing. All transfers must be booked in advance, and availability must be confirmed with our reservations team at reserve@explora.com. If you have any questions or need assistance with your reservation, please contact reserve@explora.com. Distances The journey between Torres del Paine and El Chaltén is 402 km (250 miles) and takes approximately 8 to 9 hours. The journey between Torres del Paine and El Calafate is 374 km (232 miles) and takes approximately 5 to 6 hours. Condiciones – Cupos limitados. – El servicio de traslado considera únicamente recogida y bajada de pasajeros entre Explora Torres del Paine, Chile, y Explora El Chaltén, Argentina. – Los traslados operan entre octubre y abril. Para otras fechas, consultar por opciones de traslados privados. – Explora no se hace responsable por retrasos que puedan producirse debido a cruces fronterizos o condiciones del camino.

faqs.q: Check-In & Check-Out
faqs.a: Check-in & Check-out Check-in takes place after 1:00 p.m. We recommend arriving at noon to take advantage of an afternoon half-day exploration on your first day. Check-out must be completed by 10:00 a.m. Please note that our shared transfer departs at 8:00 a.m., so we kindly ask you to have your belongings ready the night before. Unfortunately, this does not allow time for a half-day exploration on your departure day. If you’d like to enjoy a morning exploration before leaving, we’re happy to arrange a private transfer at an additional cost — just let us know in advance. Please note that lunch service is not included on check-out day.

Airlines operating this route include Aerolíneas Argentinas, Jetsmart, and Flybondy. By Vehicle from El Chaltén: If you’re traveling by private or rental car, make sure to download the directions and Google Maps route before starting your journey. The distance from El Chaltén to our lodge is 10.5 miles (17 km). How to Get Here Starting from Chile Connecting to El Calafate via Santiago: Upon arrival at Santiago Arturo Merino Benítez Airport, take a direct fly to El Calafate in Argentina with SKY Airlines, which offers two weekly flights. If you arrive in the afternoon, we recommend staying overnight in El Calafate. We will arrange to pick you up the following day according to our pre-arranged schedule Connecting to Punta Arenas or Puerto Natales via Santiago: Upon arrival at Santiago Arturo Merino Benítez Airport, take a connecting flight to either Punta Arenas or Puerto Natales. Cross into Argentina via the Río Don Guillermo crossing to reach El Calafate in Argentina. Our team will meet you there and transport you to Explora in a van. Connecting to El Chaltén via Explora Torres del Paine: From your stay at Explora Torres del Paine, you can travel with us to Explora in El Chaltén. The journey takes approximately eight hours, with a stop for meals and rest along the way. This service is part of our Explora Connects program and incurs an additional cost, which varies depending on the date of your stay. To travel ahead of the closure, our scheduled transfer now departs Balmaceda at 9:45 am, every day of the week, and arrival times have been adjusted accordingly. Arrival: Arrive on the first flight of the day, reaching Balmaceda no later than 9:15 am, in time to connect with our transfer at 9:45 am. Departure: We will take you to Balmaceda airport for flights departing from 3:00 pm onwards (as close to this time as possible to minimize waiting time at the airport). ARRIVAL TRANSFER Prior to their arrival, travelers can choose between three modalities for reaching the lodge from Balmaceda Airport: Van:The trip takes about 5 hours, along a mostly gravel road that is part of the iconic Carretera Austral. It departs Balmaceda Airport at 9:45 am every day and has no additional cost for all-inclusive programs. If travelers’ arrival times do not coincide with our transfer, we recommend they spend a night in Coyhaique and coordinate the journey to the lodge with us for the next day. Pick-up in Coyhaique: The pick-up time at the hotel in Coyhaique – between 08:00-09:00 am – will be coordinated with travelers the day before. The van will then go to pick up the travelers who arrive at the airport befor

faqs.q: Check-in & Check-out
faqs.a: Check-in & Check-out Check-in: After 13:00. We recommend arriving at noon for an afternoon exploration. Check-out: 10:00 We want you to make the most of your stay. That’s why we offer the option of a half-day exploration on your departure day before heading to the airport (if your flight schedule allows). In this case, you’ll need to check out at 07:00 before exploring, and we’ll store your luggage. *Please note: Lunch service is not included on your departure day and is available at an additional charge per person. If you’d like to request a late check-out for your convenience, please consult with our team for availability and rates. Connection to or from Torres del Paine National Park Experience the stunning scenery of Chilean Patagonia at our lodges in Torres del Paine and Patagonia National Park. Take advantage of our private 1.5-hour lodge-to-lodge flight, for our Explora guests, over the Andes Mountain Range and the southern ice field. Available every Monday and Thursday from October 3rd to mid-April, this convenient flight option provides a unique perspective of the region. Travel light with a soft suitcase weighing up to 20 kilograms. Prices start at USD 3,384 per person, one way, for a 4-night stay and USD 4,925 for a 3-night stay. For booking inquiries, contact reserve@explora.com.
