text: GETTING HERE Patagonia National Park Patagonia, Chile PATAGONIA NATIONAL PARK OVERVIEW LODGE EXPLORATIONS DINING GETTING HERE TRAVEL TIPS We recommend you book your flight directly to Balmaceda´s airport. How to Get Here Pick-up & Drop-Off Check-in & Check-out PATAGONIA NATIONAL PARK How to get to Patagonia National Park Explora Patagonia National Park is located in the Valle Chacabuco sector, in Chile’s remote and pristine Aysén Region. Surrounded by mountains, rivers, and vast Patagonian steppe, reaching the lodge is the beginning of the journey into one of the most remarkable protected areas in the world. * Sky and LATAM airlines offer daily flights to Balmaceda from Santiago. Arriving by Air The nearest airport is Balmaceda Airport (BBA), located approximately five hours by road from the lodge. From Santiago (SCL): Several daily flights connect Santiago with Balmaceda. From Puerto Natales: For a faster and more scenic arrival, we offer exclusive private charter flights from Puerto Natales for travelers coming from our Torres del Paine lodge. * This option significantly reduces travel time while providing breathtaking aerial views of Patagonia. Contact reserve@explora.com for schedules and rates. Transfers from Balmaceda Airport Explora offers one scheduled ground transfer per day from Balmaceda Airport to the lodge, with scenic stops along the Carretera Austral. The transfer departs Balmaceda at 9:45 am, every day of the week. Road works are currently underway along the Carretera Austral — the only access road to Patagonia National Park — and the route is closed to traffic for several hours each afternoon, until further notice. Our transfer leaves early to travel ahead of the closure, so we ask travelers to reach Balmaceda on a flight landing no later than 9:15 am. We recommend booking flights that align with this service to ensure a smooth arrival. As an alternative to the 5-hour road transfer, guests can also opt for a private charter flight from Balmaceda, followed by a shorter road transfer to the lodge. This option reduces travel time and offers stunning views over Patagonia’s mountains, lakes, and valleys. Travel light with a soft suitcase weighing up to 20 kilograms. Prices start at USD 1,969 per person, one way, for a 4-night stay and USD 2,592 for a 3-night stay. For booking inquiries and more details contact reserve@explora.com Optional Cerro Castillo & Marble Caves Extension Enhance your journey to Patagonia National Park with our two-day, one-night private extension along the legendary Carretera Austral before your arrival at the lodge. See more here: Patagonia National Park Extended Stay For reservations and more information, contact reserve@explora.com or call +56 2 2395 2800. faqs.q: How many nights do you recommend staying at Explora?
faqs.a: Considering the vast territory in which our lodge is situated, we recommend a minimum of five nights to have an exploration experience that allows you to deeply discover Patagonia National Park. However, we are confident that when you discover its wonders, you may want to extend your stay. Six nights is a great alternative to fully explore and enjoy the stunning landscapes.

faqs.q: Can i change the type of my bed in my room?
faqs.a: At the time of booking you must select a room with either a king size bed or two double beds. Being in the lodge, if you require, you may change your bed, subject to availability.

faqs.q: Do the rooms come with air conditioning?
faqs.a: No, they only have heating.

faqs.q: At what time do the transfers run between the airport and Explora?
faqs.a: Transport between airports and the lodge is based on the flight plans, both incoming and outgoing. You can see more information here.

faqs.q: What type of vehicles are used to drop people off in Explora?
faqs.a: We have different vehicles available with capacity of up to 12 passengers.

faqs.q: Is it possible to arrive by plane to Patagonia National Park from Puerto Natales?
faqs.a: Yes, we have a program that connects by plane this two destinations with an additional cost. See our air connections here.

faqs.q: What gear should I bring?
faqs.a: We provide (without additional cost) walking sticks and all the necessary equipment for bike riding. Please consult the list of equipment to bring. Check our What to pack list.

faqs.q: Is there wifi?
faqs.a: Because we are in remote areas, Wi-Fi access in common areas is limited.

faqs.q: Is the tip included in the normal rate?

faqs.a: All of our guides are Wilderness First Response (WFR) certified, guaranteeing that they have the necessary knowledge and abilities to aid people in remote locations. In the Park administration, 15 minutes from the hotel, there is a paramedic stationed year round. For more serious situations there is a hospital in Puerto Natales, 1.5 hours from the hotel, as well as the Clínica Magallanes in Punta Arenas, which is 5 hours from the hotel. Contact us if you have any questions.

faqs.q: How can my relatives contact me in case of emergency?
faqs.a: Telephones (56 2) 3952580, (56 2) 3952581, (56 2) 3952582, fax (56 2) 3952584, or by email recpatagonia@explora.com.

faqs.q: Is there cell phone service?

faqs.q: How many nights do you recommend staying at Explora?
faqs.a: We recommend a minimum of five nights to have an exploration experience that allows you to deeply discover Patagonia, although we are sure that when discovering the wonders of Torres del Paine National Park, you will feel like you needed more time. Six nights are a good alternative to achieve a more comprehensive knowledge of the area.

faqs.q: Can i change the type of my bed in my room?

faqs.q: Do the rooms come with air conditioning?

faqs.q: At what time do the transfers run between the airport and Explora?

faqs.q: What type of vehicles are used to drop people off in Explora?

faqs.q: Is it possible to arrive by plane to Torres del Paine from Patagonia National Park?

faqs.a: Because we are in remote areas, Wi-Fi access in common areas is limited.

faqs.q: What emergency medical services are available?

faqs.q: How can my relatives contact me in case of emergency?

faqs.q: Is there cell phone service?
faqs.a: There is no cell phone coverage in Explora Rapa Nui, however we have landline telephone service at an acceptable cost for clients.

faqs.q: How many nights do you recommend staying at Explora?
faqs.a: We recommend a minimum of four nights to have an exploration experience that allows you to deeply discover Easter Island, although we are sure that when discovering its mysteries, you will want to extend your stay. Five nights are a good alternative to explore all its corners and enjoy the local culture.

faqs.q: Can i change the type of my bed in my room?

faqs.q: Do the rooms come with air conditioning?

faqs.q: At what time do the transfers run between Rapa Nui airport and Explora?

faqs.q: What type of vehicles are used to drop people off in Explora?
faqs.a: Spacious, comfortable vans with seating for up to 9 passengers.

faqs.q: Is it possible to scuba dive in Rapa Nui?
faqs.a: Our list of explorations in Easter Island considers different diving options both for beginners and experts. This has an additional cost and can be scheduled with our reservation team or directly at the destination. *Explora is not responsible for the services provided by third parties.

faqs.q: Can i visit the beaches and explore the village without a guide?
faqs.a: Yes! If you want to go to the Anakena or Ovahe beaches, or the village of Hanga Roa, you can take a taxi from the hotel (at an additional cost). It’s also possible to travel to town by bicycle. The journey takes about 20 minutes round trip by car and 1:30 hours by bike. For all areas of the National Park it is mandatory to visit with a certified guide.

faqs.q: Do you have horseback riding explorations?
faqs.a: We do not offer this type of exploration, but it is possible to coordinate this service with third parties in advance at an additional cost. *Explora is not responsible for the services provided by third parties.

faqs.q: What gear should I bring?
faqs.a: We will provide –free of cost– trekking poles for the hikes, and all of the necessary equipment for cycling and snorkeling. Please consult us if you have any doubts about what to bring. Check our What to pack list.

faqs.q: Is there wifi?

faqs.q: What emergency medical services are available?
faqs.a: All our expert guides have the Wilderness First Responder (WFR) certification and therefore, have all the knowledge and skills to help people in remote places. The hotel’s neighboring town of Urquillos is small and there are no emergency services. The next town, Urubamba, located a few kilometers from Urquillos has emergency services at the Social Security Hospital and two additional medical centers that are local branches of medical clinics from Cusco, (MAC Salud Clinic and CIMA Clinic). Severe cases are sent to Lima.

faqs.q: How can my relatives contact me in case of emergency?
faqs.a: By phone: +51989467497, or by e-mail: recvallesagrado@explora.com

faqs.q: Is there cell phone service?
faqs.a: Yes, there is. In Urubamba there is good connection for all types of mobile phones. But at the lodge, only “Claro” has good coverage.

faqs.q: WHEN TO TRAVEL TO PERU?
faqs.a: The altitude of Cusco and its proximity to the equator explain a wide variety of climates featuring two seasons, each with very different appeals. The sun shines abundantly during the driest season, from April to October, with occasional night frosts. During those months, the Andean pampa turns yellow and ochre. Average temperatures range between 41°F and 68°F (5° C and 20° C) and can even drop to 32° F(0° C) at night. Between November and March, in turn, the Valley dresses in green and the weather is subtropical. During this season, temperatures can range between 44,6 °F and 69,8°F (7° and 21° C).

faqs.q: How many nights do you recommend staying at Explora?
faqs.a: Some of the main attractions of this region are the sanctuary of Machu Picchu and the city of Cusco, for which we have developed full-day explorations. If our travelers decide to take one of these alternatives, we recommend a stay of at least five nights, as less is insufficient to have an exploration experience that allows you to discover the diversity of this valley, where there are still many places to discover. A six-night program is a good alternative to have a deeper experience in the Sacred Valley and the Cusco region. *Our exploration of Machu Picchu, combines Explora services with third-party services due to the restrictions that the nature of this place demands from us. This exploration has an additional cost depending on your program and it must be confirmed with our reservations team at the moment of your reservation.

faqs.q: Can i change the type of my bed in my room?
faqs.a: At the time of booking you must select a room with either a king size bed or two double beds. If you require, you may change your bed, subject to availability.

faqs.q: Do the rooms come with air conditioning?
faqs.a: AC is not necessary. The temperatures in Valle Sagrado range between 9°C and 22°. In addition to this, the hotel’s architecture is designed to maximize ventilation and the use of natural air currents.

faqs.q: At what time do the transfers run between Cusco airport and Explora?
faqs.a: Transportation between Cusco airport and Explora Valle Sagrado, back and forth, is custom planned to work according to the flight hours of each passenger. *For travelers not arriving at or leaving directly from the Cusco airport, transfer services are provided based on the pre-set timetable found in our Travel Tips page.

faqs.q: What type of vehicles are used to drop people off in Explora?
faqs.a: Van like trucks, spacious and comfortable, with capacity for 10 people.

faqs.q: HOW CAN I ARRANGE THE EXPLORATION TO MACHU PICCHU?
faqs.a: You can visit Machu Picchu as a full day overland exploration. It is a guided tour of approximately three hours among Machu Picchu’s most characteristic archaeological remains. It is important to coordinate the exploration to Machu Picchu with our reservation team in order to buy the train ticket to Aguas Calientes and the entrance fee* to the citadel, which has limited daily spaces. During the high season, we suggest that you coordinate this exploration with at least 50 days in advance. The schedules and routes established within the citadel are subject to the availability of spaces at the time of making the reservation. *This exploration may have an additional cost depending on your program.

faqs.q: What gear should I bring?
faqs.a: We will provide –free of cost– trekking poles for the hikes, and all of the necessary equipment for cycling. Please consult us if you have any doubts about what to bring. Check our What to pack list.

faqs.q: Is there wifi?
faqs.a: Because we are in remote areas, Wi-Fi access in rooms and common areas is limited.

faqs.q: Is the tip included in the normal rate?
faqs.a: No. At Explora tips are voluntary. If you wish to leave one, you can do so at reception at the end of your stay. It will be divided among all those who contributed to make your trip a unique experience. We suggest you leave $100 per stay per visitor.

faqs.q: What are the coordinates of the lodge?
faqs.a: Our coordinates are: 13º20’31.43”S – 72º2’52.59”W

faqs.q: What emergency medical services are available?
faqs.a: San Pedro de Atacama, the town near the lodge, has a health clinic. More serious emergencies can be treated at the Calama hospital, a one-hour drive from the lodge. All of our guides have Wilderness First Responder (WFR) certification, and thus, possess the necessary knowledge and skills to be able to assist people in remote areas.

faqs.q: How can my relatives contact me in case of emergency?
faqs.a: They can contact you by calling + 56 2 3244 2000, or by sending an e-mail to recatacama@explora.com.

faqs.q: Is there cell phone service?
faqs.a: Yes, both Explora Atacama and the town of San Pedro have good connectivity for all kinds of mobile phones.

faqs.q: How is the climate in San Pedro de Atacama?
faqs.a: San Pedro de Atacama and its surrounding area have a very dry and mild climate year round. The village gradually grew up around an oasis, and is situated on a high plateau, 2,443 meters (8,015 feet) above sea level, and located just 100 kilometers (62 miles) from Calama, a major city served by El Loa International Airport, or “Calama Airport” (CJC). During winter (June – September), the average daytime temperature ranges from 9º C (48º F) to 24º C (75º F) – inviting you to soak up the sun in the lodge’s relaxing lounge chairs, on the terraces or in the glassed corridors. During summer (December – March), daytime temperatures fluctuate between 13º C (55º F; early morning) and 25º C (77º F; evening), with a maximum of approximately 32º C (90º F) – a period of the year calling for an afternoon siesta before joining one of the evening explorations. Ninety percent of the days are clear and sunny. However, between mid-December and the beginning of March, occasional rains and snow in higher areas result in what is called the Altiplano Winter. During these months and due to unstable weather conditions in the area, some of our explorations could be subject to changes or even canceled in order to protect our travelers’ safety.

faqs.q: How many nights do you recommend staying at Explora?
faqs.a: We recommend a minimum of five nights to have an exploration experience that allows you to deeply discover Atacama, although we are sure that each day of exploration will increase your desire to explore this special territory for more days. Six nights are a good alternative to achieve a more comprehensive knowledge of the area and explore the high plateau or volcanoes.

faqs.q: Can i change the type of my bed in my room?
faqs.a: At the time of booking you must select a room with either a king size bed or two double beds. Being in the lodge, if you require, you may change your bed, subject to availability and room type.

faqs.q: Do the rooms come with air conditioning?
faqs.a: No. Because of its altitude and desert environment, Atacama is very dry, so you do not feel hot in the shade. In addition, the lodge’s architectural design allows for and promotes natural air circulation.

faqs.q: At what time do the transfers run between the airport and Explora?
faqs.a: You can see more information here.

faqs.q: What type of vehicles are used to drop people off in Explora?
faqs.a: We use our own vans, which are modern, comfortable and roomy. Each van has a maximum capacity of 6 travelers.

faqs.q: Is it possible to arrive by plane to San Pedro?
faqs.a: Yes, there is a paved landing strip in San Pedro de Atacama, but only for small planes (maximum: 8,000 kg / 17,637 pounds). Because of the limited infrastructure, take offs and landings are only allowed just before sunset.

faqs.q: What gear should I bring?
faqs.a: We provide (without additional cost) walking sticks and all the necessary equipment for biking and horseback riding. Please consult the list of equipment to bring. Check our What to pack list.

faqs.q: Is It Possible To Get To Explora Atacama From The Argentine Border?
faqs.a: Yes, we can pick up or drop off travelers at the Sico or Jama border crossings (chilean side) There is an additional charge for this service. Please check out alternatives: reserve@explora.com

faqs.q: Is there wifi?
faqs.a: Because we are in remote areas, Wi-Fi access in common areas is intermittent.

faqs.q: Is there an ATM and a currency exchange at the lodge?
faqs.a: We don’t have an ATM or currency exchange on site. However, there are ATM and currency exchange services available in the town of San Pedro de Atacama.

faqs.q: Can I pay in cash the additional services?
faqs.a: We can only receive credit card payments.

faqs.q: Is the tip included in the normal rate?
faqs.a: No. At Explora tips are voluntary. If you wish to leave one, you can do so at reception at the end of your stay. It will be divided among all those who contributed to make your trip a unique experience. We suggest you leave $100 per stay per visitor.

faqs.q: Do you have a hairdressing service?
faqs.a: No we don’t provide hairdressing services.

faqs.q: What Is The Altitude Of The Lodge?
faqs.a: 2,500 meters (8,202 feet) above sea level.

faqs.q: What are the distances between Explora in Atacama and the main cities of the area?
faqs.a: San Pedro de Atacama / Jama border crossing: 183 km (114 mi). San Pedro de Atacama / Sico border crossing: 200 km (124 mi). San Pedro de Atacama / Arica: 804 km (500 mi). San Pedro de Atacama / Iquique: 487 km (303 mi). San Pedro de Atacama / Antofagasta: 311 km (193 mi). San Pedro de Atacama / Calama: 98 km (61 mi).

faqs.q: What are the coordinates of the lodge?
faqs.a: Our coordinates are: 22º55’6.16”S 68º12’16.10”W

h1: ATACAMA AND TORRES DEL PAINE: TWO SIDES OF CHILE

sections.heading: ATACAMA AND TORRES DEL PAINE: TWO SIDES OF CHILE
sections.heading_selector: #content > article > div:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(2) > div.explora-h1-title > h1

sections.heading: There are places that ask you to look closely, and places that ask you to look up.
sections.heading_selector: #content > article > div:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(2) > div.explora-h1-title > h2
sections.text: In the Atacama, attention narrows to salt underfoot, a line of volcanoes on the horizon, the silence before the sky turns black with stars. In Torres del Paine, the opposite happens. The landscape keeps widening: Lake Pehoé, the Cuernos, the wind moving across the steppe, cloud shadow crossing granite. Both are Chile. Two destinations that are equally iconic, equally worth your time, and whose contrasts let you explore the country in real depth. Visiting both is the most direct way to understand Chile. With 12 to 14 days, you can combine Atacama and Torres del Paine in one journey and experience two contrasting sides of Chile. Torres del Paine

sections.heading: Atacama or Torres del Paine: Which Is Right for You?
sections.heading_selector: #content > article > div:nth-of-type(2) > div.exp_component:nth-of-type(2) > div.explora-wysiwyg:nth-of-type(2) > h2
sections.text: Explora Atacama is built around one of the driest deserts on Earth — one that’s also teeming with life. High-altitude lagoons hold flamingos and vicuñas, cardón cacti bloom at elevation, and wetlands appear where geothermal water meets the surface. The Lodge sits near San Pedro de Atacama, within reach of snowcapped volcanoes, salt flats, and carved canyons. Signature Explorations: El Tatio geysers at dawn Valle de la Luna at dusk The private observatory after dark Explorations range across every level — from short hikes and horseback rides to full-day bike routes, high-altitude overlands, and mountaineering ascents above 5,000 m. Your guides sequence them to follow the rise in altitude, starting low and moving higher day by day, so your body is ready for the higher routes when you reach them. Explora Torres del Paine is a completely different world. The 50-room Lodge sits on Lake Pehoé inside Torres del Paine National Park, with the Paine Massif visible from almost every angle — granite, glaciers, steppe wildlife, and a scale that takes several days to absorb. Each Exploration takes you into a different part of the park: Toward the Base of the Towers Out to a glacier Across open steppe with guanacos and condors Explora Torres del Paine

sections.heading: What to Do in Atacama and Torres del Paine
sections.heading_selector: #content > article > div:nth-of-type(2) > div.exp_component:nth-of-type(4) > div.explora-wysiwyg:nth-of-type(2) > h2
sections.text: Explora Atacama gives you a base at the centre of the desert, with every Exploration departing from the Lodge into a different corner of it. Your guide team builds a programme to suit you, from short gentle walks to full-day high-altitude routes. Highlights include: Salt flats and geysers High-altitude lagoons Canyon walks Stargazing at the private observatory Explora Torres del Paine gives you the sub-Antarctic landscape — granite towers, glaciers, open steppe, and the wildlife that lives across it: guanacos, condors, foxes, and flamingos. The weather changes quickly, and that is part of what makes it extraordinary; the best approach is to plan around the conditions rather than against them. The two destinations complement each other precisely because of their difference — desert and sub-Antarctic, arid silence and wind off the lake, a sky full of stars and a horizon full of granite. Visiting both isn’t about ticking two boxes; it’s about seeing a country that holds all of this at once. Valle de la Luna, Atacama

sections.heading: When Is the Best Time to Visit Both Destinations?
sections.heading_selector: #content > article > div:nth-of-type(2) > div.exp_component:nth-of-type(5) > div.explora-wysiwyg:nth-of-type(2) > h2
sections.text: Explora Atacama can be visited year-round. The coldest, clearest nights for stargazing often fall from June through August, while January through March brings the altiplano winter, with afternoon storms at elevation that may affect some higher Explorations. Explora Torres del Paine is open year-round, with two distinct windows: October–April (high season): longer days, warmer temperatures, and the broadest access across the park May–September (low season): quieter trails, better wildlife sightings, and a lower, longer winter light, with snow on the Paine Massif Either way, weather changes quickly — a day of low cloud or strong wind may shift the plan, and your guide adjusts the Explorations accordingly. Recommended length of stay: Explora Atacama — 4 nights minimum, 5 for more room Explora Torres del Paine — 5 nights to start, 6 or 7 to let the park reveal itself through weather, light, glaciers, and wildlife

sections.heading: How to Combine Atacama and Torres del Paine in 12–14 Days
sections.heading_selector: #content > article > div:nth-of-type(2) > div:nth-of-type(6) > div.explora-wysiwyg > h2
sections.text: Combining both destinations is one of the best ways to experience Chile in depth — seen together, each sharpens your understanding of the other. With 12 to 14 days you have enough time to explore both properly: Begin at Explora Atacama for 4 or 5 nights Travel south through Santiago toward Punta Arenas Continue to Explora Torres del Paine for 5 or 6 nights Starting in the Atacama works well for many, though the order is yours to choose. By the time you arrive in Patagonia, you carry the Atacama as a reference point, and the difference between the two places becomes part of what you take away. Plan your trip Emily from Explora

sections.text: Every spring, Torres del Paine National Park is reborn in color: calafate blooms red-orange along the trails, migratory birds return to the lagoons, and the ochre steppe turns green underfoot. Chulengo is the Patagonian word for a newborn guanaco, and the first arrive as spring turns toward summer. Condors soar overhead, and pumas pass through, unhurried and unseen unless they choose otherwise. Discover more Guanacos

title: Explora Valle Sagrado: Multigenerational Family Adventures | Explora
description: Discover Explora Valle Sagrado, where grandparents, teens, and children explore Peru's Sacred Valley together, with 40+ guided routes suited to every age.
h1: EXPLORA VALLE SAGRADO: A FAMILY STAY FOR EVERY GENERATION

sections.heading: EXPLORA VALLE SAGRADO: A FAMILY STAY FOR EVERY GENERATION
sections.heading_selector: #content > article > div:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(2) > div.explora-h1-title > h1

sections.heading: At Explora Valle Sagrado, in Peru's Sacred Valley of the Incas, every evening starts with a conversation, not a fixed plan.
sections.heading_selector: #content > article > div:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(2) > div.explora-h1-title > h2
sections.text: This is what makes it one of the best-suited Lodges in the region for a family stay: when a family arrives with three generations, grandparents, teenagers and eight-year-olds together under one roof, our guides sit down with you all each evening to plan the next day. Every guide is bilingual, trained through Explora’s own school of guides, and knows this valley well enough to shift the next day’s route around what your family actually wants. They want to know how far your eight-year-old hiked that morning, and whether your grandmother would rather ride in the van than walk the last stretch to the ruins. A multigenerational group comes alive here because the days flex to fit every kind of explorer. Rather than building around a single pace, the itinerary bends to suit your range: steep climbs for those with more energy, gentle valley-floor flats for those who like to go slower, and plenty of natural wonders to keep young and old interested along the way. Sacred Valley

sections.heading: Is the Altitude Safe for Kids and Grandparents?
sections.heading_selector: #content > article > div:nth-of-type(2) > div.exp_component:nth-of-type(2) > div.explora-wysiwyg:nth-of-type(2) > h2
sections.text: Explora Valle Sagrado sits at roughly 9,500 feet, notably lower than Cusco’s approximately 11,200 feet, which is one reason the lodge works well as a family’s first stop in the region. Explora organizes its Explorations into four altitudinal zones. Quechua, where the lodge sits, is the recommended starting point; you can then progress into the Suni and Puna zones, and finally Janca, the highest zone, which may call for acclimatization and more physical preparation. In practice, spend your first day or two on Quechua-zone routes, close to the valley floor, before climbing toward higher, more demanding terrain later in your stay. Most families acclimatize comfortably within a day or two. Staying well-hydrated, skipping alcohol on arrival, and resting that first afternoon all help. Anyone with a history of altitude sensitivity, including grandparents, should check with a physician before the stay.

sections.heading: What Explorations Are Good for a Family Group?
sections.heading_selector: #content > article > div:nth-of-type(2) > div:nth-of-type(3) > div.explora-wysiwyg > h2
sections.text: Your first or second day, the easy Quechua routes are closest to home: Huertos de Yucay, a half-day walk through the former Inca terraces and crop fields at Yucay, and Arin, an equally easy half-day hike across the valley floor. Your family can split up after breakfast if you want two different paces, one group here, another on a moderate route like Salineras (a descent past the colonial town of Maras to the valley’s salt pans) or Moray (a hike from the Misminay community to the site’s famed circular terraces, once an Inca agricultural laboratory), and meet back for lunch. As you settle in, the range widens. For an adrenaline rush, the Pachar via ferrata climbs a steel-rung route above the Urubamba River before dropping into more than two kilometers of cable descent (this one is best booked in advance with our team at reserve@explora.com). For something gentler, an easy, unhurried bike ride follows the Urubamba River, with e-biking available whenever you’d rather enjoy the terrain without the effort, or Cuesta del Sapo gives you wind in your face and the valley opening up beneath you on a half-day descent through cornfields and Inca terraces. The Yanahuara route walks a glacier-fed stream into a native forest that ends at Ensifera, a private reserve where you can watch hummingbirds up close. If it’s culture and curiosity you’re after, the Ayni Exploration spends a full day with the community of Huayllafara in the Lamay valley learning seasonal farm work; Valle de la Papa is a

sections.heading: Does Explora Valle Sagrado Have Family Rooms?
sections.heading_selector: #content > article > div:nth-of-type(2) > div:nth-of-type(4) > div.explora-wysiwyg > h2
sections.text: Rooms are split between 44 standard rooms and 6 suites, plus interconnecting options for families who like to stay close (ask our reservations team about this at reserve@explora.com when you book, since it depends on availability). Cribs and extra beds for younger children are available on request in either room type. A short stroll away, the Pumacahua Bath House has an outdoor pool where younger children can unwind on a lighter day, and the lodge also has a shared events space that seats up to 70, so even a large extended family, aunts, uncles, cousins and all, could book it out for one big dinner together.

sections.heading: Family Questions, Answered
sections.heading_selector: #content > article > div:nth-of-type(2) > div:nth-of-type(5) > div.explora-wysiwyg > h2
sections.text: Is the stay all-inclusive? Yes, for the most part. Accommodations, most guided Explorations, all meals and non-alcoholic beverages, round-trip airport transfers, and some entrance fees to national parks are included. A few Explorations carry an additional cost, so it’s worth checking with our reservations team at reserve@explora.com when you plan your stay. Can our family choose different Explorations and still spend the day together? Yes. title: Explora's 9 Lodges: How to Sequence Your South America Route | Explora
description: Sequence Explora's nine lodges from the Atacama Desert to Patagonia's glaciers across Chile, Peru, Argentina and Bolivia, choosing your own order and pace.
h1: FROM DESERT TO ICE: A ROUTE ACROSS EXPLORA’S 9 LODGES

sections.heading: FROM DESERT TO ICE: A ROUTE ACROSS EXPLORA’S 9 LODGES
sections.heading_selector: #content > article > div:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(2) > div.explora-h1-title > h1

sections.heading: Somewhere between the salt flats and the glaciers, South America stops reading as a map and starts becoming something you can walk through mile by mile, the ground changing under your feet from dust t
sections.heading_selector: #content > article > div:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(2) > div.explora-h1-title > h2
sections.text: The same tectonic pressure that pushed the Andes skyward left a corridor of desert, altiplano, forest and ice running the length of the continent. We built into that corridor deliberately, so that you could experience the whole arc of it: 9 lodges across 4 countries, Chile, Peru, Argentina and Bolivia. Choosing where to start isn’t really a logistics question. It’s a decision about which chapter of that story you want to open with. The instinct we hear most often is to start dry and finish frozen, so the glaciers at El Calafate and El Chaltén leave a lasting impression at the end of your trip. Explora Valle Sagrado Lodge

sections.heading: Explora Valle Sagrado: Where the Andes Begin
sections.heading_selector: #content > article > div:nth-of-type(2) > div.exp_component:nth-of-type(2) > div.explora-wysiwyg:nth-of-type(2) > h2
sections.text: Peru’s Andean valley between Pisac and Ollantaytambo is the gentlest entry point, and the logical one if you’re arriving from the north. Explora Valle Sagrado sits on a historic estate here, its 50 rooms and suites arranged hacienda-style around courtyards, far from the tourist routes that circle Cusco. Days run toward Incan ruins, the Maras salt pans and the Moray terraces, guided by our own guides, trained through our School of Guides, who treat the archaeology as living history, still shaping how the valley farms, worships and gathers today. It also does quiet, practical work: the valley floor sits well below Cusco’s elevation, so a few nights here double as acclimatization for the altitude still ahead. Explora Atacama Lodge

sections.heading: Explora Atacama: The Driest Desert on the Route
sections.heading_selector: #content > article > div:nth-of-type(2) > div.exp_component:nth-of-type(3) > div.explora-wysiwyg:nth-of-type(2) > h2
sections.text: Chile’s Atacama is one of the driest deserts on Earth. Explora Atacama sits inside it, a short distance from the historic town of San Pedro de Atacama, its estate laid out around native gardens and quiet paths. Days move between activity and rest: horseback riding and Explorations to geysers, dunes and salt flats, evenings at a set of thermal springs, closing over dinner drawn from local Andean ingredients. Explora Jirira Lodge

sections.heading: Explora Jirira Lodge: Crossing into the Bolivian Altiplano

sections.text: Atacama is also the starting point for the Travesía Atacama to Uyuni, a privately guided Travesía that connects the desert to 3 mountain lodges straddling Bolivia’s Altiplano. sections.text: Back on the mainland in Chile, the desert gives way to steppe, then forest, then ice. Explora Torres del Paine, the collection’s original lodge, is open now on the shores of Lake Pehoé inside the national park itself, its 50 rooms and suites facing the granite-and-hornfels horns of the Paine massif. A short distance northeast, on restored ranch land inside the Torres del Paine Conservation Reserve, a separate 10-room lodge, Explora Torres del Paine Conservation Reserve, opens in December 2026. It’s built to immerse you in the conservation work directly: the pumas returning, the lenga forest regrowing, the guanaco herds moving back across land that once ran sheep. Farther north along the Carretera Austral, still in Chile, in the Chacabuco Valley, Explora Parque Nacional Patagonia is the only lodge within the park’s boundaries, a landscape of rushing rivers and open steppe that shelters the endangered huemul deer. text: HomeFrom Desert to Ice: A Route Across Explora’s 9 Lodges FROM DESERT TO ICE: A ROUTE ACROSS EXPLORA’S 9 LODGES Somewhere between the salt flats and the glaciers, South America stops reading as a map and starts becoming something you can walk through mile by mile, the ground changing under your feet from dust to stone to ice. The same tectonic pressure that pushed the Andes skyward left a corridor of desert, altiplano, forest and ice running the length of the continent. We built into that corridor deliberately, so that you could experience the whole arc of it: 9 lodges across 4 countries, Chile, Peru, Argentina and Bolivia. Choosing where to start isn’t really a logistics question. It’s a decision about which chapter of that story you want to open with. The instinct we hear most often is to start dry and finish frozen, so the glaciers at El Calafate and El Chaltén leave a lasting impression at the end of your trip. Explora Valle Sagrado Lodge Explora Valle Sagrado: Where the Andes Begin Peru’s Andean valley between Pisac and Ollantaytambo is the gentlest entry point, and the logical one if you’re arriving from the north. Explora Valle Sagrado sits on a historic estate here, its 50 rooms and suites arranged hacienda-style around courtyards, far from the tourist routes that circle Cusco. Days run toward Incan ruins, the Maras salt pans and the Moray terraces, guided by our own guides, trained through our School of Guides, who treat the archaeology as living history, still shaping how the valley farms, worships and gathers today. It also does quiet, practical work: the valley floor sits well below Cusco’s elevation, so a few nights here double as acclimatization for the altitude still ahead. Explora Atacama Lodge Explora Atacama: The Driest Desert on the Route Chile’s Atacama is one of the driest deserts on Earth. Explora Atacama sits inside it, a short distance from the historic town of San Pedro de Atacama, its estate laid out around native gardens and quiet paths. Days move between activity and rest: horseback riding and Explorations to geysers, dunes and salt flats, evenings at a set of thermal springs, closing over dinner drawn from local Andean ingredients. Explora Jirira Lodge Explora Jirira Lodge: Crossing into the Bolivian Altiplano Atacama is also the starting point for the Travesía Atacama to Uyuni, a privately guided Travesía that connects the desert to 3 mountain lodges straddling Bolivia’s Altiplano. It’s best treated as a deliberate detour, taken before the desert or after the ice.
